## Who I am

I'm Chan Meng (she/her), an AI agent architect and full-stack engineer based in Auckland, New Zealand. I architect AI agents, ship full-stack platforms end-to-end, and teach others to do the same.

Most AI projects demo beautifully and fall over in production. I'm the engineer you bring in so that doesn't happen: I design the agent architecture, build the platform around it, and leave your team able to keep shipping after I've gone.

I do my best work for founders who need speed, teams who need depth, and products built for people who aren't the Silicon Valley default. Right now I'm also my own client, as founder of ArchCanvas + ArchLang.

Right now I am Founder & Sole Engineer at ArchCanvas (since April 2026), and Chief Technology Officer at FemTech Weekend (since March 2025). ArchCanvas is an AI architectural designer: you describe a building in plain English and it produces a dimensioned floor plan that you refine by talking to it, live at archcanvas.uk. Underneath it is ArchLang, the open-source declarative floor-plan language I wrote, which compiles source into dimensioned drawings so every plan can be checked and edited exactly.

Before that I was AI Agent Architect at Engram (May 2026 – July 2026); Founding Principal Engineer, Activation, Execution & AI Systems at Gavigo (October 2025 – October 2026); Senior Full Stack Engineer & Website Team Lead at She Sharp (July 2025 – September 2026).

What I take on:

- Founding / Principal engineer: Embed early. Set engineering direction. Ship to production solo or as the first hire on a small team.
- AI Agent Architect: Architect agentic systems end-to-end — retrieval, memory, tool use, eval. Build the spine, hand off the gloss.
- CTO-class operator: Own the tech for an early-stage product company. Hiring plan, architecture, ship velocity.
- Lead AI-programming instructor: Design and deliver cohort-based AI engineering programs. Curriculum, teaching platform, mentorship.

I'm open to founding-team, staff IC, AI-architecture and AI-engineering-instruction work, and to selected contract builds for founders. I'm based in Auckland and work remotely or in person, including with teams in other time zones. Pricing depends on scope: write to me with what you need and I'll come back with a scope and a quote. The fastest way in is email, or a 30-minute call at https://cal.com/chan-meng/30min.

I taught maths at tutoring schools in China for about seven years before software. In 2022 I decided to rebuild my life somewhere I could breathe freely, and in 2023 I moved to New Zealand for the Master of Applied Computing at Lincoln University, which was awarded with Distinction. I built with AI from the first semester; it wasn't easy. The teaching years are why I now teach engineers to build with AI and document everything I build.

I have taught 5 AI-programming cohorts since 2024 (100+ direct learners across 5 cohorts since 2024), and received the Outstanding Mentor Award, two years running — AI Hackathon Festival 2025 and Aotearoa AI Hackathon Festival 2026. The course material is public at https://programming.chanmeng.org.

I speak Cantonese and Mandarin natively, and English (professional working proficiency) and Japanese (limited working proficiency). I have practised minimalism since 2018: "Subtraction for life, addition for thought."

Contact: hello@chanmeng.org

Elsewhere: Portfolio: https://chanmeng.org/ · LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/chanmeng666/ · GitHub: https://github.com/ChanMeng666 · X: https://x.com/chanmeng666 · YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/@ChanMeng666 · Newsletter: https://chanmeng.org/#newsletter

## Current roles

### Founder & Sole Engineer at ArchCanvas

- Period: April 2026 – present
- Location: Auckland, New Zealand (remote)
- URL: https://archcanvas.uk/
- Keywords: ArchCanvas (AI architectural designer for floor plans), ArchLang (declarative floor-plan language), Designs that compile (parametric, not pixels), Programming Language Design, Compilers, AI Agent Architecture, Vercel AI SDK, Next.js, Building in public

Founder and sole engineer of ArchCanvas (archcanvas.uk), an AI design agent that turns a plain-English brief into a dimensioned floor plan you can build from, then lets you refine it by talking. Invented ArchLang, an open-source floor-plan language (62 npm releases, 139 diagnostic codes, 4,338 tests), when drawing plans as pictures proved impossible to check — so every plan ArchCanvas draws can be compiled, checked and edited exactly.

**Impact.** Founder and sole engineer of ArchCanvas, an AI architectural designer that turns a plain-English brief into a dimensioned floor plan — and of ArchLang, the open-source floor-plan language I invented so every plan it draws can be compiled, checked and edited exactly.

**Company context.** ArchCanvas ([archcanvas.uk](https://archcanvas.uk/)) is an AI design agent for architects and self-builders: describe a building in plain language and it designs a dimensioned floor plan you can actually build from — with room labels and measurements — alongside a grounded AI rendering, then stays conversational on an infinite zoomable canvas where you refine the plan by talking to it. It is live and takes real payments on a pay-per-result model (a free first generation, then credit packs through Stripe; no subscription). Underneath it is **ArchLang** ([github.com/ChanMeng666/archlang](https://github.com/ChanMeng666/archlang) · [playground.archlang.uk](https://playground.archlang.uk) · npm [@chanmeng666/archlang](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@chanmeng666/archlang)), the open-source declarative floor-plan language I designed and wrote.

**Mission.** Make a floor plan a **program, not a picture**. In 2026 generating a pretty image of a floor plan is a commodity; what is scarce is a design that can be proven right. A picture cannot be compiled, linted or measured — text can. Because every ArchCanvas plan is real ArchLang rather than pixels, iterating means recompiling rather than re-prompting: nudge a wall, change a parameter or ask the AI to fix circulation, and exactly that thing changes.

**My mandate.** Founder and sole engineer of both the product and the language, working with AI coding agents and building in public. Everything from product positioning and pricing to the compiler, the agent loop, payments, deployment and the launch plan is mine to decide and to ship.

**Impact delivered.** **The product came first, and it taught me what was wrong with it.** I started ArchCanvas on 2026-04-08 with the obvious architecture: ask a model to draw the floor plan as an SVG. The drawings looked plausible and could not be trusted — a model drawing a picture cannot tell you whether a door collides with a wall, and it redraws the whole plan when you ask it to move one thing. So eleven weeks in I stopped and built the thing that was missing: a language. ArchLang 0.1.0 went to npm on 2026-06-24, and the next day it replaced the freehand drawing engine inside ArchCanvas. Since then the AI writes ArchLang, the compiler turns it into a dimensioned drawing, and the edits are exact and replayable.

**ArchLang — an original programming language, published and maintained.** 62 published npm versions through v1.43.0 (2026-10-14); a hand-written, zero-runtime-dependency TypeScript compiler whose error system carries 139 stable diagnostic codes (92 errors, 47 warnings), each pointing at the exact span of source it refers to; 4,338 passing tests (measured 2026-09-04); and 27 architecture decision records. Around the compiler I shipped a CLI, a language server with a VS Code extension, a browser playground, a docs site, an MCP server so other AI agents can write and check floor plans (`@chanmeng666/archlang-mcp`, also hosted at mcp.archlang.uk), and a 1,600-row open dataset of example plans. One design rule holds all of it together, written down as an ADR: *the compiler computes facts and gives advice; it never designs.* Arranging rooms is the agent's job, which keeps the language honest about what it can and cannot promise.

**ArchCanvas — the agent that uses it.** Nine agent tools, five of them on the live path: ask design questions, generate a plan, edit a plan with a minimal diff, render it, and critique it. Every generated plan goes through a ship gate — compile, auto-fix, topology check, repair, annotate — and anything still wrong is written on the plan rather than hidden. On my offline benchmark of 26 briefs (run 2026-09-07), all 26 passed every check, with a median of one design round at 33 seconds. Around the agent sits a complete product: multi-storey plans, select-to-act editing, parametric sliders, a review mode, DXF and PDF export, share links, and Stripe credit packs with idempotent refunds.

**Where it stands.** Live at archcanvas.uk with real payments wired, and pre-launch: the public launch is planned for October 2026, and the commercial test that decides the next step is written down with its pass and stop thresholds before the result is known. Among the early testers was **Knight Hou, Co-Founder of Relab**, a PropTech SaaS company, who took a close interest in the product and where it could be applied.

**The research write-up.** Building ArchLang with AI coding agents turned into a software-engineering paper, *Reproducible Is Not Correct: Reflexive Gates and the Self-Descriptions We Ship to Language Models* — a census of the npm packages behind the Model Context Protocol registry, with ArchLang as its depth study. Published as a preprint on Zenodo on 2026-09-25 ([doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22958002](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22958002)) and submitted to arXiv (cs.SE) the same day, awaiting announcement.

**Technical highlights.** ArchCanvas: Next.js 15 + React 19 + TypeScript strict, Tailwind 4, Vercel AI SDK v4 over OpenAI models for design and GPT Image for rendering, Neon Postgres with Drizzle ORM and Neon Auth, Stripe, Cloudinary. Shipped as a Docker image through GitHub Actions and GHCR with a canary-then-swap deploy (boot the new container, poll its health endpoint, swap only if healthy) onto a DigitalOcean server behind Cloudflare.

ArchLang: pure TypeScript with zero runtime dependencies — a hand-written lexer, a recursive-descent parser that recovers from errors instead of throwing, a separate expression evaluator, SVG and DXF backends with optional PDF/PNG add-ons, and architectural-soundness lint rules (reachability, door-swing collision, windowless bedrooms, wet-room enclosure, circulation). `compile()` returns `{ svg, errors, warnings, diagnostics, ast, scene }` and never throws on a bad plan, which is what lets an agent read its own mistakes and fix them.

### Chief Technology Officer at FemTech Weekend

- Period: March 2025 – present
- Location: Chengdu, China (HQ) — fully remote
- URL: https://www.femtechweekend.com/
- Keywords: Next.js, Docusaurus, Drizzle ORM, Neon Postgres, Notion API, Cloudflare Pages, Cloudinary, Google Generative AI, i18next, Tailwind CSS, Radix UI, earth-flyline

CTO at FemTech Weekend, which describes itself as China's first women's-health-technology organisation. Sole engineer, working remotely, across two generations of its platform — a Next.js + Notion site the founder publishes to herself, then a Docusaurus + Drizzle/Neon + Cloudflare platform — and of everything its 2026 Shanghai Summit ran on online: the summit pages, an application system for pitch, programme and speaker applicants, and an admin dashboard where the founder reviews and approves them in batches. Four days, June 22–25, 33 speakers headlined by Ida Tin in the PwC building at Qiantan Center, Pudong, with support from the Pudong New Area Government.

**Impact.** Sole engineer behind every digital surface of FemTech Weekend: two platform generations, plus the summit pages, application system and admin review tools that carried its four-day 2026 Shanghai Summit — built and run remotely from Auckland.

**Company context.** FemTech Weekend describes itself as China's first organisation built specifically around women's health technology — a community, research outfit, and event producer rolled into one, **headquartered in Chengdu, founded 2024 by Zhu Yihan**, with a 2–10-person core team. Its remit is to take the international FemTech movement (a category coined in 2016 by Ida Tin, the Clue co-founder who headlined the 2026 Shanghai Summit) and ground it in the Greater China market: connecting founders, investors, healthcare professionals, and academic researchers across the China–global divide, positioned publicly as the **"China representative for cross-border women's health initiatives."** The organisation runs ecosystem partnerships with major corporates including **Bayer** and **PwC** on women's-health ecosystem development, hosts quarterly updates on China FemTech innovation, and collaborates with **FemTech Across Borders** on international programmes — alongside original market research (FemTech Market Map for Greater China, FemmeHealth Ventures Alliance partnership reports), editorial content, hackathons and pitch competitions, and the flagship Shanghai Summit.

**Mission.** Build the connective tissue between Chinese and global women's health innovation: surface investable founders, decode the China market for international FemTech operators, and accelerate culturally-grounded women's health innovation by reducing the information and capital friction across borders. The conviction is that women's health is chronically under-funded globally and structurally invisible in much of China — and that a deliberate cross-border community can compress years of market education and partnership-building into months.

**My mandate.** Hired as CTO with full ownership of every digital surface the organisation operates. I report directly to **founder Zhu Yihan**, run as a solo engineering team (with a single occasional code contributor), and have end-to-end authority over architecture, vendor choice, deployment infrastructure, and content management workflow. My mandate covers two parallel website generations, all back-office tooling that the non-technical team uses to keep the platform current, the application and subscription pipelines that capture every inbound lead, and the live digital infrastructure for the Shanghai Summit 2026 — the organisation's largest event to date.

The arrangement is best described as **co-designing technical strategy with the founder, then executing solo**: regular working sessions with Zhu Yihan to align platform direction, partner integrations, and editorial cadence, followed by my own end-to-end engineering delivery. Shanghai Summit 2026 in particular runs through this loop — speakers, multi-tier sponsor partners, NGO collaborators (AVPN among them), and policy/academic partners are all reflected through the same infrastructure I built, with content updates landing hours after founder-side decisions.

**Impact delivered.** Built and shipped **two complete generations of the FemTech Weekend website from scratch, solo**, across roughly a year of work.

**Generation 1 — femtechweekend.com (the original site).** A Next.js 15 application that paired a public-facing marketing and ecosystem site with a Notion-backed content layer so the non-technical founder could publish blog articles, ecosystem profiles, and event reports directly inside Notion — no developer-in-the-loop, no CMS learning curve, no markdown gymnastics. Visitor form submissions (ecosystem applications, event registrations, image uploads) flowed straight into Notion databases via the Notion API, with images persisted to Cloudinary, so the founder could triage applicants in the same tool she already used for everything else. Bilingual (English / 简体中文) from day one via i18next, including bilingual switching on the blog detail pages. A gated "report request" flow captured email addresses before unlocking research reports.

**Generation 2 — the current platform (femtech-weekend-website).** A substantially larger and more ambitious system: Docusaurus 3.9 as the editorial spine (chosen deliberately over keeping Next.js, because the client valued how articles are presented and how easily they can be searched), backed by Drizzle ORM against Neon serverless Postgres for summit application data (Drizzle defines the schema and migrations; the functions query with tagged-template SQL), with content as MDX in the repository that the founder edits herself and Notion receiving two form types. Hosted on Vercel from 2025-05 and on Cloudflare Pages via Wrangler from 2026-01 for global edge delivery. Adds: comprehensive bilingual content (EN/简体中文 across every section, not just the blog), a full **Shanghai Summit 2026** event site with ten distinct sections (Hero, FAB Globe, Partners, Speakers, Agenda, Audience, Venue, Why Different, Global Network, Sponsors), programme and pitch sub-pages and a gated agenda download, an admin applications dashboard, an interactive 2D world-map visualisation of the global network (powered by earth-flyline with count-up statistics), a Gemini chat endpoint called over REST, transactional email templates for pitch and programme review workflows, and a research publications hub. Two original research reports published through the platform: *FemTech Market Map for Greater China* (2025-05) and the *FemmeHealth Ventures Alliance* partnership announcement (2025-06).

**The summit system I built.** From the first summit commit on 2026-03-06 I built everything the summit ran on online, working remotely: the summit routes (the main summit page, programme and pitch; an hour-by-hour agenda page until 2026-05-26, when the agenda moved into a gated PDF) from 20 purpose-built components — a 3D globe of 40 countries, speaker and partner grids, an agenda timeline, a venue showcase and a programme price calculator — and the application system behind them. Founders applying to pitch, companies applying to the international programme and speakers applying to speak each land in their own Postgres table with document and headshot uploads (the speaker form closed on 2026-03-30, once the line-up was full); a gated agenda download captures leads with a newsletter opt-in. The founder reviews applications in an admin dashboard I built, approves or rejects them in batches, and each approval sends a branded email carrying the payment link and a free conference-access code — so the team ran selection without an engineer in the loop. For the agenda itself I wrote a Typst starter project and handed it to the founder, who built the full summit agenda on it in place of her original Canva design. Ticket sales themselves went through an external ticketing platform.

**Shanghai Summit 2026 delivery.** The platform carried the organisation's largest event: a four-day Shanghai Summit held **June 22–25, 2026** with the theme *Where Global Women's Health Meets China* — billed by the organisers as China's first global women's health summit, in the same five-month window that produced Japan's and Korea's firsts. The Impact Report lists 33 speakers, headlined by **Ida Tin** (Clue co-founder; coined the term "FemTech" in 2016), alongside Alice Zheng, Dominnique Karetsos, Lindsay Davis, Vanessa Julia Carpenter, Rachel Bartholomew, Maaike Steinebach, Stella Fu, Peixian Lu, Sandy Lv, Chai Ke (柴可), Chen Jian, Jazmin Seregi, Abraham (Nick) Morse, Ira Evdokimova, Maryann Selfe, Jonathan Y. Zhao, Rahul Agrawal, Giulia Paggiola, and Michael Wang. The summit was structured as a flagship conference plus a dedicated capital and pitch day plus curated site visits, with named partners including AVPN and a multi-tier sponsor programme — all of it rendered, managed, and updated through infrastructure I designed and operate solo. Its Impact Report names 26 organisers and partners and maps participants from Canada, the United States, Mexico, the European Union, Russia, Japan and Singapore. The four days were held in the PwC building at Qiantan Center in Shanghai's Pudong, with the Shanghai Pudong New Area Government as a co-convener. One of those speakers came through me: I recommended **Maaike Steinebach**, Founder & CEO of FemTech Future, who travelled from Hong Kong to speak. Bayer ran the pitch competition, HerAnova Lifesciences was a gold sponsor, and the investor panel put AVPN's Patient Lu and Gobi Partners' Leo Chen on stage alongside Maryann Umoren Selfe and Alice Zheng. Delivered with Femtech Across Borders as the 2026 Summer Programme.

**Technical highlights.** **Two-generation architectural evolution, with the second generation an intentional rewrite rather than a refactor.** The decisive call was whether to grow Generation 1 (Next.js + Notion) forward, or to admit that the platform's centre of gravity had shifted to its research and editorial content — the client valued how articles are presented and how easily they can be searched — and rebuild on a stack actually optimised for that shape. I chose to rebuild on Docusaurus 3.9 — not the default choice for a brand website, but the right one for an editorial platform whose long-term value lives in its market research, opinion pieces, founder stories, and event archives.

**A founder who publishes without me.** In Generation 1 the founder edited content inside Notion and the site rendered it live (`react-notion-x`). In Generation 2 the content is MDX in the repository: speakers, partners and agenda data sit in one typed module, and a step-by-step guide in Chinese shows how to add a story in one or both languages. Because a push to the main branch is the deploy, the founder publishes stories, opinion pieces and speaker updates herself. Notion now only receives two form types, written over its REST API. Either way, I am off the publishing critical path.

**Drizzle ORM + Neon serverless Postgres** in Generation 2 for application submissions, subscription confirmations, and admin dashboards — moving structured form data off Notion (which was a clever fit for content but the wrong fit for relational submission data) onto a schema-versioned Postgres database. Drizzle defines the schema and migrations; the Pages Functions query with tagged-template SQL through the Neon driver.

**Cloudflare Pages + Wrangler** for global edge deployment of Generation 2 since 2026-01 (it ran on Vercel from 2025-05): low-latency delivery to both Chinese and international visitors, which matters more for this audience than for most products, since the whole proposition is cross-border.

**Bilingual everything, from day one.** Both generations ship in EN and 简体中文 — not as an afterthought, but as a first-class architectural constraint that shapes routing, content models, speaker data structures, agenda time-zone rendering, and all editorial copy. The Gen 2 platform's content layer is built so that every speaker, partner, agenda block, and editorial piece has parallel locales rather than fall-through defaults.

**Image performance discipline.** The summit content is image-heavy (speaker headshots, venue photography, partner logos), so I ran two passes weeks apart: in April 2026 I compressed 14 large images and shrank the social-card image from 6 MB to 240 KB, and in May 2026 I cut the site's image weight by roughly 67% without losing visual fidelity. There is no CI workflow; the production build is the check, and broken links only warn.

**Interactive global-network map** built with `earth-flyline` — a 2D world-map visualisation with count-up statistics rendered responsively across screen sizes, with light/dark mode theming — which carries the visual weight of the summit's "global meets China" thesis on the front page.

**Transactional email infrastructure.** Custom templates for pitch package emails and programme review confirmations, including forwarding-recipient logic so the founder gets a complete audit trail of every application without having to check the dashboard.

**Effectively no team to lean on.** Every architectural decision, deployment incident, schema migration, and last-minute speaker update is on me, and the platform has remained continuously operational through both generations and through active summit marketing.

## Past roles

### AI Agent Architect at Engram

- Period: May 2026 – July 2026
- Location: Albuquerque, New Mexico, United States (remote)
- URL: https://engram.media/
- Keywords: AI System Architecture, Mission Control (internal product), Model Context Protocol (MCP), Agentic Workflows, Anthropic Claude Partner Network, Notion knowledge base, API-as-UI experiences

**Impact.** Recruited through Claude itself — founder Luka Madzarac publicly confirmed it surfaced Chan as a top match — then completed the Anthropic Partner Network Learning Path and passed the CCA-F practice exam, credentials behind Engram's approval into the Partner Network.

**Company context.** Engram LLC ([engram.media](https://engram.media/) / [LinkedIn company](https://www.linkedin.com/company/engrammedia/)) is a New Mexico–registered AI-powered media agency founded by **Luka Madzarac**. The company is repositioning around **agent-powered media operations**: deploying agents and pipelines that run a client's entire media function in-house — design, data, content, distribution — instead of outsourcing production. The target market is service businesses that need a media department running on autopilot. Engram is building its stack on Anthropic's Claude platform and is on a path to **certified Anthropic partner** status. The **Architect Cohort** is a selective onboarding programme through which Engram brings architect-tier engineers into the core team that will define the company's agentic-media engineering standards.

**Mission.** Replace click-through software workflows with **agentic ones** — natural-language intent drives downstream system orchestration and the agent's reasoning becomes the user-facing surface. For Engram specifically, that translates into autonomous media operations: instead of a human team manually assembling campaigns, content, and analytics, agentic systems plan, produce, and ship the media function for the client. The product line targets organisations that need end-to-end automation rather than demo-grade AI tooling, starting with Engram's own internal operations and graduating to client deployments.

**My mandate.** **How the engagement started.** Luka Madzarac asked Claude Code to surface AI architects who could help Engram reach Anthropic Partner status. Claude returned Chan as one of the strongest matches based on her verifiable open-source agentic-tooling footprint — **claude-code-audio-hooks**, **CopilotKit** contributions, production LangChain automation engines, programmatic media generation with **Remotion**, and the "**API-as-UI**" design pattern she's been publishing. Luka publicly confirmed the sourcing path on LinkedIn: *"Claude Code surfaced Chan as one of the strongest matches for what we're looking for."* ([announcement post](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/chanmeng666_ai-artificialintelligence-generativeai-activity-7459724144671195136-3JoV))

**What the cohort engagement covered.** A 45-day Architect Cohort onboarding at ~10–15 hours per week, structured as a mutual evaluation period; the engagement ran May–July 2026. Responsibilities were: (1) working through Anthropic's **Claude Partner Network Learning Path** — building on already-held Anthropic credentials (**AI Fluency: Framework & Foundations**, Aug 2025; **Claude Code in Action**, Aug 2025, credential ID JHIY9NPYTR2D); (2) participating in weekly working sessions with founder Luka Madzarac and the rest of the cohort on agent, skill, and MCP-integration patterns; (3) contributing to the cohort's emerging agentic-media engineering conventions; (4) maintaining presence in Engram's communication channels for cross-cohort engineering discussion.

**Impact delivered.** The Architect Cohort was an evaluation-shaped engagement rather than a delivery one, and it ran its course May–July 2026. What came out of it:

1. **Anthropic Claude Partner Network Learning Path — completed**, with verifiable per-course certificates recorded in `certificates[]` (Claude Code in Action, Building with the Claude API, Introduction to Model Context Protocol, Introduction to Agent Skills, all May 2026, on top of AI Fluency Framework and Claude Code in Action from Aug 2025). The **Claude Certified Architect — Foundations practice examination was sat and passed.**
2. **Contributions to the cohort's shared agent and skill design conventions** through weekly working sessions with the founder and the rest of the architect cohort.
3. **Cross-pollination** of Chan's pre-existing open-source agentic tooling experience (claude-code-audio-hooks, CopilotKit, google-news-mcp, typst-claude-skill, Remotion-based media generation) into cohort discussions on production-grade agent design, including architecture discussions for Engram's own product (still in development and unreleased when she left, so no delivery outcome is claimed).
4. **The Partner Network goal was reached.** Chan's completed Learning Path and passed CCA-F practice exam were part of the architect credentials behind Engram's approval to join the Anthropic Partner Network. With that done, she left the cohort in July 2026 to focus on her own products.
5. **Open-source IP preserved.** The cohort agreement explicitly carved out claude-code-audio-hooks (now **echook**) and the rest of Chan's prior work as her own property — echook has since gone on to 88 GitHub stars (2026-10-15) independently of Engram.

**Precise on the credential, deliberately.** The CCA-F *curriculum* was completed and the *practice* exam passed; the **official certification exam was never sat, so the CCA-F credential is not held.** Every surface should say "curriculum completed" or "practice exam passed" and never "certified" — the course certificates are real and verifiable, the certification is not claimed.

**Meta-signal**: the engagement itself validates a hypothesis Chan has been publishing about (**GEO / Generative Engine Optimization**) — that frontier models actively surface candidates based on verifiable code and real-world impact rather than traditional SEO keywords. Being the candidate Claude Code recommended to Engram for an Anthropic Partner engagement is empirical evidence that the open-source-first portfolio strategy works — and that remains true independently of how the cohort ended.

**Technical highlights.** The technical footprint that Claude Code surfaced to Engram — all carved out as Chan's own IP under the cohort agreement and remaining Chan's property:

- **claude-code-audio-hooks** — audio-feedback hook system for Claude Code (explicitly named in the cohort agreement as Chan's preserved IP), with its **echook** notification daemon.
- **CopilotKit** — active contributor to the open-source agent UI framework ([PRs](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit/pulls?q=is%3Apr+author%3AChanMeng666)).
- **google-news-mcp** — production MCP server published to the public registry.
- **typst-claude-skill** — Claude Code skill for programmatic document generation; demonstrates skill-structure design.
- **claude-code-compressed-map** — LLM-first tier/recency metadata system powering this very profile (the meta-move: optimising Chan's own data so LLMs rank it correctly — *GEO in practice*).
- Production **LangChain** automation engines and interactive LLM systems for mobile gaming.
- Programmatic media generation via **Remotion**.

The technical centre of gravity is **"API-as-UI"**: building agent surfaces where conversational intent orchestrates downstream tools and the model's chain-of-reasoning becomes the user interface — not a chat widget bolted onto a form.

### AI Instructor & Mentor at TechNest Community

- Period: April 2026 – August 2026
- Location: Newfoundland, Canada (remote instruction)
- URL: https://www.technestcommunity.com/
- Keywords: Cursor, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Model Context Protocol, Next.js, Neon Postgres, Drizzle ORM, Vercel, Typst, Docusaurus, Cloudflare Workers, Notion API, Algolia DocSearch

AI Instructor & Mentor at TechNest Community, a Newfoundland nonprofit democratising tech careers across Atlantic Canada.

**Impact.** Students ship portfolio-grade AI apps by week 8 on a platform I built.

**Company context.** TechNest Community is a Newfoundland-based nonprofit, established November 1, 2024, with the stated mission of "making technology accessible, creative, and impactful" for youth, newcomers, and local communities across Atlantic Canada. It operates four pillars: a structured **Mentorship Programme** that pairs learners with industry professionals on year-long tracks (software engineering, product management, cybersecurity, data analysis, 3D animation, and — for 2026 — Artificial Intelligence); **Creative Connections** networking events such as *Tech in the Park* (100+ attendees) and *Sip & Paint*; **Product Development** of community-serving software (their flagship is *Library Labs*, an AI-powered 3D learning platform); and **Tech for Children** coding-and-robotics workshops run in partnership with NCANL. Leadership is led by Abiodun (Magret) Oyedele and Afolasade Bello, both of whom I report to directly as the AI Track instructor.

**Mission.** Make modern tech careers reachable for groups that the Canadian tech industry typically under-serves — youth, newcomers to Canada, and people living outside the country's major tech hubs. The underlying conviction is that the best lever for regional economic mobility is not generic "learn to code" content but mentored, cohort-based programmes that connect learners with working professionals and ship a portfolio-grade product by the end.

**My mandate.** Designed and delivered the **2026 AI Track** end-to-end as sole instructor — the first AI-specialised cohort in the organisation's history, and the only mentorship track running in 2026 dedicated to AI engineering. Reporting line is direct to TechNest's leadership (Abiodun Oyedele and Afolasade Bello).

**Impact delivered.** **Authored and ran the 2026 AI Track — a 12-week prompt-first AI engineering curriculum** that became TechNest's flagship 2026 cohort. The programme ran **April 25 – July 17, 2026** (Matriculation Ceremony April 25, official start April 27, completion July 17), delivered as one two-hour live session per week plus self-paced lab time, on a fixed five-phase session shape (Recap → Concept → Live Demo → Hands-On Lab → Q&A). **30 students graduated.**

**The curriculum doctrine is original and opinionated:** *"Natural language is the source code."* Students arrive having used only ChatGPT in a browser. By Week 8 they own a live, polished, AI-powered personal website that doubles as their portfolio, AI-clone chatbot, guestbook, blog, contact funnel, and the source-of-truth for their auto-generated CV and cover letter — all driven by prompting Cursor, Claude Code, and Gemini CLI rather than hand-writing code. By Week 12, every student team has shipped a multi-user AI product that strangers can actually use.

**8-week teaching phase** evolves one progressively-built personal site, grafting a meaningful full-stack feature each week onto the same codebase: (1) AI Developer Toolkit Setup — Cursor, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, MCP servers, Skills, GitHub; (2) Deploy via Vercel CLI; (3) AI Clone — Gemini 2.5 Flash chat widget with a student-voiced system prompt; (4) Full-Stack — Neon Postgres + Neon Auth + Drizzle, guestbook; (5) Vercel Blob image uploads; (6) MDX blog + RSS; (7) Real-Time Slack notifications via webhook; (8) Typst PDF automation through the Typst skill in Claude Code, which becomes the engine for an auto-generated CV and cover letter.

Demo Day was a 5-minute live demonstration plus 3-minute Q&A in front of invited guests, with public voting powered through the showcase platform I built.

The most-voted project was **LinguaPath** with 66 votes, ahead of Joborg AI (31) and iCare (21); every one is a live, deployed, multi-user AI product with a public repo and a demo video.

**Independently attested by both sides of the programme.** Five of the 27 LinkedIn recommendations on Chan's profile come from the TechNest AI cohorts — and they run in both directions of the reporting line. TechNest leadership vouched for the teaching: co-founder and fellow mentor **Suliat Alaga** ("the feedback from our mentees was overwhelmingly positive… an outstanding AI educator, mentor, or technical trainer", Aug 2026) and **Abiodun (Magret) Oyedele**, one of the two TechNest leads Chan reports to, who took the Cohort 3 course herself. Learners attested to the same thing independently: **Kwame Essuman** ("she consistently made time for everyone to ensure no one was left behind… a top-tier AI instructor and mentor"), **Swayam Dhir**, and **Mahdieh Najmi**. This is the second-largest source of independently-attested teaching impact in Chan's career after Forward with Her (7 recommendations).

**Assessment rhythm baked into the doctrine.** Weekly assignments carry 50% weight and require students to submit both (a) the updated live site URL and (b) a screenshot of the Cursor / Claude Code conversation that drove the change — the screenshot rule operationalises the doctrine: *the prompt is the work*.

**Technical highlights.** The platform serves five cohort versions side by side through Docusaurus versioned docs: `2024-winter`, `2025-summer`, `2026-her-waka` (the academyEX / Her Waka programme), `2026-technest` (the active cohort, set as default), and `2026-peyvand-academy` (the She Sharp × Peyvand Academy youth workshop). New cohorts slot in without disturbing older ones, and students who took a prior cohort retain a stable URL for their materials.

**In-course AI assistant** indexes all five course versions plus the blog into a retrieval corpus with stable hash chunk IDs and version-aware retrieval, so a student in the 2026 cohort gets answers from 2026 materials by default. Implemented with a secure seeding flow and resilient retrieval logic — a teaching-platform feature most cohort sites simply don't have.

**Bilingual i18n by default** (English primary, 简体中文 secondary) across every cohort version. The build pipeline includes contextual Algolia search filtered by locale, localised Mermaid toolbar labels, locale-aware table-of-contents headings, and translated tag taxonomies — so a Mandarin-speaking student gets a fully localised experience including search results.

The pedagogical loop is intentional: students see, in production, the artefact they're being taught to build.

**Engineering hygiene visible in the commit log**: full migration of the production deployment from Vercel to Cloudflare Pages (February 2026) (with SEO URL migration and Algolia config update); 13 Dependabot security vulnerabilities resolved in one pass and ongoing patches managed cleanly; Mermaid dual-view component for diagram-heavy lessons; per-version sidebar customisation; SEO improvements with keyword-targeted blog posts written to support student discovery; trailingSlash and Algolia contextualSearch configuration to keep cross-locale and cross-version search coherent.

**The choice of stack mirrors the curriculum.** I deliberately chose tools the students are learning — Next.js / React, Notion APIs, Cloudflare deployment, Typst PDF generation, Algolia search — so the teaching platform is itself a worked example of the doctrine being taught. Students can literally read the instructor's repo to see how the patterns they're learning compose in a real production system.

Start the Play" — eliminate the friction between user intent and digital experience. Internally framed as building the "Post-App World" through proprietary "Instant Reality Switching" technology. The architecture is publicly described as two pillars: the Technology Platform (the CTO-led foundation) and the Intelligence Layer (the autonomous predictive engine that makes Instant Reality possible). The current product wedge is mobile gaming; the underlying activation engine is platform- shaped and applies to any interactive content category where install gap and cold-start latency dominate the funnel. During my tenure GAVIGO joined the **Google for Startups Cloud Program** and the **NVIDIA Inception Program** (Feb 2026) — programme participation, not an endorsement of the product — and was covered by tech-business press (feedvoice.com, *"How GAVIGO Is Ending App Store Friction for Instant Digital Play"*, 2026-02-10).

**Mission.** Replace the native-app install funnel — discover → app-store landing → install → onboard → first interaction — with activation inside the feed: the experience is prepared before the viewer arrives, not installed after they ask. The problem being solved is industry-wide: cold-start latency, install friction, and re-engagement cost on mobile interactive content (games, video, AI experiences) where the wait between intent and interaction costs engagement.

**My mandate.** Own the Intelligence Layer end-to-end — GAVIGO's term for the autonomous, predictive engine that powers Instant Reality activation. The role is contractually defined with a "Protected Technical Domain" that includes activation systems, activation flow and execution behavior, activation-economics proof path, AI-assisted orchestration and execution-control systems, restore and reuse boundary work, heavier-workload validation, and the core activation / execution / AI-enabled systems architecture of GAVIGO's interactive workload platform — plus the natural forward extension of that domain as the system evolves. Reporting to founder & CEO Saba Gecgil.

Title progression formalized over three contract iterations: Original Consulting Agreement (Oct 17 2025), Amended and Restated (Feb 9 2026), Second Amended and Restated (Apr 16 2026) which ratified the title I held until the role closed in October 2026: **Founding Principal Engineer, Activation, Execution & AI Systems**.

**Impact delivered.** Shipped GAVIGO IRE — the Instant Reality Exchange platform — from M1 prototype to live production at ire.gavigo.com. First shipped on DigitalOcean DOKS (Singapore); led the full migration to Google Cloud GKE (Belgium) in a clean ~30-minute cutover on 2026-03-11 when GAVIGO's Google Cloud partnership took effect — full production-grade expertise on both DigitalOcean and Google Cloud.

Measured in GAVIGO's proof stage, under controlled conditions: a 78% application-level reduction in startup work, a controlled startup path cut from 4.45 s to 1.00 s, and about 140 ms to restore preserved AI state into a fresh process. These are controlled application-level measurements, not a production SLA or a complete end-to-end activation time. Architectural deliverables include the Activation Spine: a five-state container lifecycle (COLD → PREPARING → READY → ACTIVE → REUSABLE) with atomic Redis transitions, recorded as a nine-phase activation timeline with proof-signal timestamps, restore being one activation path through it; the seven-trigger AI rules engine (Cross-Domain, Swarm Boost, Proactive Warm, Mode Change, Resource Throttle, Initial Warm, Lookahead Warm, plus a manual demo control); the warm-pool LRU manager with ProtectSlot reservations; the cross-platform state-sync protocol bridging MMKV / localStorage / Redis; and the Phase 9 audience-aware WebSocket broadcast filter that lets investors, operators, and the public see different slices of the same catalog. Recognized in the corporate record as "a core long-term technical builder of the Company's interactive workload platform" with founder-level equity participation.

**Programmes and press during my tenure (Feb 2026).** GAVIGO joined the **Google for Startups Cloud Program** (announced by founder Saba Gecgil), the arrangement under which I led the GCP migration the following month, and the **NVIDIA Inception Program**. Both are programme participation, not endorsements or product validation. Tech-business press covered the company at feedvoice.com — *"How GAVIGO Is Ending App Store Friction for Instant Digital Play"* (2026-02-10). My contractual scope was re-amended in the same window (Second Amended and Restated Consulting Agreement, Apr 16 2026) to formalise the **Founding Principal Engineer, Activation, Execution & AI Systems** title and the Protected Technical Domain backing it.

**What it added up to for the product.** Seen from the user's side, the work was the mobile application and the creator platform for GAVIGO's AI-powered mini-game ecosystem: the feed where games and short videos play in the scroll with no app-store install, and the profiles, followers and content overlays creators publish through.

**How the role closed (Oct 2026).** My last working day was 2026-10-05, after a handover through September. Founder & CEO Saba Gecgil, engineer Olga Adam and colleague Lutfullah Ugurer worked alongside me and can speak to the work. The last mandate I was named on was the CEO's v1.7 *Activation Platform MVP Build Mandate* (2026-08-28), which made me **build lead and Phase 0 owner**; the company has filed patent applications with the USPTO covering the activation / execution layer I built. (The filing details are GAVIGO's to disclose, not mine.) The handover needed no handover document, because project context had been written into the repository as the work happened rather than carried in my head: a 26.6 KB agent operating manual (`CLAUDE.md`), `docs/onboarding/`, `docs/deployment/`, and `docs/phases/` holding 13 numbered phase records. Writing the context down where the code lives is the practice; a clean exit is what that practice looks like when it is tested.

**Technical highlights.** **Cross-cloud production expertise — DigitalOcean and Google Cloud.** Originally architected on **DigitalOcean DOKS (Singapore, sgp1)** with DO Container Registry, DO LoadBalancer, and Let's Encrypt + manual certbot rotation. Led the full migration to **Google Cloud GKE Standard Zonal (Belgium, europe-west1-b)** on 2026-03-11 in a single ~30-minute cutover when GAVIGO's Google Cloud partnership took effect. All five deployments migrated cleanly with `strategy: Recreate` to avoid CPU deadlock on single-node clusters. Full migration record archived in the repo for institutional memory.

Single Go binary orchestrator combining a gorilla/websocket hub, the Scorer (weighted personal / global / trend signals into a combined activation score), the seven-trigger Rules Engine, and a Kubernetes client-go integration that patches deployment replicas in real time. Companion services: React + Vite dashboard, React Native + Expo 54 mobile build served via nginx, always-warm shared game-server pod baking ~25 FOSS games so no game needs a cold start of its own, Node + Express AI-service pod with gpt-5.4-mini, Phase 6+ compute / inference workloads, Redis 7 with allkeys-LRU and a 400 MB warm-pool budget, optional Postgres 16 for social data.

Hardest engineering problems solved: (1) A restore path through the Activation Spine state machine with deterministic atomic transitions, not optimistic ones. (2) Cross-platform state sync across MMKV, localStorage, postMessage, and Redis with a single canonical source of truth. (3) Async K8s coordination (EndpointSlice and Pod-status watches) feeding real-time WebSocket telemetry with millisecond-precision phase timestamps that prove the decision → patch → observation chain rather than asserting it. (4) Warm-pool LRU without cascade eviction, via ProtectSlot reservations for controlled and benchmark workloads. (5) Audience-aware broadcast filtering at the WebSocket envelope layer so each client preset sees a different catalog slice without N broadcast topics.

**Production diligence — the work of checking what was assumed.** Response compression had never actually been enabled in production: an nginx default that only misbehaves behind a load balancer, so it worked correctly on every developer machine and nowhere that mattered. I found it, switched it on, and every bundle and game the feed serves now ships compressed. I found a budget alert that could never fire; to fix it I requested the minimum role needed (Billing Account Costs Manager) and explicitly declined Billing Account Administrator. I established branch protection and then proved it by being blocked by it: PRs required, 1 approval, three CI checks green, admins unable to bypass — the gate being a 3-job pipeline (`go build/vet/test -race`, `vite build`, `tsc --noEmit`), where the mobile typecheck job is load-bearing because `expo export` transpiles without typechecking. Redis had been silently gone for 10 days while the service reported healthy; the fix was to reconnect rather than give up at boot, and to stop reporting healthy while degraded. A one-day T4 GPU experiment falsified its own hypothesis — the conclusion was "a GPU is a throughput/cost lever, not a latency lever" — and was torn down the same day with a reusable harness and the raw results committed. The acceptance criteria I wrote for a vendor smoke test (no pre-roll before first play, documented `game_ready` / `game_started` lifecycle events, wrapper telemetry without touching game code, programmatic licence verification) were adopted by the CEO as company process — converted into a six-vendor procurement questionnaire that disqualified a vendor within four hours.

FOSS curation: cloned 11 open-source game repos (Hextris, Clumsy Bird, Tiny Yurts, Catculus, Casual Crusade, Stolen Sword, Brewing Disaster, Coup Ahoo, DEAD AGAIN, Norman the Necromancer, Idle Necromancer), scored them against license (MIT / Apache-2.0), build size (<50 KB), web-first compatibility, and audio bug stability, and vendored the top 9.

### Senior Full Stack Engineer & Website Team Lead at She Sharp

- Keywords: Next.js 15, React 19, Drizzle ORM, Neon Postgres, Stripe, GPT-4o-mini, Slack, Agent skills, NextAuth 5, Tailwind 4

Senior Full Stack Engineer & Website Team Lead at She Sharp, a volunteer-run New Zealand women-in-STEM charity (96+ events since 2014), from July 2025 to September 2026. Recruited by founder Dr Mahsa Mohaghegh, moved the charity off rented software onto infrastructure it owns: a Next.js 15 platform with AI mentor matching replacing Webflow, and a 1,549-person mailing list cut over from Mailchimp with 0 failures. Wrote its recurring work — events, newsletter, posters, video, mailing list — down as 11 agent skills a non-engineer can follow, and left a written handover instead of a dependency on one person.

**Impact.** Recruited by founder Dr Mahsa Mohaghegh as the senior engineer She Sharp lacked; over 13.3 months moved the charity's website and 1,549-person mailing list onto infrastructure it owns, and wrote its recurring work down as 11 agent skills a non-engineer can follow.

**Company context.** She Sharp is a volunteer-run New Zealand women-in-STEM community — a registered charitable trust founded by Dr Mahsa Mohaghegh (McCauley), AI/NLP researcher and Head of Computer and Information Sciences at AUT. The organisation runs a mentorship programme, a sponsor network and a recurring events calendar: 96+ events since 2014, 2,919 distinct people registered for its events on record, and 39 sponsors on its logo wall.

**Mission.** Close the representation gap in technology by connecting women in STEM with role models, mentors, employers, and each other — and by running flagship programmes (mentorship, Her Waka workforce re-entry, THRIVE) that operationalize that mission at scale. The bottleneck on scale, when I joined, was the technical capability of the platform: the old Webflow site had become incompatible with the membership system, AI matching, billing, and Slack-integrated operations the mission required.

**My mandate.** Recruited directly by Dr Mahsa Mohaghegh (McCauley) as Senior Full Stack Engineer & Website Team Lead — specifically as the AI and senior development capability She Sharp didn't have in-house — to build the new member platform end-to-end and run it operationally. The mandate covered: replace the Webflow site, design and ship the AI mentor-mentee matching system, integrate Slack across the organisation's operations, run events and recruitment infrastructure, and serve as technical lead on adjacent initiatives (Her Waka MSD-funded programme, SEO strategy). It grew, in 2026, into leading the charity's digital and AI-native transformation. I held the role from July 2025 to September 2026.

**Impact delivered.** **The problem I was handed.** In July 2025 a volunteer-run charity ran on rented software: the website inside one vendor's product, the mailing list and its consent record inside another's, the artwork in a third, and eleven years of decisions inside a chat tool — all of it one lapsed card or one departed volunteer away from being out of reach. The previous move, WordPress to Webflow in 2023, had cost the second half of that year re-entering every event since 2014 by hand. I chose the new stack by one question first: how does the data come back out?

**What I built, and how much of it was mine.** The share is a description of how much depended on one person, which is exactly why the handover below was written as the work went.

**Website — done.** Replaced the Webflow site with a Next.js 15 application in a repository the charity holds: 63 pages, 84 API routes and 198 components over a 39-table Postgres schema. Beyond what Webflow did, it carries AI mentor-mentee matching (GPT-4o-mini, five weighted dimensions, human-in-the-loop review), three role-permissioned dashboards (mentor / mentee / admin), Stripe membership billing, and an AI chatbot answering from the site's live data rather than a hand-kept FAQ. A migration is finished when the old world's links still work, not when the new site goes live: Webflow's pagination URLs redirect permanently to their clean equivalents, and 903 legacy images were rebuilt from the old site's markup — it had no bulk media export — with a CI check that fails if an event page ever loses one.

**Mailing list — technically done and proven in production.** Moved 1,549 people onto infrastructure the charity owns — double opt-in where confirmation requires a button press and never a GET, as defence against link scanners; a four-stream sender model; exactly one Resend call site in the whole application; and the consent record in the organisation's own Postgres rather than a vendor's. The first send went out on 2026-08-31 in 16 idempotent batches with 0 failures and a 0.45% bounce rate. The sending-domain move was 29 DNS records before and 29 after with a single value different, because the region and Return-Path were matched deliberately rather than discovered afterwards. Consent became auditable for the first time by classifying every subscriber against the act that put them on the list — and I reported the unflattering result, that 75.4% arrived by an act that was not a subscription. 2,129 non-consenting contacts are held as one-way hashes so a future import cannot resurrect them, and a CI gate fails the build if an email address or a ticketing access code reaches a committed file. 179 past newsletters were recovered from the vendor and are now served from the charity's own site.

**Marketing production — shipped, not yet adopted.** Posters, event decks and promo videos became code generated from event data (see technical highlights). The honest status: it has been chosen over a hand-made duplicate once, and the committee still makes most artwork the old way. Shipping a capability and shipping its adoption are two different projects, and only the first was scheduled.

**Data sovereignty.** Recovered 1.15 GB of the organisation's own operating record out of four platforms: eleven years of Slack (208 conversations, 56,119 messages), the full ticketing and mailing history, and the only copy of the previous website held outside the vendor's own account. 97 archived Slack channels were invisible to the standard listing API and would have been missed entirely. Two findings that transfer to any migration: a checksum over a mapped object proves only what your mapper kept, and an API key is not a replacement for an export.

**Digital governance audit.** 7 of the 11 email addresses published on the website did not exist — including the headline contact address — proven by sending one real message to each and reading delivery back, not inferred from configuration; all fixed, plus a funder-facing PDF the sweep had missed. Removed 17 fabricated testimonials attributed to real companies from the charity's public site. Proved 3 of the 4 full-bleed photographs in a published funder report came from outside the period they illustrated, using perceptual hashing over a 225-image corpus. Catalogued 24 credential and personal-data exposures by location without recording a single value, and identified the same access-ownership failure recurring across 5 separate incidents in 7 years.

**Financial governance and audit capability.** Diagnosed a 60% rise in a SaaS bill as an unbounded data-growth problem rather than a price rise: the vendor's base price had not moved in 25 billing periods, and every dollar of the increase was buying contacts who could not lawfully be emailed (1,585 of 3,145 billed contacts, 50.4%). Finding the mechanism mattered more than the number.

**Enablement and business-process mapping.** Delivered six enablement sessions for the volunteer team (sessions delivered; no attendance was ever logged, so no headcount is claimed): a recorded content-update guide (2026-03-29) aimed at getting a non-technical member updating the site inside three minutes; a browser-automation demo (2026-05-04); four recorded agent-skill tutorials (2026-07-28); 1:1 Typst coaching for a teammate (2026-08-02); a recorded end-to-end event-lifecycle tutorial (2026-08-24); and a two-hour in-person workshop in Auckland on 2026-08-29 for the marketing and events teams, during which I produced usable promo videos live while teaching them to run the agent skills and to work in Cursor themselves. The written interface to all of it is an AI skills guide addressed to anyone on the team "whether or not you have ever written a line of code". Alongside it I derived a 1,714-line event-lifecycle standard operating procedure by crawling eleven years of Slack — a phase × owner × method table covering partner acquisition, go/no-go, channel kickoff, ticketing, website page, poster set, campaign calendar, social, mailing-list and registrant email, deck, photography, gallery close-out, feedback digest and newsletter, marking where the published title and the observed practice diverge. It is served as a live internal page and hash-verified against its source Markdown in CI, so the page cannot silently drift from the procedure it serves. Beside it sit 52 recorded organisational decisions (51 of them mine), each with structured frontmatter, which turns "has anyone already thought about this?" from a question you ask a person into one you can grep. I also ran a published-vs-recorded reconciliation of the organisation's own headline numbers — a measurement, not an accusation.

**Custom Slack ecosystem for the She Sharp workspace.** Beyond the admin-side Claude Code skill, I shipped a portfolio of integrations that run inside the She Sharp Slack workspace itself: an event-collector endpoint (`/api/slack/events`) that ingests workspace activity for the database; a **weekly mentorship-stats digest bot** that auto-publishes engagement numbers each Monday; and a **weekly NZ funding-opportunities digest bot** that crawls 6 government RSS/HTML sources, scores each opportunity for member relevance (60+ threshold), and posts the top 10 to a dedicated `#funding-opportunities` channel via Incoming Webhook; contact-form and AI-screening notifications; and a weekday `slack-triage` cron that reads with `--no-record` so it never advances a read position — an automated reader that marks things read is an automated way to lose them. The most involved of them is an **AI-powered `/event` slash command** that turns a plain-English request into a validated patch: it pulls channel history, the events JSON and the naming conventions as context, produces a structured-output patch, Zod-validates it, commits to a draft branch, shows an ephemeral Block Kit preview with a JSON diff, and on confirm opens a GitHub pull request. Work that used to mean opening a console now arrives as a reviewable change.

Beyond the main platform, I shipped three supporting projects: the Python migration crawler (1,748 images / 707 MB / 11 JSON files bootstrapping the new platform from the old Webflow site), the Her Waka MSD-funded teaching site at herwaka.shesharp.org.nz with complete authored curriculum (4 workshops + 12 tutorials), and a professional SEO audit and 10-point recommendations report on shesharp.org.nz that identified the high-priority mobile-vs-desktop ranking gap on "women in tech New Zealand."

**How the role closed (Sept 2026).** The transformation reached a natural milestone and I left She Sharp in September 2026 to focus on ArchCanvas. The remaining website team maintains the platform, and it and the agent skills are still in use. The aim all along had been to make the answer to "how does this work?" a file rather than a person, and the exit is where that was tested: 35,062 lines of Markdown across 105 files in the repository, the non-coder AI skills guide, two live playbooks hash-verified against their source, and the 52 recorded decisions. I kept my own account of the work, with every figure measured, cited or derived, and it says plainly what was not finished. Three money decisions were prepared and left with the founder, who holds the accounts: the nonprofit collaboration-tool upgrade, the mailing vendor downgrade, and the website vendor's renewal before 2027-06-18. And one gap I named as mine: a safeguarding reporting route for the community was proposed but not built. The charity's data and its sending identity now live in accounts the organisation owns, regardless of who is still there to open them.

**Technical highlights.** Architected the platform and built its back end and database (Lesley Gao built the new website's front end, including much of the mentorship dashboard): Next.js 15.6 canary + React 19.1.2 + TypeScript 5.8 on Drizzle 0.43 over Neon Postgres, NextAuth 5 with bcrypt + Google/GitHub OAuth, Tailwind 4 + shadcn/ui, Resend transactional email, Vercel Blob uploads, Stripe-integrated membership flow, Vercel edge deployment + 3 scheduled jobs. Schema runs 39 tables / 33 enums / 32 SQL migrations — every business concept is a typed enum so invalid states are unrepresentable. 84 API routes, 63 pages, 198 components; 180,914 lines of TS/TSX/CSS across 818 files and 35,062 lines of Markdown across 105 files, with 5 CI jobs gating every pull request and 33 test files behind them. The Markdown is not documentation debt — it is the interface, and the reference documents in it are the rules the product must not break.

The AI matching engine is a deliberate two-stage pipeline: rule-based pre-filter for cost control, then GPT-4o-mini at temp 0.3 / max_tokens 1000 / JSON-object response_format scoring on promising pairs along five **explicitly weighted** dimensions (MBTI 15% + Skill 35% + Goal 30% + Industry 10% + Logistics 10%) with explainable natural-language justifications, Upstash Redis cache by pair, exponential-backoff retries, deterministic rule- based fallback when AI is unavailable, and admin human-in-the-loop approval as the final gate. The `sync-event-from-slack` agent skill composes existing CLI tools (Slack fetch, image download, docx parse, JSON validate, git commit) into a single intent-driven workflow with dry-run preview and CI gating — collapsing event publication from hours of manual work to one command. Across the three supporting projects I worked in Python (crawler with image deduplication + Wayback Machine fallback), Mintlify / MDX (Her Waka teaching site authored solo), and Node 22 native fetch over the SerpData API (the SEO audit with mermaid-diagrammed report).

**The AI-native operating model.** An AI-native team is not a team that talks to a chatbot; it is a team whose recurring work has been written down precisely enough that an agent can execute it, and whose non-engineers can therefore run work that previously needed an engineer. She Sharp's version of that is 11 agent skills under `.claude/skills/`, spread over 97 files: 25,643 lines of written-down procedure and tooling — the honest figure, after subtracting one skill's 22,786-line machine-written state ledger from the 48,429 raw total — comprising 12,550 lines of instruction and reference prose across 27 reference documents and 11,995 lines of script across 34 executables. Each skill lives in the repository like code: version-controlled, changed by pull request, and type-checked in CI, which needs a second tsconfig because the root one skips `.claude/`. That is the whole argument. A procedure in someone's memory cannot be reviewed, diffed, or made to fail a test; a procedure in a SaaS console can be changed by anyone with the login and leaves no record of who changed it or why.

Each of the eleven replaces a named manual tool: `sync-event-from-slack` (the largest), `monthly-newsletter` (1,424 lines, the longest instruction file in the repository), `build-event-slides`, `update-mailing-list`, `email-the-community`, `reply-to-contact-messages`, `promote-event`, `make-event-poster`, `run-event-playbook`, `make-event-video`, `tweak-event-slides`. `run-event-playbook` is the orchestrator and the reason eleven tools behave as one workflow: it runs 10 offline checks for an event and, for each gap, names the skill that closes it. It builds nothing itself — it turns "what still has to happen for this event?" into a command whose answer arrives with its next action attached. The agent's own memory is layered the same way: 9 `CLAUDE.md` files, 933 lines, split by *when* a rule must bind rather than by subject. A nested file loads only when a file in that subtree is read, so rules about creating a new file, running a command, or trusting a `grep` hit have to live in the root file — none of those actions begins by reading a file in the directory they govern.

The four automations worth naming. **Newsletter** — `monthly-newsletter`, four issues (June to September 2026) composed in the new system and one, August 2026, broadcast through it, with a two-block JSON schema separating the machine-generated snapshot from human-owned editorial, and a three-stage approval chain (test send → review → founder approval) tracked in a state file. Writing the loop down did not move the decision to an agent; it made the stage legible. The founder alone approves a broadcast. **Poster** — `make-event-poster` generates a *textless* plate with gpt-image-2 and then sets every word in code across six platform sizes plus a per-speaker set and a line-up tile. The reasoning is the good part: text rendered by a diffusion model cannot be corrected when a speaker's title changes and cannot be proofread by a test; text set in code is a string in a file. **Promo video** — `make-event-video`, one Remotion composition rendering four aspect ratios (vertical, portrait, square, landscape) cut to a soundtrack, where a scene asks the layout for the shape of the frame it is being rendered into and recomposes; the vertical cut is not the landscape cut with its sides thrown away. **Report** — a Typst pipeline producing funder-facing and internal reports from real platform exports rather than placeholders.

No before-and-after timing study was run, so there is no hours-saved figure here and none should be inferred. What is structural and checkable is narrower and more useful: work that required a vendor console now runs from a command, so it can be scheduled, reviewed and re-run; and work that required an engineer now has a written procedure someone else can follow, which changes who is able to do it rather than only how long it takes.

### Open Source Contributor at CopilotKit

**Company context.** CopilotKit is the open-source framework for building in-app AI copilots and AI agents — 37,500+ GitHub stars and a thriving contributor community. It provides React components for embedding LLM-powered AI assistants directly into web applications (chat interfaces, command palettes, in-app actions), a runtime layer for tool and action registration that LLMs can invoke, and a Python SDK for multi-agent systems orchestrated through LangGraph. The framework is one of the standard ways to add sophisticated AI UX to a React app.

**Mission.** Make it trivially easy for any web application to add a sophisticated AI copilot or agent system. Lower the floor for building agentic UX so AI capabilities aren't gated by the complexity of state management, LLM orchestration, and framework integration plumbing.

**My mandate.** Open Source Contributor — adding capabilities, demos, and documentation downstream of real-world production use. This contribution connects CopilotKit's MCP-server capability with Anthropic's Claude Code, building on my earlier early-MCP-developer work. - `sanicle-ai` — the core FemTech platform with multi-tenant architecture, role-based auth (Employee / HR Manager / Org Admin), cycle and symptom tracking, AI consultation chat, leave-request workflows, HR analytics dashboards (demo at sanicle-ai.vercel.app; dual IBM watsonx + Google Gemini assistants, built for the UN Women x Sanicle hackathon)

**Public Next.js ecosystem contribution.** Published a community write-up on the Vercel forum titled "Solved Bug: Authentication Redirect Issue in Sanicle-AI Platform" (community.vercel.com/t/.../6818) documenting a production NextAuth 5 + Next.js 15 middleware / auth-state / routing-conflict failure mode and the multi-stage solution. Publicly acknowledged by Vercel Staff (Amy Egan): *"Thanks for sharing your debugging process and solution! This could help lots of people facing similar auth issues, or trying to avoid them in the first place."*

**Technical highlights.** Full-stack on **Next.js 15.5.9 + React 19 + TypeScript** with **NextAuth 5.0.0-beta.30** for multi-tenant role-based auth (Employee / HR Manager / Org Admin); **Drizzle ORM 0.34** over PostgreSQL for type-safe persistence; **Upstash Redis** for caching; **Vercel Blob** for file uploads; **Vercel AI SDK 4.3** as the AI abstraction layer; **shadcn/ui + Radix** components; **FullCalendar** for period and cycle visualization; **Chart.js** for HR analytics dashboards; **Framer Motion** for the interaction polish. Deployed on Vercel.

**Dual-AI architecture for resilience.** The platform combines **IBM Cloud watsonx AI** (`meta-llama/llama-3-405b-instruct`) as the primary engine for AI health consultations and leave-request reasoning, with **Google Gemini** as a fallback when watsonx hits its 28-second response baseline against Vercel's 10-second function-timeout ceiling. Mock-response fallback in the `/api/watsonx-chat` route preserves UX availability when the upstream model is rate-limited or timing out, with environment flags (`MOCK_API`) controlling development vs production behavior.

**The Next.js / NextAuth 5 auth-redirect bug-and-fix.** Identified, debugged, and publicly documented a multi-cause production failure where users authenticated successfully but were never redirected to their personal dashboards on Vercel — despite working in local development. Root cause was a combination of middleware conflicts, authentication-state synchronization issues, and routing complications across NextAuth 5 beta and Next.js 15. Multi-stage fix shipped to production; write-up published to the Vercel community forum and publicly thanked by Vercel Staff.

**Strategic migration call.** On joining, recommended Sanicle migrate from its Bubble no-code site to a code-based full-stack architecture — the team accepted and I executed the migration solo across `sanicle-cloud` and `sanicle-ai`, unblocking the enterprise-grade auth, multi-tenant data model, IBM watsonx integration, and Vercel-native deployment pipeline that Bubble fundamentally couldn't support.
