### Chief Technology Officer at FreePeriod

- Period: November 2024 – June 2025
- Location: Guangzhou, China (remote)
- URL: https://www.linkedin.com/company/free-period/
- Keywords: Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Radix UI, Framer Motion, Recharts, Zustand, Google Maps API, Cloudflare Pages, i18n

CTO at FreePeriod (Guangzhou, China; HKUST(GZ) Lab of Future Technology incubated), the public-health startup tackling period poverty through sanitary-pad dispensers, reproductive-health education, and policy advocacy under founder Julia Zhu. FreePeriod's dispensers now serve the public areas of 10 store locations in Guangzhou.

**Impact.** Solo CTO of a Guangzhou period-poverty startup combining software with off-grid hardware (solar-powered free-period-product dispensers) — site live through seven external recognitions in one cycle: four prizes, two programme selections and a grant.

**Company context.** FreePeriod is a Guangzhou-based public-health startup tackling period poverty and menstrual access through a combined hardware, software, and advocacy approach. Founded in 2024 by Julia Zhu (朱楠) and incubated at the **Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) Lab of Future Technology**, the company designs and deploys emergency sanitary-pad dispensers based on vending-machine technology for public spaces, runs reproductive health education programmes, and advocates for "women-friendly places" that supply free sanitary products in public restrooms — organised under the founder's strapline that *sanitary pads should be public infrastructure, like toilet paper, not a luxury purchase*. The team is 2–10 strong and operates as a university-incubated venture with strong academic and competition backing.

**Mission.** Normalise menstrual products as a free, universally-available public good — starting in mainland China, where period poverty is still under-discussed and where women in transit, on campus, in low-income workplaces, or in emergencies routinely face access gaps. The theory of change is to combine concrete hardware deployments (so the access gap is visibly solved in specific real places) with reproductive health education (so the cultural conversation moves) and policy advocacy (so the commitment institutionalises). The March 2024 policy win installing free sanitary pads in HKUST(GZ) women's restrooms is the proof-of-model the rest of the strategy builds on.

**My mandate.** Brought in as CTO in November 2024 to own every piece of FreePeriod's digital presence. Reporting directly to founder Julia Zhu, my mandate covered the public website end-to-end — architecture, build, deployment, and ongoing maintenance — alongside the digital infrastructure that supports the company's advocacy and product-rollout work (location directory of dispenser installations, advocacy document distribution, product demonstration, event scheduling, bilingual content for cross-border audiences). Solo engineering team throughout.

**Impact delivered.** The site is the public face of every product, advocacy, and education thread the company runs.

**What the site has to do, and does:** present the dispenser product and the company's mission to a press- and grant- evaluator audience (the company collected four prizes, two programme selections and a grant in its 2024 cycle); host an interactive **Google Maps directory** of dispenser locations and women-friendly places so visitors can find free menstrual products near them; serve a product introduction video and downloadable advocacy documents (research summaries, policy briefs, partnership decks); run a Google Calendar embed for community-event scheduling; and operate fully bilingually (English / 简体中文) for both domestic Chinese audiences and the international academic, competition, and grant ecosystem the company sits inside.

**Stayed on the site post-tenure as the long-term technical custodian** — the founder kept me on for ongoing infrastructure work after the active CTO engagement ended in June 2025. In that capacity I shipped the **production migration from Vercel to Cloudflare Pages** in April 2026 (re-pointing DNS, rebuilding the static export pipeline around `wrangler pages deploy`, updating CI), upgraded Next.js to 15.5.9 to clear all then-open Dependabot security alerts in a single pass, refined the i18n layer to handle developer-credit footer attribution in both locales, and kept locations data current as new dispensers were installed.

**Joined during the company's external-validation cycle.** During the period of my active CTO tenure and immediately leading into it, FreePeriod accumulated a striking concentration of recognition: **Best Award at Japan's 12th International Conference on Social Sciences and Humanities** (2024); **Third Prize in the HKUST Sustainable Smart Living Competition** (2024); **Best Social Media Award at FemTech China's inaugural Women's Health Technology Challenge**; **First Prize at the Shenzhen Nanshan District Philanthropic Creative Star Contest**; selection into **Tencent's Technology Venture Capital Program**; selection into **Tsinghua University's SDG Open Innovation Marathon**; and the **HKUST Entrepreneurship Bridge Grant**. The site I built was the public artefact those judging panels were clicking through.

**Technical highlights.** **Static-export Next.js 15 + TypeScript** site deployed as a fully static bundle (the build script wipes `.next` and `out/` then writes a clean static export), which is the right shape for a high-traffic, low-mutation marketing-and-advocacy site sitting in front of grant judges, press, and policy stakeholders. Cheap to host, instantly cacheable, and trivial to move between hosts — a property I exercised when I migrated production from Vercel to Cloudflare Pages via `wrangler` in April 2026 without rebuilding the application.

**Google Maps as a directory primitive.** Rather than building a custom database-backed location service, I used `@react-google-maps/api` with a hand-curated TypeScript module (`locations.ts`) as the source of truth for dispenser and women-friendly-place installations. Each install or location update flows through a Git commit, so the founder gets full audit history of where and when each pin moved, and the Maps-rendered front end stays one PR away from edits. Several commits in the log are `Update locations.ts` — that's the rollout cadence visible in version control.

**Bilingual i18n by design, not bolt-on** — Chinese and English run side by side across the marketing copy, the dispenser product descriptions, the impact narrative, the advocacy document previews, and the footer credit. The audience split is genuinely bilingual (domestic Chinese policy and partner audiences on one side; international academic, competition, and grant audiences on the other), so the language layer is a first-class architectural concern, not a translation afterthought.

**Document and video preview pipelines** for the policy briefs, research summaries, partnership decks, and the company's product introduction video — in-browser preview plus downloadable original — so external evaluators can review artefacts without leaving the site.

**Radix UI primitives + Framer Motion** for accessibility- correct interactive components (dialogs, toasts, checkboxes, popovers) with motion polish, and **Recharts** for impact- metric visualisations on the dashboard. **Zustand** for the small amount of client-side state the marketing surface needs (language toggle, dialog state).

**Engineering hygiene maintained through the long tail.** Even after the active CTO engagement ended I kept the site secure and modern: a clean Dependabot-driven Next.js 15.5.9 upgrade resolved all then-open security alerts in a single commit; the Cloudflare Pages migration was executed without downtime; i18n strings stayed current with footer attribution changes; and locations data continued to track installations as the company rolled out.

**Software-meets-hardware integration as a deliberate skill surface.** FreePeriod is not a pure-software play — the product is a vending-machine-class hardware deployment for emergency sanitary pads, with solar-powered variants for lower-grid-access locations, deployed across public spaces and partner institutions. My engineering job was to make the software side of that combined operation legible and useful: the live Google Maps dispenser directory that lets users locate the nearest installation; the bilingual advocacy document distribution flow; the live product-demo interface; and the locations dataset that tracks each rollout. This was an explicit exercise in shipping software that is judged not on technical novelty but on whether it makes physical-world deployments visible, addressable, and trustworthy to non-technical audiences.

The app integrates with CORDE's Workbench central operations platform via the API contract Kullum Ladley documented: **14 API documents on eight topics, revisions included**, plus one written priority list (15 files, each prefixed `YYYYMMDD_Kullum_...`), covering Workbench API calls, reading logs, log creation, mobile-app authentication, log extension fields, file upload, log completion and the group completion workflow — all captured under version control as the API/ folder of the team's documentation repository.

Translated CORDE's abstract user stories into concrete Azure DevOps work items; co-designed the database schema by reconciling two team-developed plans against CORDE's existing database slices into a unified version; survived two UI library re-evaluations (Native Base → React Native Elements → Native Base) and chose Native Base for its Figma-component-library integration so design and implementation stayed close; ran the demo cadence in front of Barry Clark and the CORDE technical team every week across five months; and moved the team from a one-branch policy (agreed June 2024) to a main branch plus a develop branch with pull requests in mid-July 2024, merging most of those pull requests into main myself.

**Handed over, still carried on for CORDE.** In mid-September 2024 one teammate stepped back, and the client's test rounds, fixes and release builds for the last month fell to me. In October 2024 Luke Shi took the project over in his own fork of the repository and has carried it on for CORDE since, with releases into 2026. The platform upgrades in that fork since 2024 (React Native upgrades, Android 16 KB page-size compliance, pre-commit hooks) are his work, not mine; my later commits to the original repository are documentation only.

**Technical highlights.** **React Native 0.74 + TypeScript + Native Base** on the client (the version at handover), deliberately chosen over Expo because the project's offline-first requirements pushed against Expo's managed workflow (and over React Native Elements because Native Base shipped a Figma component library that let the team do design-first then implement against the exact components). The native-only mode also opened the door to Android-native development where the offline pipeline needed it.

**SQLite as the system of record for the moment of work.** Local-first storage of text + photo + GPS coordinates + timestamps captured in the field, with a synchronisation pipeline that reconciles back to CORDE's Workbench central database when connectivity returns. What the code does: the local id and the server id are separate columns, so a log created offline never collides with one the server issues; each log carries its own sync status and retry count; a background queue retries uploads on timers; attachments go through the separate file-upload protocol in Kullum's API documents; and a pull replaces the local copy with the server's. A failed upload is not re-queued and there is no conflict prompt: both were the next things to build.

**Heavy native-integration surface:** geolocation + geolocation-service (foreground and background), camera- roll, image-picker, document-picker, file-system, secure keychain storage, native maps, react-native-permissions for the Android permission flow, base64 encoding for the on-the-wire payloads. The dependency list is twice as long as a typical RN app because field-data-collection in Canterbury's rural water-infrastructure context genuinely touches that much of the device.

**API integration discipline.** Apifox for shared interface testing across the team; Swagger as the contract source from CORDE; a `test-sharepoint-connection.js` script as evidence of a SharePoint-touching corner of CORDE's document workflow; Azure DevOps as the work-item store Barry Clark and the CORDE team worked from; per-week question sets compiled into documents and reviewed before each offline meeting so CORDE's time was used efficiently.

**The documentation repo is the artefact.** A second repository (`team-corde`) ran in parallel as the project's living memory — every weekly meeting decision, every UI-library evaluation, every database-schema iteration, every CORDE email exchange's outcome, captured in version-controlled prose.

## Flagship projects

### ArchLang

An original declarative floor-plan language that compiles .arch source into professional, dimensioned floor plans — 'Typst/LaTeX for architecture.' Zero-dependency, isomorphic TypeScript (hand-written lexer + recursive-descent parser), errors returned as data not thrown, with architectural-soundness linting, human-circulation analysis, a deterministic repair pass, five export formats (SVG/DXF/PDF/PNG/text), an agent-native CLI, full LSP + VS Code extension, and a client-side playground. Published to npm; the compiler engine behind ArchCanvas.

- URL: https://archlang.uk/
- Repository: https://github.com/ChanMeng666/archlang
- Started: June 2026
- Status: production
- Tech stack: TypeScript 5.7 (ESM, zero runtime dependencies), Hand-written lexer + recursive-descent parser + expression evaluator, tsup (build), Biome 2.5 (lint/format), Vitest 2.1 + fast-check (property tests) + pixelmatch (visual regression), Optional lazy add-ons: @resvg/resvg-js (PNG), clipper2-wasm (geometry), pdfkit (PDF), LSP (hover/completion/rename/signature), VS Code extension (ChanMeng.archlang, TextMate grammar), Vite + CodeMirror 6 playground (100% client-side), VitePress docs, GitHub Action (renders ```arch fences to images)
- npm package: @chanmeng666/archlang v1.43.0 (62 published versions through 2026-10-14, 27 ADRs)
- Tests: 4,338 passing, 0 skipped, across 216 test files (measured 2026-09-04)
- Primitives: 15 element kinds (wall · room · door · window · opening · furniture · dim · column · stair · elevator · escalator · roof · void · outdoor · fence), read from the element registry 2026-10-15, + fixture-symbol catalog
- Export formats: 5 — SVG + DXF (zero-dep) · PDF + PNG (lazily-loaded optional add-ons) · text-only plan
- Diagnostics: 139 stable E_*/W_* codes (92 errors · 47 warnings), each carrying a byte span + a machine-applicable fix
- Lint rules: 8 architectural-soundness rule modules (reachability, door-swing collision, windowless bedroom, wet-room enclosure, circulation)
- CLI: ~20 subcommands, all with --json + deterministic exit codes (0 ok / 1 IO / 2 source / 3 usage)
- Downstream: the compiler engine behind ArchCanvas, which consumes frozen-API contracts (data-arch-id anchors, diffPlans()) verbatim

ArchLang is a small language for floor plans: you describe walls, rooms, doors, windows, and furniture in plain text, and it compiles to a precise, dimensioned drawing — SVG, DXF, PDF, PNG, or a text-only plan. The same source always produces the identical drawing, so widening a bedroom is a one-number edit instead of re-drawing. It also checks whether a plan is actually livable (can you reach the bathroom? does a bedroom have a window?), and is the floor-plan engine behind the AI design agent ArchCanvas.

**Impact.** Describe a floor plan in plain text — walls, rooms, doors, windows — and get a precise, dimensioned architectural drawing back. Change one number and exactly one thing moves. It also checks that a plan is actually livable, and powers ArchCanvas, an AI design agent.

**Problem.** Floor plans live in two unsatisfying states: hand-drawn in heavy CAD tools, or generated as raster images. Both make the thing you most want to do — a precise, parametric edit — expensive: widening a bedroom means re-drawing, or re-rolling an image and hoping the rest survives. Neither is authorable by an AI agent, because there is no deterministic text representation an agent can write, verify, and tweak. And an image never *knows* whether the plan it depicts is actually habitable — whether a bathroom is reachable only through a bedroom, whether a door swings into another door, whether a bedroom has a window. ArchLang exists to make a floor plan a **program**: exact, deterministic, diff-able, agent-authorable, and checkable for architectural soundness.

**Audience.** Three audiences. Architects and self-builders who want plans that are precise and reproducible rather than hand-drawn approximations; design-tool builders who need a floor-plan engine they can embed (ArchCanvas is the first); and AI agents that need to author and verify plans without ever rendering an image — for which ArchLang exposes its entire language in one ~2k-token spec page, returns a plan "as facts" (rooms, areas, adjacency, door connections, circulation) over `describe --json`, and scores a plan against a written brief with `validate --intent`.

**Product logic.** You write `.arch` source. The coordinate model is integer millimetres with an SVG-convention origin; elements are placed either absolutely (`room 4000x3000 at (0,0)`) or **relationally** — `right-of`, `left-of`, `above`, `below` with `align` and `gap`, resolved by deterministic topological arithmetic so the layout stays consistent under edits. The language is genuinely programmable: `let` bindings, pure value-functions, `for`/`if`/`while`, arrays, string interpolation, optional metric unit suffixes (`4m`/`40cm`), and `import` + `component` for reuse — all expand-time and pure (no runtime, clock, or I/O), so output is byte-for-byte deterministic.

Compilation is a returned value, not a side effect: `compile()` hands back `{ svg, errors, warnings, diagnostics, ast, scene }` and **never throws** on a bad plan — every diagnostic carries a byte span and a machine-applicable `fix`, and the SVG is simply left empty. On top of the compiler sit several analysis surfaces: a **lint** pass over eight architectural-soundness rules (reachability, door-swing collision, windowless bedroom, unenclosed wet room, too-narrow door…); a **circulation** analysis that models how a person actually walks the plan on a clearance-eroded nav grid (per-room walk distance, narrowest pinch, path circuitousness) with an optional route overlay; a deterministic **repair** pass that nudges furniture out of walls and door swings and emits a change log; an **intent** check that scores the plan against a written brief and returns a pass/fail exit code; and a **suggest** surface that emits candidate door/window statements to fix reachability problems. All of it is reachable from a ~20-subcommand CLI where every command supports `--json` and returns deterministic exit codes, plus an LSP, a VS Code extension, four render themes, accessibility annotations, and a fully client-side playground.

**Business logic.** ArchLang is free and open-source, MIT, published on npm as `@chanmeng666/archlang`. Its strategic role is twofold. As an artifact it is a credential — an original programming language with a hand-written compiler, a 139-code diagnostic system, domain-specific static analysis, and full IDE tooling, built and versioned with engineering discipline (27 ADRs and 62 published versions by 2026-10-14). As infrastructure it is the **engine that makes a commercial product possible**: ArchCanvas (the AI design agent) depends on it, writing parametric ArchLang rather than freehand SVG so that its select-to-act editing, parametric sliders, and semantic diffs all work — capabilities that only exist because the underlying plan is a deterministic program. Agent access is designed CLI-first: a CLI costs zero context until it is called, whereas an MCP tool schema sits in an agent's window permanently. ArchLang still publishes an optional MCP server (`@chanmeng666/archlang-mcp`, on the official registry) so MCP-native hosts can discover it, but keeps the SDK quarantined in that one package so the core stays zero-dependency. Since 2026-10 the same server is also hosted at mcp.archlang.uk (ADR 0026), for hosts that take a URL and cannot start a local process; it is the only scripted Worker in the repository, and the two public sites stay static.

**Technical approach.** A pure-TypeScript, zero-runtime-dependency compiler: a hand-written lexer (line/col tracking), a recursive-descent parser that recovers rather than throwing, and a separate expression evaluator, all isomorphic so the same code runs in Node and in the browser — the playground sends nothing to a server. The heavy or native pieces (resvg for PNG raster, clipper2-wasm for polygon geometry, pdfkit for PDF) are **optional and lazily imported** behind bundler-ignore guards, so a browser bundle never tries to resolve them and a default install pulls none of them. Output determinism is enforced with property tests (fast-check) and visual-regression tests (pixelmatch). The diagnostic layer — 139 stable `E_*`/`W_*` codes, each with a byte span and a suggested fix, surfaced as data and even as a self-describing error-SVG card — is the deliberate foundation of the agent story: an LLM can author a plan, read the structured errors, and self-correct in a tight loop without a human or an image in the middle.

**Outcomes.** The surface area is unusually complete for a solo language project — 15 element kinds, 5 export formats, 8 lint-rule modules, a circulation analyzer, a repair pass, an intent-scoring channel, a ~20-command CLI, a full LSP, a VS Code extension, an optional MCP server (also hosted at mcp.archlang.uk), a client-side playground, a docs site, a published HuggingFace dataset of self-verifying repair trajectories, and a GitHub Action that renders every ```arch fence in a repo's Markdown. Most tellingly, it is already load-bearing: ArchCanvas's in-browser use of the core drove real hardening, proving the engine under a downstream product rather than in isolation.

**My role.** I invented the language and wrote everything — the language design, the hand-written lexer / parser / evaluator, the 139-code diagnostic system, all five export backends, the lint / circulation / repair / intent / suggest pipelines, the LSP and VS Code extension, the CodeMirror playground, the docs site, the MCP server, and the npm packaging. Outside users have since filed issues, and the first outside pull request (a PDF Unicode-font fix) was reviewed and merged on 2026-09-23.

### ArchCanvas

'Your AI architectural designer — dimensioned floor plans you can actually build from.' An AI design agent that turns a natural-language brief into ONE strong floor plan — written as parametric ArchLang (Chan's own DSL), compiled to real dimensioned SVG, plus a GPT-Image rendering grounded on that exact plan — then refined conversationally on an infinite zoomable canvas where edits morph in place. Select-to-act editing, a review mode that overlays circulation and pins critique, parametric sliders, and export of the whole design history as a real git repo. Refinement mutates the plan in place — it never regenerates it.

- URL: https://archcanvas.uk/
- Started: April 2026
- Status: live
- Tech stack: Next.js 15.3 (App Router) + React 19 + TypeScript 5.8, Vercel AI SDK (ai 4.3, @ai-sdk/openai) + OpenAI 6.45 — orchestrator on gpt-5.6-terra since 2026-07-31 (off GPT-4o, then gpt-5.5); a separate, env-configurable designer model writes the plan; vision on the same tier, GPT Image grounded renderings (one model, gpt-image-2, for every view since 2026-09-01), @chanmeng666/archlang ^1.42.0 (Chan's own declarative floor-plan compiler, consumed as a package), Neon Postgres + Drizzle ORM (13 tables, schema-push), Stripe 17 (credits ledger, dual live/test mode), Cloudinary (rendering storage), react-zoom-pan-pinch (infinite zoomable canvas), isomorphic-git + memfs + fflate (export design history as a real git repo, in-memory), jose (JWT/JWKS auth), Zod validation · shadcn/ui + Tailwind 4 + Framer Motion + GSAP, Docker canary-then-swap deploy over SSH (DigitalOcean VPS, Traefik + Let's Encrypt, Cloudflare Full-Strict)
- Surfaces: 13 pages · 28 API route handlers · 71 components · 205 source files
- Database: 13 Drizzle tables on Neon (projects · designFrames · agentThreads · credits · creditTransactions · shares · generationAttempts · uploads · stripeWebhookEvents · newsletterIssues · agentTurnSteps · funnelEvents · renderAttempts), read from the schema 2026-10-12
- Agent tools: 9 (7 user-facing: askDesignQuestions · generateFloorPlanDSL[new plan] · editFloorPlanDSL[minimal diff] · generateRendering · critiquePlan · analyzeReference[vision] · analyzeFloorPlan)
- Generation unit: one generation = plan + grounded rendering + critique, produced as a single atomic set; edits, parametric tweaks, re-renders, and review mode all operate on that set without re-generating it
- Deploy: private repo → GitHub Actions → GHCR → canary-then-swap over SSH (boot canary, poll /api/health, swap only if healthy) on a DO VPS behind Traefik + Cloudflare

ArchCanvas is an AI design agent for architects and self-builders. Describe a building in plain language and it asks a few questions, then designs one dimensioned floor plan you can actually build from — with room labels and measurements — alongside a realistic AI rendering of it. From there it stays conversational: on an infinite zoomable canvas you refine the plan by talking to it, scrub through every past version, and export the whole design as files or as a full change history.

**Impact.** An AI design agent for architects and self-builders: describe a building in plain words and it designs a dimensioned floor plan you can actually build from, plus a realistic rendering — then you refine it by talking, on an infinite zoomable canvas.

**Problem.** AI floor-plan tools produce pretty pictures you cannot build from and cannot precisely edit. An image-generated plan has no real dimensions, no guarantee a wall is straight, and no handle to grab when you want the kitchen two metres wider — you re-prompt and hope. Meanwhile professional CAD is powerful but slow and expert-only, and neither world lets you simply *talk* to your design. ArchCanvas closes that gap: a plan you can converse your way to, that is nonetheless a real, dimensioned, buildable artifact you can keep editing precisely.

**Audience.** Architects and designers who want to move fast from brief to a credible dimensioned plan, and self-builders / renovators who have a vision but not CAD skills and need something they (or their builder) can actually work from. Because every plan is a real floor-plan program underneath, the same product serves a careful professional nudging a wall thickness with a slider and a first-timer who just wants to describe their dream house and see it — and refine it — in plain language.

**Product logic.** The studio runs in two acts. **Act I** is a full-screen briefing conversation: the user picks a typology (residential, accessible clinic, open-plan office, passive house) and describes the build; the agent asks two-to-five clarifying questions inline, then generates ONE plan — deliberately not a grid of options — as parametric ArchLang, compiles it to a dimensioned SVG with `data-arch-id` anchors, renders a grounded AI visualization, and critiques it. That single turn is the only point at which the agent is asked for a brand-new plan.

**Act II** is a canvas-first studio, and nothing in it regenerates. Edits are conversational and **morph the plan in place** — the parent geometry fades to a dashed ghost, a semantic-diff chip shows what changed, and a version-lineage timeline lets you scrub the history. **Select-to-act**: click a room, door, or window and a floating action bar offers verb chips (Enlarge / Shrink / Widen / Move) plus agent-suggested scoped edits. A **Parametric Tweaks** panel turns the plan's own variables (room sizes, counts, wall thickness) into live sliders that recompile instantly with no AI call at all. **Review mode** toggles a walking-circulation overlay (routes, pinch points) and pins anchored critique findings, each with a one-click "have AI fix" — display-only, never auto-applied. The finished design exports as SVG/PNG/DXF/PDF, or as a full versioned change history whose log *is* the design conversation.

**Business logic.** The unit of work is one generation turn — plan + grounded rendering + critique, produced as a single atomic set — and everything downstream of it is refinement rather than regeneration. That split is deliberate: a design task's value is lumpy (you want a few strong plans, then iterate on them for a long time), so every edit, parametric tweak, re-render, and review action mutates the existing frame in place, and the model is re-invoked only when the user genuinely asks for new work. The advantage is the ArchLang pairing: because plans are a deterministic program rather than pixels, ArchCanvas can offer editing, tweaking, diffing, and change-history export that an image-generation competitor structurally cannot.

**Technical approach.** A single Next.js 15 monolith (React 19, TypeScript 5.8) over a 13-table Drizzle schema on Neon Postgres, with Stripe credits, Cloudinary rendering storage, and jose-based auth. The AI layer is an orchestrated tool-agent on the Vercel AI SDK: the orchestrator was deliberately migrated off GPT-4o (which under-used tools and wrote non-parametric DSL), first to gpt-5.5 and on 2026-07-31 to **gpt-5.6-terra**; the plan itself is written by a separate designer model (its own env-configurable constant, so the designer can move without moving the orchestrator), and reference-image vision moved off GPT-4o to the same tier on 2026-08-15. Its tools center on `generateFloorPlanDSL` — write parametric ArchLang, compile it through the `@chanmeng666/archlang` package (^1.42), pass a ship-gate, save a frame — with `editFloorPlanDSL` as the minimal-diff follow-up. Renderings are **grounded**: the compiled plan is rasterized and sent as the grounding image to GPT Image 2 so the render matches the real geometry instead of hallucinating a layout. Since 2026-09-01 one image model renders every view; resilience comes from two request shapes (a grounded edit, then a text-only generate), not from a second model. `designFrames` stores each version's ArchLang source, compiled SVG, rendering URLs, lint warnings, review findings, and a self-referential `parentFrameId` for lineage — which is exactly what the in-memory change-history export (isomorphic-git + memfs, zipped with fflate) walks root-to-tip. Deployment is a canary-then-swap over SSH: build a Docker image, push to GHCR, boot a health-checked canary, and swap traffic only if `/api/health` passes — otherwise abort untouched.

**Outcomes.** On the founder-run offline benchmark of 26 briefs (2026-09-07) all 26 plans passed every check, at a median of one design round. The product is unusually rigorous about testing its own thesis — a `generationAttempts` telemetry table tracks first-pass ArchLang validity per model, and a `bench` harness runs briefs through both the DSL pipeline and a legacy freehand-pixel pipeline as a control group (now with timing and token axes), so the "DSL beats pixels" claim is measured, not asserted. It is also the proving ground that hardened ArchLang: real in-browser use of the compiler drove concrete upstream fixes, most recently the 1.18 topology work.

**My role.** Sole author of the entire product — the two-act studio and canvas UX, the AI orchestrator and its tools, the grounded rendering chain, the ArchLang integration, the schema and credit/billing system, the change-history export, the falsifiability instruments, and the canary-then-swap deployment. And of ArchLang itself, the floor-plan language it is built on — invented eleven weeks into this product, when drawing plans as freehand SVG proved impossible to check. Sole engineer, working with AI coding agents.

### Tam-AI-Ti

Development commission from Riria (Missy) Te Kanawa, Māori Executive Lead — Strategy & Governance at ASB Bank (former KPMG NZ National Māori Sector lead) — an AI Financial Wellness Coach grounded in Te Whare Tapa Whā that proved Māori users will engage with a culturally-native AI agent (19-user cohort, 4 months, bilingual te reo Māori).

- URL: https://tamaiti.whiri-ai.com/
- Demo: https://youtu.be/NtT7_q6xhlk
- Started: October 2025
- Status: production
- For: Whiri-AI
- Tech stack: Next.js 15.5 (App Router + Turbopack build; route handlers on the Node.js runtime), React 19.1 + TypeScript 5 (100% strict typing across 48 tables / 494 columns), Drizzle ORM 0.44 + drizzle-kit 0.31 (10 schema files: users · assessments · goals · daily-engagement · ai-coach · whanau · maramataka · whakatauki · financial-coach · index; 22 SQL migrations 0000-0021 generated by drizzle-kit, 0012 extended by hand with the pgVector HNSW indexes), Neon Postgres (HTTP serverless adapter `@neondatabase/serverless` 1.0), pgVector — 1536-dim `text-embedding-3-small` embeddings on 4 tables (goals · goal_progress · journal_entries · ai_coach_messages), CopilotKit 1.10 (backend + runtime + react-core/react-ui/react-textarea) — deliberately optimised from 8 AI-enabled routes down to 3 focused ones (Dashboard CRUD wellness + Journal fill + Journal History search), OpenAI 6 SDK — three-model composition: `gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18` for CopilotKit actions (temp 0.3, deterministic), `gpt-4o-2024-11-20` for journal enhance/translate/insights (temp 0.5-0.8), the GA Realtime model `gpt-realtime` ("verse" voice) over WebRTC for the Financial Coach with server-side VAD + 500ms silence detection and `gpt-4o-mini-transcribe` transcripts, @openai/agents 0.1 (OpenAI Agents SDK), NextAuth v5 (beta 29) + @auth/drizzle-adapter 1.10 — Google OAuth 2.0, database sessions (30-day duration, not JWT), react-hook-form 7.62 + @hookform/resolvers 5 + Zod 3.25 validation across all API inputs, @vercel/blob 2.0 — avatar storage; ioredis 5.7 — Redis cache for dashboard queries (sessions live in Postgres); Resend 6 + @react-email/components 0.5 — transactional email, react-easy-crop 5.5 — avatar crop preview; recharts 3.2 — Hauora trend charts; - Research cohort: 19 users, no test or staff accounts among them (Oct 2025 – Mar 2026)

An AI financial-wellness coach for Māori communities, built on the Māori holistic-health model Te Whare Tapa Whā — the cultural framework lives in the database schema, not as surface styling. Users get voice coaching and journaling in both te reo Māori and English, guided through wellbeing check-ins and money goals framed around family, spiritual purpose, and health rather than numbers alone. Built solo for a development commission from Riria (Missy) Te Kanawa, Māori Executive Lead — Strategy & Governance at ASB Bank; a 19-person cohort used it over four months (Oct 2025 – Mar 2026), producing 181 bilingual journal entries, 35 voice coaching sessions, and over 500 transcribed coaching messages.

**Impact.** A te reo Māori AI coach for financial wellbeing, built on the Māori holistic-health model Te Whare Tapa Whā — encoded in the database, not added as decoration. A 19-person research cohort used it over four months: voice coaching plus 181 bilingual journal entries.

**Problem.** Mainstream financial apps treat money as decontextualised numbers — budgets, balances, projections. For many Māori users that framing is culturally mismatched: money is inseparable from *whānau* wellbeing, spiritual purpose, and holistic health. Generic budgeting tools strip out the very framework that makes financial decisions meaningful, leaving Māori communities — who face disproportionate financial stress in Aotearoa — choosing between tools that fit their wallet but not their worldview, or no tool at all. Tam-AI-Ti exists to test a direct question: can an AI financial coach built natively on Māori cultural wisdom, rather than retrofitted with cultural decoration, engage a population that mainstream financial technology systematically underserves?

**Audience.** Māori adults working on their financial wellbeing, served along two account types: individual goal-setters (Full Account) and *whānau* supporters who can witness and encourage from the sidelines through a five-tier permission system (view profile, view goals, view journal, send messages, receive celebrations). Research cohort to date: 19 verified participants recruited by Missy Te Kanawa, active over a four-month window (Oct 2025 – Mar 2026), producing 181 bilingual journal entries, 35 voice coaching sessions, 146 AI coach messages, and 74 daily Hauora check-ins. Te reo Māori and English are first-class throughout. Future audience: the broader Māori adult population — *rangatahi* entering working life, parents managing *whānau* finances, *kaumātua* passing on financial wisdom — for whom culturally-rooted tools are scarce.

**Product logic.** The product is architected on Te Whare Tapa Whā, the Māori model of holistic wellness with four walls (Wairua/spiritual, Tinana/physical, Hinengaro/mental, Whānau/family) standing on a foundation (Whenua/land). Every feature traces back to this house.

A user starts with the **26Q assessment over nine named psychological factors** — `self_belief`, `long_term_focus`, `resilience`, `self_control`, `growth_mindset`, `financial_confidence`, `social_comparison`, `mindfulness`, `gratitude` (with `mindfulness` reverse-coded to capture Present Bias) — mapped to personalised recommendations. They then select up to three focus areas, choose one of three account types (Full / Supporter / Both), and proceed to set financial goals through one of **seven SMART action plans (Options A-G)**: A Spending Reduction, B Savings Increase, C Savings Rate, D Debt Reduction, E Income Growth, F Budget Review, G Accountability Partner. Each plan has its own dedicated React component family (SpendingTracker / SavingsTracker / DebtCalculator / IncomeTracker / BudgetReviewCalendar / MeetingsTracker etc. — 38 goal components total) and its own type-specific tracking fields in the schema, rather than a generic JSON-note column. A `GoalCardFactory` / `ProgressTrackerFactory` / `OverviewFactory` pattern dispatches the right component for each goal's `option` field.

They check in daily across **eleven Hauora dimensions** mapped directly to the four walls: `sleep_hours`, `water_litres`, `food_quality`, `exercise_hours` for Tinana; `wairua_time_spent`, `wairua_human_connection`, `wairua_taia_connection` for Wairua (Whenua integrated through Taiao/environment connection); `hinengaro_mauri_tau` (mindfulness), `hinengaro_ako` (learning) for Hinengaro; `whanau_check_in`, `whanau_quality_time` for Whānau. Each metric is a typed integer-scale column with a Māori-language identifier — not a UI label sitting on top of a culturally-neutral schema. They journal morning intentions (Hauora intentions across all 5 dimensions + 3 gratitude items + financial reflections) and evening reflections through the Kūmete framework (what you contributed + what you received, Tahi-Rua-Toru tomorrow goals, emotional check-in), all bilingually in te reo or English, with real GPT-4o enhancement (4 enhancement types × 3 intensity levels), translation (macron-correct ā/ē/ī/ō/ū), and 5-dimensional AI insight extraction (Emotions / Themes / Hauora / Patterns / Growth).

They meet an **AI Financial Coach on OpenAI's Realtime API** by voice (`gpt-realtime`, "verse" voice, server-side VAD + 500ms silence detection, `gpt-4o-mini-transcribe` transcripts) — a conversation partner that never reduces money to numbers but consistently frames every financial decision through all four walls of the Hauora model. Audio is deliberately *not* stored; only text transcripts persist (a cost optimisation that preserves searchability without per-minute audio storage). The AI surfaces **74 Whakatauki proverbs across 37+ categories** by theme via `/api/whakatauki/search`, references the **Maramataka 30-day lunar calendar with 4 traditional activity types** — *Toitoi* (spiritual/cultural: karakia, whakapapa, wānanga), *Hi ika* (water-based: ocean/river fishing, shellfish, seaweed), *Pouraka* (hunting: bird hunting, forest foraging, game tracking), *Mahi māra* (gardening/planting) — for cultural timing, and ties financial decisions back to family and spiritual purpose. Whānau members can be invited via email-token-based invitations with a **5-tier permission system** (`canSeeGoals` · `canSeeProgress` · `canSeeMood` · `canSeeAchievements` · `canSendMessages`) to encourage and witness without intruding.

**Business logic.** Currently a research-pilot product, not yet commercial. A development commission from Riria (Missy) Te Kanawa in her role as Māori Executive Lead — Strategy & Governance at ASB Bank. The theory of change: if a financial-wellness tool authentically reflects Māori cultural frameworks — rather than skinning generic financial technology with cultural decoration — it can drive engagement and outcomes for a population mainstream products miss.

The hypothesis sits inside Riria (Missy) Te Kanawa's broader body of work on Māori economic prosperity. She is lead author of KPMG New Zealand's *Maui Rau* report series on how Māori can advance prosperity for their people, has spoken at the National Māori Governance Summit, contributes to The Spinoff, and brings two decades of experience as a Chartered Accountant and management consultant. Former Partner at KPMG NZ leading the National Māori Sector; now Māori Executive Lead — Strategy & Governance at ASB Bank, the role in which she commissioned this build. Tam-AI-Ti is the working artifact for that thesis — evidence that culturally-native technology can serve where culturally-decorated technology cannot.

Paths forward remain open: iwi partnerships, Māori community organisations, and institutions seeking to authentically serve the Māori sector.

**Technical approach.** Solo full-stack build on Next.js 15.5 with Turbopack and TypeScript 5 (100% strict typing across the entire 48-table / 494-column schema). Drizzle ORM 0.44 over Neon serverless Postgres with pgVector for 1536-dimension `text-embedding-3-small` semantic search across four embedded tables (`goals.goal_embedding`, `goal_progress.note_embedding`, `journal_entries.content_embedding`, `ai_coach_messages.content_embedding`). Authentication via NextAuth v5 (beta 29) with `@auth/drizzle-adapter` 1.10 — Google OAuth 2.0, database sessions (30-day duration, not JWT), CSRF protection, role-based access control across three account types (full / supporter / both).

**The schema is deliberately split across 10 module files** — `users.ts`, `assessments.ts`, `goals.ts`, `daily-engagement.ts`, `ai-coach.ts`, `whanau.ts`, `maramataka.ts`, `whakatauki.ts`, `financial-coach.ts`, and `index.ts` — totalling ~924 lines, each file owning a domain boundary. **22 SQL migrations (0000-0021)**, generated by drizzle-kit and extended by hand where Drizzle could not express the change (0012 adds the pgVector HNSW indexes), track every schema change: 0015 restructured the Hauora metrics from mixed data types to consistent integer scales (better alignment with Māori wellness philosophy: removed `exercise_minutes` / `calm_minutes` / `outside_minutes` and added 7 new Hauora-aligned integer fields); 0020 added the financial coach tables (`financial_coach_sessions` 8 cols + `financial_coach_messages` 5 cols); 0021 added period-based tracking (`current_period_start`, `current_period_end`) so Options F (Budget Review) and G (Accountability Partner) operate as recurring rather than one-shot goals.

The AI layer is a deliberate **three-model composition** chosen for cost-and-quality fit:

- **CopilotKit 1.10** drives in-app tool actions on `gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18` at temperature 0.3 — deterministic and cheap for tool calls (45 AI actions across 12 hooks in the shipped code, counted 2026-10-15, after the goals assistant's 28 were cut).
- **`gpt-4o-2024-11-20`** handles high-quality journal enhancement (`enhanceJournalContent`: 4 enhancement types × 3 intensity levels at temp 0.6-0.8, max 1500-3000 tokens), bilingual translation (`translateJournalContent`: EN ↔ te reo Māori with macron-correct ā/ē/ī/ō/ū preservation at temp 0.5, max 2000 tokens), AI insight extraction (`extractJournalInsights`: 5-dimensional analysis at temp 0.3, structured JSON), reflection-question generation (`generateReflectionQuestions`: 5 question types at temp 0.7), and semantic similarity search (`findSimilarEntriesAI`).
- **OpenAI Realtime API** (the GA `gpt-realtime` model, "verse" voice, WebRTC through the OpenAI Agents SDK with a short-lived client secret) powers the voice Financial Coach with server-side VAD and 500ms silence detection; `gpt-4o-mini-transcribe` writes the transcripts. Voice sessions store text transcripts only — a cost optimisation that preserves searchability without per-minute audio storage.

**CopilotKit was deliberately optimised from 8 AI-enabled routes down to 3** (Dashboard with 4 CRUD wellness actions; Journal with the fill-journal action; Journal History with search + analysis). Goals / Maramataka / Resources / Onboarding / Auth routes were intentionally *disabled* for the AI assistant — security on auth, performance on cultural pages, and cleaner UX on goal management. That's anti-feature-bloat discipline: removing AI surface area was treated as a feature.

**Culture is in the schema, not the UI.** Every one of the eleven Hauora dimensions is a typed column with a Māori-language identifier (`wairuaTaiaConnection`, `hinengaroMauriTau`, `whanauCheckIn`, `wairuaTimeSpent`, `whanauQualityTime`, etc.); the seven SMART action plans are first-class types `a`–`g` with **15 type-specific tracking fields** in `goal_progress` rather than a generic JSON blob; the 74 Whakatauki proverbs are an indexed, embedded library searchable by theme through `/api/whakatauki/search?q=...&category=...`. The Maramataka schema (6 tables, 49+ columns) models the 30-day lunar cycle, 8 main moon phases, the 4-activity key system, daily energy levels, and Gregorian-to-Maramataka calendar mapping. **48 tables, 494 columns, 76 API route files, 100+ endpoints across 20 modules, 38 pages, 115+ React components** (44 main + 38 goal-specific + 28 shadcn/ui + 5 cultural). Route handlers on Vercel's Node.js runtime; Vercel Blob for avatar storage with `react-easy-crop` 5.5 client-side crop preview; Redis (ioredis 5.7) caching dashboard queries, with sessions kept in Postgres; Resend 6 + `@react-email/components` for transactional email; `recharts` 3.2 for Hauora trend charts.

**Outcomes.** Production-deployed at **tamaiti.whiri-ai.com**, in active operation since October 2025. Research-cohort engagement (Oct 2025 – Mar 2026, roughly four months): 19 verified users (no test or staff accounts among them), 181 bilingual journal entries, 18 active financial goals, 146 AI coach messages, 35 voice coaching sessions with over 500 transcribed messages, and 74 daily Hauora check-ins. Sustained multi-month engagement on a pre-commercial product with no marketing channel — a meaningful early signal for a research pilot.

**March 2026 production migration**: a zero-downtime cutover from my personal Vercel Hobby account to the client's Whiri-AI Pro team account — GitHub repo transfer, Vercel Blob + KV re-creation, Google OAuth re-config, custom-domain DNS cutover through Cloudflare, blob-data migration, Resend sender-domain re-verification, and `NEXTAUTH_SECRET` preservation so existing user sessions survived. The app first moved to the client's apex domain, then to the subdomain she chose, and every registered user was emailed the new address. Documented as a reusable 12-step playbook covering every component and the rationale for not using Vercel's built-in Project Transfer.

**22 schema migrations shipped** in lock-step with feature work, none rolled back — the most consequential being 0015 (Hauora-metrics restructure to consistent integer scales), 0020 (Financial Coach voice tables) and 0021 (period-based tracking converting Options F/G from one-shot to recurring goals). Vercel's automated React Server Components security fix was merged as PR #2 (Dec 2025).

Project status: fully built, deployed and in operation. After about four months of cohort use, and the agreed maintenance period, it was handed over in full: the client runs it herself. It sits within Missy Te Kanawa's wider published work on Māori economic prosperity — KPMG NZ *Maui Rau* report series (lead author), Māori Governance Summit talks, The Spinoff contributing author — as the working artifact for the thesis that culturally-native technology can serve Māori communities where culturally-decorated technology cannot.

**My role.** Solo independent developer with full ownership of the entire stack and lifecycle. Introduced to the project by Dr Mahsa McCauley (Mohaghegh), founder of She Sharp (New Zealand's leading women-in-STEM nonprofit) — Missy approached Mahsa for a developer recommendation and Mahsa referred me from the She Sharp engineering team, where I serve as Senior Full Stack Engineer and Website Team Lead.

Engagement model: Missy as client, directing the product structurally (feature requests, surveys, "include the Maramataka lunar calendar," "add a Financial Coach feature") and funding the work directly; I designed, built, deployed, and maintained the entire system, and ran the data analysis. Voice was my own initiative, not part of the brief: when testers asked to speak rather than type, I proposed a voice coach and shipped it in November 2025. Throughout development I sent feature-demo videos at every milestone so Missy could review progress without needing a technical background. Post-launch, I produced teaching videos enabling Missy to use Cursor to do her own database reads and basic data analysis, and walked her through the live database. When the agreed maintenance period ended (February 2026) she chose to keep the app running, and I handed it over in full in March 2026: repository, hosting, domain and email moved to her accounts, and she runs it herself.

Carried Shanghai Summit 2026 (June 22-25, 33 speakers headlined by Ida Tin — Clue co-founder who coined the term "FemTech" in 2016): 10-section summit homepage, programme and pitch sub-pages and a gated agenda PDF, 3 summit application forms (programme/pitch/speaker) writing to typed Postgres tables plus ecosystem applications into Notion, double-opt-in newsletter wired to a Resend segment, admin dashboard with batch review + brand-styled approval/rejection email automation, Gemini-powered chatbot, bilingual EN/简体中文 across every surface.

The website and application system for FemTech Weekend, China's first women's-health-technology community. It carried the community's Shanghai Summit 2026 (June 22–25) with a bilingual English / 简体中文 event site, online application forms, a newsletter, and a founder-run admin dashboard, all on fast edge hosting for audiences inside and outside China.

**Impact.** The bilingual website and sign-up system for FemTech Weekend — China's first women's-health-tech community — which carried Shanghai Summit 2026 and its 33 speakers, led by Ida Tin, who coined the term FemTech.

**Problem.** FemTech Weekend is China's first community built specifically around women's-health technology — part community, part research outfit, part event producer — headquartered in Chengdu, founded 2024 by Zhu Yihan, with a 2-10-person core team. Its remit is to take the international FemTech movement (a category named in 2016 by Ida Tin, the Clue co-founder who headlined the 2026 Shanghai Summit) and ground it in the Greater China market: connecting founders, investors, healthcare professionals, and researchers across the China-global divide. The community publishes original market research (the FemTech Market Map for Greater China and FemmeHealth Ventures Alliance reports) and runs recurring updates on China FemTech innovation.

Two website generations have lived inside a ~13-month window. That shift culminated in Shanghai Summit 2026 — a four-day flagship event, June 22-25, 2026, themed Where Global Women's Health Meets China. The summit needed its own first-class digital infrastructure: a speaker lineup (33 in the summit's Impact Report), an agenda, application pipelines, an ecosystem partner directory, a sponsor programme, and a press-ready editorial surface — all bilingual EN / 简体中文, all edge-delivered across the China-global divide, and all operable by a non-technical founder when I am not in the loop.

**Audience.** Three concentric audiences. Founders, investors, and ecosystem operators in women's-health technology — the people who apply to the programme, pitch competition, speaker pool, or ecosystem directory; subscribe to the newsletter; and read the research reports. They span Chinese and international markets, so every primary surface ships bilingually. Shanghai Summit 2026 attendees and prospective attendees — 33 speakers headlined by Ida Tin, plus partners (PwC, Bayer, AVPN and others), multi-tier sponsors, and a delegate audience drawn from the global femtech community. The FemTech Weekend internal team — primarily founder Zhu Yihan, who publishes stories, opinion pieces and speaker updates herself as MDX in the repository, without developer involvement, and reviews applications through the ADMIN_API_KEY-protected admin dashboard, approving ecosystem applicants via the brand-styled email automation built into the platform.

**Product logic.** The platform is organised around four parallel surfaces the founder operates independently, plus a fifth founder-only surface (the admin backend).

Surface 1 — the editorial spine. Docusaurus 3.9 with three blog-plugin instances: blog/ (research reports, currently 2 published — FemTech Market Map for Greater China 2025-05, and FemmeHealth Ventures Alliance 2025-06), opinions/ (commentary), and stories/ (founder profiles). Choosing Docusaurus over keeping Next.js was deliberate: the client valued article presentation and article search, which Docusaurus provides out of the box (MDX, blog collections, DocSearch), and that outweighed the loss of Next.js's rendering flexibility.

Surface 2 — the Shanghai Summit 2026 event site. A 10-section homepage at /shanghai-summit/ (SummitHero → FABGlobeSection → PartnersGrid → SpeakersGrid → AgendaTimeline → WhoShouldAttend → VenueShowcase → WhyDifferent → GlobalEcosystem → SponsorsSection, bookended by SummitCTA), with the venue set to the Qiantan Center, Shanghai. Sub-pages cover the programme application and the pitch-competition application (with deck upload). The hour-by-hour agenda page was retired on 2026-05-26: the route redirects, and the full agenda is a PDF behind a lead-capture modal that records interest to its own table. Speaker data lives in a typed src/data/shanghai-summit.ts module so non-technical edits go through a single source of truth.

Surface 3 — the application pipelines. The three summit forms each have a typed table on Neon Postgres (schema defined in Drizzle) and their own Cloudflare Pages Function: pitch_applications, programme_applications (including the China-engagement fields — china_objectives, china_relevance, china_concerns, etc.) and speaker_applications; the speaker page was taken offline on 2026-03-30 once the line-up was full, with its table and API kept. Ecosystem submissions are written to Notion over its REST API. Every summit submission gets a reference_number, defaults to status: 'submitted', and is reviewable in the admin dashboard. PDFs (pitch decks, company overviews) and headshots upload to Cloudinary's REST API through four dedicated upload-* endpoints, keeping object storage detached from Postgres row size.

Surface 4 — the newsletter system. subscribe-newsletter.js creates a Resend contact with explicit segment assignment, handling the "contact already exists" path via the contact-to-segment join endpoint, then sends a brand-styled HTML welcome email (with a plain-text fallback for accessibility). A second endpoint, confirm-subscription.js, runs the double-opt-in flow so subscribers verify intent before joining the active segment.

**Business logic.** The platform's job in this economy is to be the trust-signal-bearing public surface that lets a Western founder, a Chinese investor, a corporate partner, or a prospective speaker take the organisation seriously within seconds of arrival — and the operational substrate that lets the 2-10-person core team triage applications, publish editorial, and run the summit without scaling headcount. Every architectural choice on Gen-2 is downstream of those two demands.

**Technical approach.** Docusaurus 3.9 as editorial spine, a Drizzle-defined schema on Neon for summit application data, Cloudflare Pages Functions for the entire server side. The functions query Neon with tagged-template SQL through the Neon driver; Drizzle supplies the schema and migrations. No Node backend, no container, no separate admin app — the whole platform is one Docusaurus site with colocated Pages Functions handling every server-side concern.

16 Cloudflare Pages Functions, ~5,373 LOC of server-side JavaScript, organised by intent: 4 application submitters (submit-programme/-speaker/-pitch/-ecosystem.js), 2 newsletter endpoints (subscribe-newsletter.js, confirm-subscription.js — Resend Contacts API, segment assignment, 409-conflict fallback, double-opt-in), 4 Cloudinary uploaders (upload-headshot/-image/-company-overview/-pitch-deck.js), 3 admin endpoints (admin/applications.js, admin/batch-review.js, admin/send-approval.js — each checks X-Admin-Key against ADMIN_API_KEY before any DB write), 1 Gemini chatbot (chat-stream.js), 1 PDF intake (pdf-form-submit.js), and 1 agenda lead-capture (submit-agenda-download.js).

Drizzle schema, 4 tables, 4 migrations: 0000_luxuriant_riptide → 0001_programme_overhaul (China-engagement column family) → 0002_speaker_overhaul → 0003_agenda_downloads (summit-agenda lead capture). Tables share a common pattern: identifying fields → typed domain fields → uploaded asset URLs → admin lifecycle (status defaulting to 'submitted', status_updated_at, admin_notes, reference_number), created_at via defaultNow(). Schema at src/db/schema.ts.

Email automation discipline. Every transactional template is hand-authored HTML plus a plain-text twin, brand colours baked in, table-based layout that renders cleanly in Outlook and Gmail. Every interpolated string passes through an escapeHtml helper before reaching the template. Resend is called over its REST API directly (no SDK), so the same code runs unchanged on the Cloudflare Workers runtime.

Gen-1 used Notion as its CMS; Gen-2 keeps its content as MDX in the repository, which the founder edits herself through Git with a guide written in Chinese, so the developer is off the publishing critical path. Notion only receives two form types, written over its REST API; Gemini and Cloudinary are also called over REST, not their SDKs, so the same code runs on the Workers runtime. Bilingual everything from day one — EN and 简体中文 as a first-class constraint shaping routing, content models, speaker data, and agenda rendering. Image performance discipline — two passes weeks apart: on 2026-04-10, 14 large images compressed and the social-card image cut from 6 MB to 240 KB; on 2026-05-12, the repository's image weight cut by about 67%. Hosted on Vercel from 2025-05, then Cloudflare Pages + Wrangler 4.0 from 2026-01 for global edge delivery; local dev composes docusaurus start with wrangler pages dev so functions run against the same edge runtime as production; Node 22.x pinned in engines.

**Outcomes.** Production-deployed at femtechweekend.com and operating the full organisational pipeline (ecosystem applications, newsletter, summit forms, research distribution) across both EN and 简体中文 audiences. Shanghai Summit 2026 ran June 22–25, 2026 with the platform as its sole operational substrate.

Commit cadence shows active delivery, not maintenance: recent work includes growing the confirmed speaker lineup, setting the venue to Shanghai's Qiantan Center, building the gated "download full agenda" lead-capture flow (new endpoint + agenda_downloads table), and rebuilding the social/OG card — all solo, on a live site marketing a flagship event.

The platform demonstrates a design call worth flagging: Generation 2 was a deliberate rewrite, not a refactor. The client valued how articles are presented and how easily they can be searched, so it was rebuilt on Docusaurus 3.9 — not the default choice for a brand website, but the right one for an editorial platform whose long-term value lives in its market research, opinion pieces, founder stories, and event archives. Two original research reports have been published through it — FemTech Market Map for Greater China (2025-05) and the FemmeHealth Ventures Alliance partnership announcement (2025-06) — both functioning as lead-generation artefacts and thought-leadership positioning in Chinese and international markets.

**My role.** I am Chief Technology Officer, hired 2025-03 by founder Zhu Yihan (hire date is a career fact, not repo-verifiable), with full ownership of every digital surface the organisation operates. I hold end-to-end authority over architecture, vendor choice, deployment infrastructure, content-management workflow, application and subscription pipelines, and the live infrastructure for Shanghai Summit 2026.

I wrote the entire Drizzle schema, every migration, all 16 Cloudflare Pages Functions, every email template (HTML + plain-text twins, brand-coloured, XSS-defended), the admin dashboard, the summit application forms, the Shanghai Summit 10-section homepage plus sub-pages and gated agenda, the Notion form integrations, the bilingual EN / 简体中文 routing and content layer, the Gemini chatbot, the earth-flyline global-network visualisation, and the image-performance pass. I operate the production Cloudflare Pages deployment and make every speaker / sponsor / agenda update directly on main, reporting to founder Zhu Yihan and collaborating with the 2-10-person core team on editorial calendar, summit programming, and ecosystem partnerships.

### Eatropolis Website

Solo-built freelance commission (signed 4 May 2026 agreement with Chow Luck Club Ltd; PM Armand Bentigan) for the official `eatropolis.co.nz` event website — Auckland's one-day culinary festival on **2026-10-10 at Shed 10, Queens Wharf, Tāmaki Makaurau**, featuring **30+ award-winning chefs**. Production-grade in the literal contract sense: a nine-day contracted build with two-phase public reveal schedule (Phase 1 teaser 2026-05-22, Phase 2 full site 2026-06-05), engineered to handle **1,000 concurrent visitors** under k6 load testing per contract, hardened for the **NZ Government Web Accessibility Standard 1.2 (WCAG 2.2 AA)** with **Tātaki Auckland Unlimited (TAU)** review gates, deployed to **Cloudflare Workers via OpenNext** (the official 2026 Next.js-on-Cloudflare path, not the legacy Pages adapter), with Resend (DKIM/SPF/DMARC live, mail-tester 10/10), streaming OpenAI chat + Whisper + TTS gated behind Cloudflare Turnstile + KV per-IP rate-limit, GA4 + CF Web Analytics behind a NZ Privacy Act 2020-compliant cookie banner, and a **GitHub- as-CMS** content workflow with one-click `✏️` Web-Editor links so the non-technical client edits MDX + JSON directly in the browser.
