The live public website for Eatropolis — Auckland's one-day culinary festival on 10 October 2026 at Shed 10, featuring 30+ award-winning chefs — solo-built under a signed freelance contract with Chow Luck Club Ltd. It runs on Next.js and Cloudflare's edge network, meets the NZ Government's WCAG 2.2 AA accessibility standard, and includes a voice-enabled AI guide that answers visitor questions about dishes, tickets, and getting there. It launched publicly in June 2026 after passing a 1,000-visitor load test with zero errors, and the non-technical client now edits all site content themselves.

**Impact.** The live site for Eatropolis, Auckland's official one-day culinary festival — 30+ award-winning chefs at Shed 10 on 10 Oct 2026. Commissioned work, reviewed by the council's development agency: WCAG 2.2 AA, a voice-enabled AI event guide, a 1,000-visitor load test, zero errors.

**Problem.** Auckland-based Chow Luck Club Ltd — producer of the Eatropolis culinary festival, supported by Tātaki Auckland Unlimited on behalf of Auckland Council Events — needed a real, production-grade public website for its one-day festival on 2026-10-10 at Shed 10, Queens Wharf, Auckland, featuring 30+ award-winning chefs. The brief, set in a signed 4 May 2026 commercial agreement, called for a custom-designed site at eatropolis.co.nz released in two visibility phases (a teaser landing first, then the full site), conformance to the NZ Government Web Accessibility Standard 1.2 (WCAG 2.2 Level AA) with Tātaki Auckland Unlimited review gates before each launch, load-testing to 1,000 concurrent visitors, strong mobile performance, SEO plus AI-crawler discoverability, full contact and enquiry forms with branded email, an AI event assistant, privacy-compliant analytics, and — critically — a way for the non-technical client to edit every word on the site themselves after handoff. All delivered solo by one freelance developer in a nine-day contracted build, with three months of post-launch maintenance included.

**Audience.** Three concentric audiences. Festival-goers — the public, arriving from search, social, and partner sites; mobile-first; with traffic spikes around ticket release and event day. The Eatropolis ecosystem — 30+ culinary partners and their award-winning dishes, plus multi-tier sponsors (Principal / Al Fresco / Associate / Community), the ticketing partner, and media — each with pages on the site they review before launch. The Chow Luck Club team and Tātaki Auckland Unlimited reviewers — the non-developer client signatory Bee Keng Koh, day-to-day project manager Armand Bentigan, and the review committee that gates each public launch on accessibility and content. The content-editing workflow assumes none of these reviewers will ever open a terminal: every editable field is reachable through a single ✏️ link into GitHub's browser-based editor. The client took this up during the teaser phase (19 May – 2 June 2026), making a dozen of their own content edits this way before the full launch.

**Product logic.** The product is one website with a two-phase visibility schedule, not two separate builds. The same Cloudflare edge worker serves both phases; what changes is which pages are publicly reachable.

Phase 1 (teaser): only the /coming-soon page is public — a "Something Big is Cooking" teaser with partner attribution, key event facts, and a newsletter sign-up connected to the email service. Everything else sits behind a Cloudflare access lockdown, with a narrow bypass rule publishing just the handful of paths the teaser needs.

Phase 2 (full site, live since 2026-06-05): the lockdown was lifted on launch morning and the full site went public in one step, with a single launch-announcement email sent to everyone who had signed up during Phase 1.

The full site spans the marketing pages: Home (a full-screen hero, an autoplay video at launch and a rotating dish-photo slideshow since the client's change of 2026-09-17; scroll-through origin story, restaurant logo carousel, "Your Day at Eatropolis" steps, ticketing block, sponsor wall, final call-to-action); Dishes (a filterable grid of signature plates, several of them 2026 Iconic Auckland Eats Award winners); Culinary Partners (filterable restaurant grid with featured spotlights); Experiences; Event Info (date, time, location, schedule, getting-there guide); Our Partners (four-tier sponsor showcase); Contact (general and partnership enquiry forms); plus legal pages. Tickets are sold off-site through Universe (a Ticketmaster company) — the site links straight out to the Universe checkout rather than hosting its own ticket page.

Three form pipelines, all server-side: General Enquiry, Partnership Enquiry, and Newsletter sign-up. All forms are protected by Cloudflare Turnstile (an anti-spam check that's gentler on users than reCAPTCHA), and all confirmation and notification email flows through hand-authored, brand-styled templates — a visitor acknowledgment plus a full-submission notice to the client for both general and partnership enquiries, a newsletter welcome, a one-click unsubscribe confirmation, and the launch announcement.

The AI event assistant is a floating chat widget that streams answers from an OpenAI model, with voice input (speech-to-text) and voice reply (text-to-speech). It's pre-loaded with the event's own content — dates, location, tickets, partners, FAQs, transport — compiled at build time, so it can't invent prices, dates, or partner names; every answer is grounded in the same content the client edits. It's rate-limited per visitor with Cloudflare's key-value store plus a Turnstile pre-check. The AI layer is written behind a single provider abstraction, so the whole chat stack can switch from OpenAI to Anthropic Claude in one line.

The content layer is the project's deliberate design call. The brief asked for a "CMS structure"; the solution is GitHub-as-CMS through the browser editor, deliberately rejecting spreadsheets and licensed CMS products (Sanity, Strapi, Payload, Contentful) to avoid adding third-party dependencies. Every editable field has a direct ✏️ link that opens GitHub's web editor; the client edits, saves, and the site auto-rebuilds in a few minutes. At handoff the content was 40 MDX files (dishes, partners, FAQs, sponsors — each with schema-validated frontmatter) plus 16 JSON files for page copy, all type-checked at build time.

**Business logic.** This is a commercial freelance commission — not a personal or passion project. Delivery is anchored to a signed contract with a three-stage schedule, each stage tied to a developer deliverable rather than to reviewer sign-off, so review delays don't stall progress.

Scope discipline is the second design axis. The contract enumerates exactly what's in scope (the site, design system, animation layer, three forms, one launch broadcast, the AI widget, SEO plus AI-crawler discoverability, performance and load testing and security hardening, analytics, WCAG 2.2 AA conformance, Cloudflare hosting, initial content seeding, handoff and training, and three months of maintenance). Everything outside that — extra pages, custom ticketing, multilingual versions, a blog, ongoing email campaigns, a formal third-party accessibility audit, future-year event refreshes, deep CRM work — sits under separately-quoted add-ons or hourly engagement after the maintenance window ends. The warranty is capped at that same window. I wrote the contract myself (in Typst, compiled to PDF), so the scope discipline is by design: a nine-day contracted solo build inside a clearly bounded commercial perimeter that doesn't bleed into future event years.

The client side is worth surfacing too. Chow Luck Club Ltd runs the festival as a private event business; Tātaki Auckland Unlimited (Auckland Council's culture, business, and economic-development arm) supports it on behalf of Auckland Council Events. That relationship is why the contract is explicit about WCAG 2.2 AA conformance with review gates — Tātaki Auckland Unlimited has its own public-sector accessibility obligations. The contract draws a clean line between what the website technically conforms to (automated audits, manual checks, a written conformance statement — in scope) and the formal third-party audit and self-assessment that Tātaki Auckland Unlimited files as an organisation (out of scope).

**Technical approach.** Stack: Next.js 16.2.5 (App Router, React Server Components) with React 19.2, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS 4 (design tokens consumed as CSS custom properties), deployed to Cloudflare Workers via @opennextjs/cloudflare — the current official path now that the Pages adapter is legacy. The choice is contract-driven: the client owns the Cloudflare account, and the whole stack (hosting, DNS, anti-spam, email routing, analytics, access control) runs there, with the worker moved to Cloudflare's Workers Standard plan (2026-05-09) once the free tier's limits blocked the build: its bundle-size ceiling stopped the database-and-email deploy, and its per-request CPU limit stood in the way of the 1,000-visitor load profile.

Data layer: Drizzle ORM against a Neon serverless Postgres database, with the schema split into three domain modules (chat / email / forms, re-exported from one index) behind four repository modules for type-safe query boundaries. Persistence is a full email-lifecycle audit: form submission → send attempt (with idempotency keys) → delivery/open/bounce/complaint webhook events. End-to-end newsletter round-trip was verified at 5.96 seconds from form submit to Gmail delivery confirmation.

Content layer: MDX for long-form editorial content plus Zod schemas that validate both frontmatter and page-copy JSON at build time. A prebuild step compiles every content file into a typed manifest that powers the AI assistant's knowledge — so the AI knows every dish, partner, and FAQ without any runtime database reads.

Email: Resend with 7 hand-authored, brand-styled email templates. The domain has SPF, DKIM, and DMARC live, with a DMARC dashboard for ongoing monitoring; mail-tester scores 10/10. Inbound webhook signatures are verified, and webhook traffic is carved out of the pre-launch lockdown with a dedicated bypass rule.

AI: the Vercel AI SDK behind a one-file provider abstraction (lib/ai-provider.ts), currently on an OpenAI model for streaming chat, plus speech-to-text for voice input and text-to-speech for voice reply. All three paths are gated by (1) a Turnstile pre-check, (2) a per-visitor rate limit in Cloudflare's key-value store, and (3) the build-time content manifest as grounding, so the assistant can't fabricate facts.

Tickets: sold off-site through Universe (a Ticketmaster company); the site links straight to the Universe checkout with UTM-tagged outbound links so the client can attribute ticket traffic. (An earlier on-site Ticketmaster Discovery API integration was removed once the festival moved to Universe.)

Analytics and consent: Cloudflare Web Analytics (privacy-friendly, cookie-free) plus Google Analytics 4 with configured conversion events, both loaded in manual snippet mode behind a NZ Privacy Act 2020 cookie-consent banner — nothing tracks until the visitor accepts. GA4 was later moved to Consent Mode v2 so real, consented traffic is measured correctly.

Performance: contract target of Lighthouse mobile ≥ 90 across categories, pursued by trimming font weights, lazy-mounting the AI assistant, and deferring hero-video sources; images run through a custom AVIF/WebP optimisation pipeline, because OpenNext on Workers does not run Next's image optimiser. Mobile Performance on the dishes page went from 71 to 84; the home page, carrying the client's full-screen autoplay video, stayed below target, and dropping the video on phones was left as the client's design call (he replaced it with a photo slideshow in September 2026). Accessibility, SEO, and best-practices scores land at or above 90 on the measured routes.

Load testing: a k6 profile to 1,000 concurrent visitors was run against the live site over five minutes (113,320 requests) with a 0.00% error rate — a clean pass on the contract's under-1% error threshold.

Accessibility: automated and manual gates. The automated suite is 39/39 axe-core Playwright tests passing across the accessibility, mobile-nav, and target-size specs. The manual layer covers keyboard-only navigation, focus visibility, heading hierarchy, alt text, semantic HTML, and screen-reader spot-checks, including a standards-based keyboard pattern for the nav dropdown menu. One brand-colour contrast issue (a harbour-blue at 4.13:1, below the 4.5:1 minimum for normal text) was fixed by adding a darker variant for text use and keeping the saturated blue in decorative, non-text roles only. A written WCAG 2.2 AA conformance statement was delivered at handoff.

Pre-launch lockdown: before launch, all routes sat behind Cloudflare Zero Trust Access, with allowlisted reviewers signing in via email one-time-passcode and four path-scoped bypass applications exposing what had to stay public (the teaser and its newsletter path, the email webhook, the legal pages, the hero video). On 2026-06-05 the lockdown was opened and the full site went public.

Deploy pipeline: GitHub Actions on every push to main (Linux only — the OpenNext build chain has Windows incompatibilities), running install → lint → build → deploy in roughly 55–70 seconds end-to-end.

**Outcomes.** Live and public at eatropolis.co.nz since 2026-06-05. The pre-launch access lockdown was opened on launch morning and the full site went public in one step, with a single launch-announcement email sent to every Phase 1 newsletter subscriber. The newsletter pipeline was verified end-to-end (form → database rows → email service → Gmail delivery webhook) in 5.96 seconds.

The 1,000-visitor k6 load test passed with a 0.00% error rate over 113,320 requests in five minutes (the response-time percentile ran above target, attributable to a single local test runner rather than server errors). Lighthouse accessibility, SEO, and best-practices scores meet or exceed 90 on the measured routes; mail-tester scores 10/10.

The GitHub-as-CMS workflow was proven before launch: during the teaser phase (19 May – 2 June 2026), the non-technical client independently made a dozen content edits — home page, coming-soon, tickets, announcement copy — through the browser editor, exactly as the workflow intended.

The handover held. On the eve of launch I trained the client's creative producer, Armand Bentigan, in a recorded session to make changes with an AI coding agent: pull, change and check locally, push. He has maintained the site himself since, through the festival on 10 October 2026: the partner lineup, a sponsor carousel, and a dish-photo slideshow that replaced the home-page hero video. Ahead of the festival I also showed him how to draft and bulk-send the event invitations through the site's own email service the same way.

The build also produced handoff documents most freelance projects skip: a ticketing setup guide, a WCAG conformance statement, a content-editing guide, a content inventory, a non-developer handoff guide, and a running decision log with architecture diagrams. Post-launch maintenance covered analytics hardening (adopting GA4 Consent Mode v2, and root-causing zero Cloudflare-analytics data to visitor-side tracker blocking rather than a code defect) and ongoing content additions, including new Iconic Auckland Eats Award-winning dishes.

**My role.** Sole freelance developer under a signed 4 May 2026 agreement between Chan Meng (Auckland-based) and Bee Keng Koh for and on behalf of Chow Luck Club Ltd, with Armand Bentigan as day-to-day project manager. Three-stage delivery schedule, each stage anchored to a developer deliverable rather than reviewer approval. The later commits there are the client's: a dozen browser-editor content edits during the teaser phase, and, since the handover, Armand Bentigan's own maintenance with an AI coding agent after the training session and maintenance guides I gave him; that work is his, not mine. The entire Cloudflare account is the client's, with my login added as an administrator — all infrastructure is client-owned, so end-of-maintenance handoff is a credential rotation rather than an account transfer.

End-to-end ownership covered: drafting the contract myself (in Typst, compiled to PDF); product architecture; the marketing-site information architecture and design system (brand hierarchy Black / Red / White, harbour blue as a subtle accent per the accessibility recalibration); the full Cloudflare Workers + OpenNext deploy pipeline with GitHub Actions auto-deploy; the Zero Trust access rules for the pre-launch and bypass schedule; the Drizzle + Neon persistence layer; the API routes for newsletter, contact and partnership forms, and the streaming chat + voice + feedback endpoints; the 7 brand-styled email templates; the AI assistant with its build-time content manifest; the Universe ticketing link-out; the analytics-plus-consent setup; the WCAG 2.2 AA conformance pass (39/39 axe-core tests plus manual verification); the 1,000-visitor k6 load-test profile; the GitHub-as-CMS workflow with per-field ✏️ editor links; the handoff document package plus the running decision log; and the handover training. Day-to-day coordination ran over WhatsApp with the project manager and formal documents over email with the client signatory.

### GAVIGO IRE

Founding-engineer MVP for GAVIGO Inc. (Delaware C-Corp) — the 'Instant Reality Exchange' activation and execution layer: an AI orchestrator keeps the next game in a TikTok-style feed on standby and activates it as the viewer arrives, on Kubernetes, with no app-store install; shipped to production and migrated DOKS→GKE

- URL: https://ire.gavigo.com/
- Started: October 2025
- Status: production
- For: GAVIGO Inc.
- Tech stack: Go, gorilla/websocket, Kubernetes, DigitalOcean DOKS (initial), Google Kubernetes Engine (post-migration), client-go (K8s API), Artifact Registry, GCE Ingress + Global HTTP(S) LB, React 18, Vite, React Native, Expo 54, WebSocket, Redis 7, PostgreSQL 16, Supabase, gpt-5.4-mini
- Application-Level Reduction: 78% (controlled proof-stage measurement: same workload and output, less application-level work) Not a production SLA.
- Controlled Startup Path Comparison: 4.45s → 1.00s (controlled proof-stage measurement) Not a production SLA.
- Preserved AI State Restore: ~140ms (preserved AI state restored into a fresh process; controlled proof-stage measurement) Not a production SLA.
- Measurement boundary: Real, controlled application-level measurements, not a production SLA or a complete end-to-end activation time
- Cloud platforms: DigitalOcean DOKS → Google Cloud GKE
- Cross-cloud cutover: ~30 min downtime (2026-03-11)
- Games: 23 across 4 studios (+2 ML/compute workloads)
- Related projects: GAVIGO Website

GAVIGO IRE is the founding-engineer MVP for GAVIGO Inc., a Delaware startup (founder & CEO Saba Gecgil) building a way past the app-install step: scroll a phone feed and a game plays right in the scroll, with no app-store install. Behind the feed, an AI orchestrator watches every scroll, keeps the next game on standby on a Kubernetes cluster and activates it as the viewer arrives; scroll back and the session is reattached rather than rebuilt. Built as the founding-engineer platform — the activation and AI-orchestration systems behind that feed — deployed to production on Google Cloud after a live migration from DigitalOcean. In GAVIGO's proof stage the work measured a 78% application-level reduction in startup work, a controlled startup path cut from 4.45 s to 1.00 s, and about 140 ms to restore preserved AI state: controlled application-level measurements, not a production SLA or a complete end-to-end activation time.

**Impact.** Founding-engineer build for GAVIGO, a Delaware startup: scroll a phone feed and a game plays right in the scroll, with no app-store install. An AI orchestrator on Kubernetes keeps the next game on standby and activates it as you arrive; scroll back and the session is reattached.

**Problem.** The native-app paradigm puts a friction tax on every interactive digital experience: discover an app → app-store landing page → install → onboard → first interaction. By the time the user reaches the thing they actually wanted, the moment has passed. For games, video, and AI experiences — where the wait between intent and interaction costs engagement — the install gap is the single largest leak in the funnel. GAVIGO's thesis, in its own marketing language: we are building the "Post-App World," eliminating the friction between user intent and digital experience through proprietary "Instant Reality Switching" technology.

**Audience.** Two surfaces run in production today. **Consumer surface**: end users on ire.gavigo.com and the mobile build scroll a TikTok-style vertical feed of 23 self-hosted games across four in-house studios (Arcade Zone, Puzzle Lab, Reflex Arena, ML Lab) plus a bundled video catalog — every game served from one always-warm pod, no external game-portal iframes. **Investor / operator surface**: the React dashboard at the same domain shows the orchestrator's AI decisions, the container state machine (COLD → PREPARING → READY → ACTIVE → REUSABLE), warm-pool budget, activation-quality metrics, and a side-by-side iframe of the mobile app — purpose-built for live demos to investors and partner evaluators. A Phase 9 audience-segmentation feature filters visibility per role (public / investor / operator presets) at WebSocket broadcast time, and a Phase 11 partner-pilot layer adds per-session telemetry and an operator-gated proof report for named-partner trials. The ultimate addressable surface is any market where the wait between intent and interaction costs engagement — mobile games, short-form video, AI chat, generative content.

**Product logic.** A user scrolls a vertical feed; the orchestrator watches focus events stream over a WebSocket hub, scores each candidate piece of content on three weighted signals (personal attention 0.4, global attention 0.4, trend / virality 0.2), and when the combined score crosses a 0.6 threshold, fires one of seven AI triggers — Cross-Domain, Swarm Boost, Proactive Warm, Mode Change, Resource Throttle, Initial Warm, Lookahead Warm (plus a manual demo control) — each of which patches Kubernetes deployment replicas through the K8s client-go API to scale a game container to READY before the user taps.

When the user arrives, the experience has already been prepared — either served from a single always-warm shared game-server pod or restored from the Reusable pool of recently-active containers. (The orchestrator's own path timings are engineering telemetry, not public performance figures, and are not quoted here.) State survives across scrolls via a postMessage protocol on web and MMKV storage on native; both reconcile against Redis as a single source of truth through the Activation Spine: a five-state container lifecycle (COLD → PREPARING → READY → ACTIVE → REUSABLE) with atomic transitions, recorded as a nine-phase activation timeline in which restore is one path. When mobile gaming meets the install gap, the GAVIGO answer is to remove the install step.

**Business logic.** GAVIGO Inc. is a Delaware-incorporated C-Corp, founder Saba Gecgil. The product wedge is mobile gaming (public tagline: "Skip the Store. Start the Play") — but the underlying activation engine is platform-shaped: any interactive content category where the install gap or cold-start latency is the dominant funnel leak. The defensibility is architectural, not feature-level: a proprietary Activation Spine plus a measured restore path is the kind of capability that compounds rather than decays. GAVIGO frames its architecture publicly as "Two Pillars": the Technology Platform (CTO-led foundation) and the Intelligence Layer (the autonomous predictive engine that makes Instant Reality possible). I own the Intelligence Layer side of that architecture under the title Founding Principal Engineer, Activation, Execution & AI Systems.

**Technical approach.** The orchestrator is a single Go binary (gorilla/websocket hub + Scorer + Rules Engine + K8s client-go patcher) deployed to a managed Kubernetes cluster. Companion pods: a React + Vite dashboard, a React Native / Expo mobile-web build served from an nginx pod, a single always-warm nginx game-server pod baking the 25-entry catalog (23 web games across four studios plus 2 ML/compute workloads) so no game needs a cold start of its own, an AI-service pod (Node + Express calling OpenAI `gpt-5.4-mini`, with a simulated-response fallback when no key is set) that scales 0→1, Redis 7 (allkeys-LRU eviction, 400 MB budget) for warm-pool state and activation metrics, and optional PostgreSQL 16 / Supabase for social data.

**Cross-cloud production experience: DigitalOcean and Google Cloud.** The platform shipped first on **DigitalOcean Kubernetes (DOKS) in Singapore (sgp1)** — DO Container Registry, REGIONAL LoadBalancer, Let's Encrypt with manual certbot renewal — chosen for cost-efficient prototype-to-production iteration. When GAVIGO's Google Cloud partnership came into effect, I led the full migration to **GKE Standard Zonal in Belgium (europe-west1-b)** on 2026-03-11: Artifact Registry replacing DO Container Registry, GCE Ingress + Global HTTP(S) LB with Google-managed certs (auto-renewal replacing 80-day certbot toil), a FrontendConfig HTTPS redirect, a BackendConfig `timeoutSec: 86400` to keep activation WebSocket sessions alive, service types reshaped from LoadBalancer-per-frontend to ClusterIP-behind-Ingress, and a GCP global static IP. All five deployments migrated with `strategy: Recreate` to avoid CPU deadlock on single-node clusters; total downtime was **~30 minutes**. GCP remains the only production cloud; a separate AWS account (with a live GPU **spot** quota) runs nothing in production and is reserved for short, torn-down inference/runtime experiments.

Hard problems solved. **A restore path** through a deterministic five-state Activation Spine with atomic Redis transitions and phase-by-phase timestamps that prove the decision → K8s patch → client-observation chain. **Warm-pool LRU without cascade eviction** via ProtectSlot reservations. **Cross-platform state sync** between MMKV (native), localStorage / postMessage (web), and Redis (server) with a typed protocol bridging iframe ↔ WebView. **Async K8s coordination with real-time telemetry** — EndpointSlice / Pod-status watches feed `activation_ready` broadcasts with millisecond-precision timestamps. **Audience-aware broadcast filtering** (Phase 9) so public / investor / operator viewers each see a different slice of the catalog. **Partner-pilot telemetry and CI discipline** (Phase 11): per-session records joining WebSocket session ↔ user ↔ device ↔ activation count, typed failure classes, time-to-playable p50/p95, an operator-gated proof report, and the project's first CI pipeline (`go build/vet/test -race`, `vite build`, `tsc`). Every activation path is benchmarked on real Kubernetes rather than asserted.

**Outcomes.** Production-deployed at ire.gavigo.com. First shipped on DigitalOcean DOKS (Singapore), then migrated to Google Cloud GKE (Belgium) on 2026-03-11 in a clean ~30-minute cutover when GAVIGO's Google Cloud partnership came into effect — production-grade expertise demonstrated on both clouds. Measured in GAVIGO's proof stage, under controlled conditions: a 78% application-level reduction in startup work, a controlled startup path cut from 4.45 s to 1.00 s, and about 140 ms to restore preserved AI state into a fresh process. These are controlled application-level measurements, not a production SLA or a complete end-to-end activation time: infrastructure work such as scheduling, container creation, networking and readiness also affects the full path. Catalog: 23 self-hosted games across four studios plus 2 ML/compute workloads and a 197-video bundle. Phase 9 audience-segmentation and Phase 11 partner-pilot telemetry are live. Role formalized over three contract iterations (Original Oct 17 2025; Amended Feb 9 2026; Second Amended Apr 16 2026), each escalating recognition of my technical ownership.

**Programmes and press.** GAVIGO takes part in the **NVIDIA Inception Program** and the **Google for Startups Cloud Program** (the arrangement under which the GCP migration of March 11 was done), and was profiled by tech-business press (feedvoice.com, 2026-02-10). These are programme participation and press coverage, not endorsements or product validation.

**My role.** Founding Principal Engineer, Activation, Execution & AI Systems (prior: Core Engineer), reporting to founder & CEO Saba Gecgil. Joined Oct 17 2025 and stepped down Sep 1 2026; the final title and scope were formalized by the Second Amended and Restated Consulting Agreement effective Apr 16 2026.

The contract defined a "Protected Technical Domain" that anchored my role: activation systems, activation flow and execution behavior, the activation-economics proof path, AI-assisted orchestration and execution-control systems, restore and reuse boundary work, heavier-workload validation and transition work, and the core activation, execution, and AI-enabled systems architecture of GAVIGO's interactive workload platform — plus the natural forward extension of that area as the system evolves. Recognized in the contract record as "a core long-term technical builder of the Company's interactive workload platform" with founder-level equity participation.

### She Sharp

Production platform that moved a volunteer-run NZ women-in-STEM charity (charitable trust CC57025, 96+ events since 2014) off Webflow and spreadsheets onto a member engine it owns. GPT-4o-mini AI mentor matching (5-weight scoring + admin review), three role-permissioned dashboards (mentor / mentee / admin), Stripe billing, and a custom Slack ecosystem (event-collector bot, weekly mentorship-stats digest, NZ government funding crawler, Claude `sync-event-from-slack` skill) that turns manual event publishing into a reviewable one-command change.

- URL: https://www.shesharp.org.nz/
- Started: July 2025
- Status: production
- For: She Sharp
- Tech stack: Next.js 15.6 canary (App Router, Turbopack dev), React 19.1.2, TypeScript 5.8, Drizzle ORM 0.43, Neon Postgres (serverless pool), NextAuth 5 beta (Google + GitHub OAuth + bcrypt credentials), @auth/drizzle-adapter, OpenAI GPT-4o-mini (temp 0.3, max_tokens 1000, JSON-object response_format), Upstash Redis (AI match cache + queue), Stripe 20 (Customer Portal for self-service membership management), @slack/web-api (event-collector + interactive handlers), @octokit/rest (Slack-skill auto-commits), Claude agent skill: sync-event-from-slack, Resend (transactional email), Vercel Blob (uploads; replaced Cloudinary on 2026-09-06), Tailwind CSS 4.1, shadcn/ui + Radix UI (20+ primitives), @dnd-kit (kanban-style admin workflows), Recharts 3 + @number-flow/react (dashboard analytics), Framer Motion + Lenis (landing-page polish), Three.js + OGL (hero shader effects), Zod 3 (validation everywhere — Slack-bot LLM output gating, form schemas), React Hook Form + @hookform/resolvers, Vercel Edge Network + Vercel Cron
- Merged pull requests: 251
- Build window: 2025-07-22 → 2026-09-01 (13.3 months active)
- API routes: 84 (app/api/**/route.ts)
- Pages: 63 (app/**/page.tsx)
- Components: 198 (components/**/*.tsx)
- TypeScript: 180,914 lines across 818 files
- Database schema: 39 pgTables, 33 pgEnums
- SQL migrations: 32 (0000_soft_the_anarchist → 0033_crazy_morg)
- Lib modules: matching, slack-bot, stripe, funding, programmes, recruitment, invitations, mentorship, email, auth, db (11 namespaced)
- Cron jobs: 3 scheduled in vercel.json at handover (weekly-mentorship-stats, weekly-funding-crawl, event-feedback-digest); the process-queue route exists but was never scheduled
- Funding crawler sources: 6 NZ government feeds (beehive RSS, data.govt CKAN, GETS RSS, MBIE HTML, Treasury RSS, women.govt HTML)
- AI matching weights: MBTI 15% + Skill 35% + Goal 30% + Industry 10% + Logistics 10%
- AI matching score range: 0-100 overall + 5 per-dimension subscores + confidence (high/medium/low)
- AI retry policy: 3 attempts with exponential backoff (1s × 2^n), batch concurrency 5, 100ms inter-batch delay
- Distinct event registrants: 2,919 (on record, per the transformation record's published-vs-recorded table)
- Sponsors on logo wall: 39
- Events since 2014: 96+
- Migration crawler assets: 1,748 images / 707 MB / 11 JSON files / 85 events + 50 Humanitix tickets + 15 podcasts + 121 photo galleries + 7 press articles + 118 pages
- Related projects: HER WAKA, Aotearoa AI Hackathon 2026, Touch the World, Talk to Code

Member platform I led the build of for She Sharp, a volunteer-run New Zealand women-in-STEM charity (a registered charitable trust). It handles member sign-ups and billing, runs the events calendar, and matches mentors with mentees using AI scoring backed by a human reviewer, replacing a Webflow site and spreadsheets the team had outgrown. Mentorship applications have been paused by the charity since June 2026, reversibly; the matching code stays in place for re-opening.

**Impact.** The digital and AI-native transformation of a volunteer-run New Zealand women-in-STEM charity: moved off rented software onto infrastructure it owns, with event setup, newsletters, posters, video and the mailing list rewritten as 11 agent skills a non-engineer can run.

**Problem.** She Sharp is a volunteer-run New Zealand women-in-STEM nonprofit — a registered charitable trust founded by Dr Mahsa Mohaghegh (McCauley), AI/NLP researcher and Head of Computer and Information Sciences at AUT, after she experienced first-hand the gap of being part of the 20% minority of women in technology. It has run 96+ events since 2014, with 2,919 distinct people registered for them on record. The original website was a Webflow build, and Webflow had become the bottleneck: the capabilities the mission required — membership tiers, mentor / mentee / admin role permissions, AI-driven mentor matching, Stripe billing, Slack-integrated operations, automated event management, recruitment pipelines, audit logging — are precisely what no drag-and-drop site builder can express. The volunteer team was running its community through spreadsheets, Slack threads, and manual outreach. She Sharp needed a real platform.

**Audience.** Active members of the She Sharp community: women in technology at every career stage, from undergraduate students considering STEM majors through senior engineers serving as mentors. The platform supports three role-permissioned dashboards (mentor, mentee, admin) plus dual-role compatibility — a mid-career engineer can simultaneously mentor juniors and be mentored by a senior, without special-cased data modelling. Additional audiences served on adjacent surfaces: Her Waka programme participants (women re-entering the workforce, served by the dedicated MSD-funded teaching site at herwaka.shesharp.org.nz), volunteer and ambassador candidates (screened through the AI recruitment pipeline), sponsors (39 on the logo wall; sponsor packages tied to event visibility and member access), and She Sharp's operational team (Slack-integrated workflows).

**Product logic.** The new platform replaces the old Webflow site with a real member system anchored on three coexisting dashboards. A user signs up via email/password (bcrypt) or OAuth (Google + GitHub), then independently activates any combination of mentor, mentee, or admin roles — duality is the **schema-level design principle**, not a special case. The `user_roles` table has one row per (user, role_type) tuple with its own `is_active`, `verified_at`, and `activation_step` columns, so a mid-career engineer can simultaneously mentor juniors and be mentored by a senior with zero special-cased data modelling. The dashboard layer (`(dashboard)/dashboard/{mentor-profile,mentee-profile, mentorship,meetings,admin,account}`) reads the active-roles set and composes role-specific cards into a single unified view.

**The headline feature is the AI mentor-mentee matching engine**, implemented as a two-stage pipeline in `lib/matching/`. Stage one is a rule-based pre-filter that rapidly scores candidate pairs on basic compatibility (skill set intersection, industry overlap, location/ meeting-format compatibility). Stage two passes promising pairs to GPT-4o-mini at `temperature: 0.3`, `max_tokens: 1000`, with `response_format: { type: 'json_object' }`, against an explicit scoring rubric defined in `lib/matching/prompts.ts`:

  - **MBTI Compatibility — 15%** (cognitive function complementarity, communication style)
  - **Skill Alignment — 35%** (mentor's expert skills vs mentee's learning goals, expertise depth vs learning breadth)
  - **Goal Alignment — 30%** (career trajectory compatibility, mentor's ability to guide toward stated goals, shared values)
  - **Industry Match — 10%** (direct + adjacent + transferable industry knowledge)
  - **Logistics — 10%** (meeting format, location proximity, time availability)

Each call returns a 0-100 overall + per-dimension subscores + natural-language explanation + recommendation + confidence (high / medium / low) + matchingFactors (strengths / challenges / growthOpportunities), Zod-validated against `AIMatchResponseSchema` before persistence. **Three production-hardness layers wrap the OpenAI call**: (1) **Upstash Redis cache** keyed by mentor:mentee pair so repeat scoring is free; (2) **exponential-backoff retries** (3 attempts, 1000ms × 2^attempt, with rate-limit/timeout classification); (3) a **deterministic rule-based fallback** with the same weighted formula that activates when OpenAI is unavailable, explicitly marking `confidenceLevel: 'low'` and `recommendation: 'manual review'` so admins know to look closer. Batch processing caps at 5 concurrent calls with 100ms inter-batch delay to respect API limits.

Matches above threshold surface to admin (`/api/admin/matching`) for human approval before pairing — conservative human-in-the-loop automation, not speculative auto-pairing. A **mentee matching queue** (`lib/matching/queue-service.ts`) holds unmatched mentees in priority order when mentor capacity is full; its re-evaluation route (`/api/cron/process-queue`) exists but was never added to the production cron schedule, so re-evaluation runs when an admin acts. Since 2026-06-19 the charity has paused mentorship applications, reversibly, behind a coming-soon page. Meetings are typed (intro / regular / milestone / final), tracked with action items (JSONB), notes, feedback, and 1-5 ratings.

**The Stripe-integrated membership flow has a novel activation architecture**: it doesn't instantly grant access. The architecture is **form → checkout → invitation code → activation**. A prospective mentee fills the public mentee form (`/api/forms/mentee/public`), which creates a `mentee_form_submissions` row. They get redirected to Stripe Checkout. On `checkout.session.completed` webhook, the system creates a `membership_purchases` record AND generates a unique `invitation_code` (`createPaymentInvitationCode`) which is emailed via Resend. The user must redeem the code to activate their account, guaranteeing email ↔ payment ↔ account linkage and preventing orphaned accounts. Self-service via Stripe Customer Portal. Webhook signature verification on every event. Membership lifecycle transitions update `user_memberships` + `activity_logs` atomically.

The platform also runs She Sharp's events infrastructure (workshops, training, networking, social, THRIVE programmes — online, in-person, or hybrid, with capacity, waitlist, and QR check-in via `/api/qr`), three membership tiers, a tiered resource library with download access control + access logs, transactional email via Resend, AI-screened volunteer recruitment (`lib/recruitment/ ai-screening.ts` against `/api/admin/recruitment/[id]/ai-screen`), sponsor inquiries with inline forms, and comprehensive audit logging (JSONB diffs via `deep-diff` on every admin action).

**A custom Slack ecosystem is deeply integrated** through three coordinated surfaces. (1) **Read-only event-collector bot** with scoped tokens (`channels:history`, `channels:read`, `groups:history`, `groups:read`, `files:read`, `users:read`, `pins:read`, `bookmarks:read`) — no destructive scopes by design. (2) **Three scheduled Vercel Cron jobs**: `weekly-mentorship-stats` posts engagement digest to `#mentorships` (recently hardened to survive cold Neon connection pools), `weekly-funding-crawl` runs the NZ government funding crawler over **6 official sources** (Beehive RSS, data.govt CKAN, GETS RSS, MBIE HTML, Treasury RSS, women.govt HTML) with dedup + relevance scoring + keyword filtering, posting a curated Slack digest, and the daily `event-feedback-digest` collects event feedback for the team. (3) **Interactive Slack event handlers** at `/api/slack/events` and `/api/slack/events/interactive` for in-Slack workflows.

**The most distinctive Slack-side piece** is a Claude agent skill named `sync-event-from-slack` living at `.claude/skills/sync-event-from-slack/`. It automates the previously- manual work of turning a Slack event channel into a published event page: it reads channel messages, thread replies, pinned items, bookmarks, speaker `.docx` bios (via `mammoth`), cover posters, and speaker headshots; downloads images and renames them per convention; composes a structured `EventV3Schema` JSON entry against a strict Zod schema; runs `verify-image-paths` as a CI gate; and on approval commits to git or opens a PR. **The skill defaults to dry-run** — no file writes, no git, no network side-effects beyond reading Slack — unless the user explicitly says "go ahead and apply". Event publication has gone from hours of manual editing to a single command, with the AI bot's structured output Zod-validated as the last line of defense before any git write.

The events surface now also carries fully data-driven event pages — for example the Aotearoa AI Hackathon Festival 2026 page (hosted by AUT in partnership with She Sharp and the AI Forum NZ), with a judging panel, schedule, prizes, sponsors, and photo galleries composed from a single Zod-validated `EventV3Schema` entry rather than hand-built markup.

**Business logic.** The platform is the operational substrate that lets each channel scale without proportional staff load: dashboards, matching, membership lifecycle, communications, recruitment, and event management are automated. The organisation's ability to grow its programmes with a volunteer team depends directly on this technical capability.

**Technical approach.** Next.js 15.6 canary (App Router, Turbopack dev) + React 19.1.2 + TypeScript 5.8 over Drizzle ORM 0.43 on Neon Postgres (serverless connection pool), authenticated via NextAuth 5 beta with bcrypt credentials and Google + GitHub OAuth (via `@auth/drizzle-adapter`), deployed on Vercel's edge network with documented sub-second TTFB. Tailwind CSS 4.1 + shadcn/ui + Radix UI (20+ primitives) for the UI; Framer Motion + Lenis + Three.js/OGL for landing-page polish; @dnd-kit for admin kanban workflows; Recharts 3 + @number-flow/react for dashboard analytics.

**The schema runs to 33 pgEnums across 39 pgTables** — a deliberate type-safety investment. Membership tiers (free / basic / premium), mentorship-relationship states (pending / active / paused / completed / rejected), meeting types (intro / regular / milestone / final), event types (workshop / networking / training / social / thrive), location types (online / in_person / hybrid), career stages (undergraduate → postgraduate → early_career → mid_career → senior → career_transition), MBTI 16 personality types, recruitment stages, invitation-code redemption states, activity-log action types — every business concept is a typed enum rather than a string column, so invalid states are unrepresentable at the database level. **32 SQL migration files** (0000_soft_the_anarchist → 0033_crazy_morg) applied via a custom safe-migration wrapper with pre-deployment snapshots and rollback SQL generation.

**84 API routes** across `app/api/**/route.ts` covering auth (12 routes including OAuth callbacks, password reset, email verification), admin (24 routes for matching/mentee-mentor reviews/ recruitment/programmes/users/permissions/analytics/zombie-cleanup), mentorship lifecycle (apply / approve / relationships / meetings), events (browse / register / my-registrations / QR check-in), forms (mentee / mentor / volunteer with public-vs-authenticated variants), Stripe (checkout / donate / webhook), Slack (events / interactive), cron (weekly-mentorship-stats / weekly-funding-crawl / event-feedback-digest scheduled; process-queue built, never scheduled), resources (download with access control), notifications, file uploads (CV + profile photo, on Vercel Blob since 2026-09-06). **63 pages, 198 components**, 180,914 lines of TypeScript across 818 files.

**The AI matching engine** combines a deterministic rule-based pre-filter with GPT-4o-mini for high-potential pairs only. The `lib/matching/` namespace has clear separation: `prompts.ts` holds the system rubric and per-pair prompt builder, `openai-service.ts` owns the LLM call with retry/cache/fallback, `cache.ts` interfaces Upstash Redis, `queue-service.ts` manages the FIFO/priority queue for over-capacity scenarios, `service.ts` orchestrates the full match flow, and `types.ts` defines `AIMatchResponseSchema` (Zod) that every LLM output must satisfy. Cost stays predictable because Stage 1 filters out incompatible pairs before they reach the LLM; outputs stay explainable because the rubric is explicit; availability stays high because the rule-based fallback uses the same weighted formula. Admin override is the final gate.

**Slack integration** uses **scoped read-only tokens** by design (`channels:history`, `channels:read`, `groups:history`, `groups:read`, `files:read`, `users:read`, `pins:read`, `bookmarks:read` — never `chat:write` from the collector). The `sync-event-from-slack` agent skill composes existing CLI tools (Slack fetch → image download with rename → docx parse via `mammoth` → JSON validate against `EventV3Schema` Zod → git commit via `@octokit/rest` or local) into a single intent-driven workflow. **Strict Zod validation is the last line of defense before any git write** — an invalid LLM patch is rejected with a Slack- friendly error, never persisted. The `weekly-funding-crawl` cron runs `lib/funding/{fetcher,dedup,scoring,keywords}.ts` over 6 government RSS/HTML sources, scores by relevance keywords, dedups across sources, and posts a curated Slack digest. The recent `weekly-mentorship-stats` hardening (`84f788f`) is a small but revealing detail: Neon's serverless pool can return stale connections to a cold Vercel Cron worker, so the cron now retries once on the specific `ECONNRESET`/`Connection terminated` error class before failing the run.

**File storage on Vercel Blob** (it replaced a Cloudinary account on 2026-09-06, as part of moving every service into accounts the charity owns); **transactional email via Resend** with role-specific templates (mentorship-emails.ts + recruitment-emails.ts + membership confirmation); **payments via Stripe** with Customer Portal for self-service membership management; **audit logging** uses `deep-diff` to capture JSONB before/after on every admin mutation.

The role spans beyond the main platform. Three supporting projects round out the contribution. **she-sharp-crawl** — a Python crawler (BeautifulSoup4, Requests) that migrated content from the old Webflow site: 1,748 images totaling 707 MB across 11 modular JSON files, covering 85 SheSharp events, 50 Humanitix ticketed events (with banner images upgraded 500 px → 1,600 px), 15 podcasts, 121 photo galleries, 7 news / press articles, and 118 site pages. Image deduplication and Wayback Machine fallback for dead links. **her-waka** — the Mintlify-powered teaching site at herwaka.shesharp.org.nz for the MSD-funded Her Waka programme; I authored both the platform and the curriculum (four workshops covering AI & Future of Work, #IAmRemarkable + Vibe Coding, Cybersecurity, Personal Branding, plus 12 self-paced tutorials at five difficulty tiers). **serpdata-api-test** — a professional SEO audit on shesharp.org.nz built on Node 22 native fetch over the SerpData API, running ~20 live Google queries across eight analysis sections (brand visibility, topical keyword rankings, NZ competitor matrix, mobile-vs-desktop gap, cross-market reach, SERP feature inventory) plus a 10-point prioritized recommendations report (e.g., "SheSharp ranks #4 desktop / not in mobile top 10 for 'women in tech New Zealand' — high-priority technical SEO gap").

**Outcomes.** Production-deployed and running She Sharp's full member lifecycle across my 13.3 months on it (first commit 2025-07-22, measured to 2026-09-01) — in active build-out, not maintenance, until I left the charity in September 2026; the platform stays in production as its live site, with mentorship applications paused by the charity since 2026-06-19. The platform now runs She Sharp's membership, mentorship, events, sponsor relationships, volunteer recruitment pipeline, and internal team operations across **84 API routes, 63 pages, 198 components, 32 SQL migrations, 180,914 lines of TypeScript, and an 11-namespace `lib/` library** (matching, slack-bot, stripe, funding, programmes, recruitment, invitations, mentorship, email, auth, db) — the technical infrastructure for an organisation that has run 96+ events since 2014.

The most recent build-out extended the public site into a photo-rich "Editorial" visual system and full event pages — including the Aotearoa AI Hackathon Festival 2026 page (AUT × She Sharp × AI Forum NZ, 7–8 August 2026 at AUT City Campus), assembled from a single Zod-validated event entry. **The Her Waka programme launched in March 2026** with NZ Ministry of Social Development funding, using the dedicated teaching site I built (herwaka.shesharp.org.nz) and the curriculum I authored — 4 workshops + 12 tutorials in 5 tiers. **The SEO audit** identified actionable competitive gaps, notably the desktop/mobile ranking disparity on "women in tech New Zealand." **The migration crawler** enabled a clean cutover from Webflow without losing institutional knowledge. **The Slack-bot + agent-skill pairing** replaced an hours-long manual event-publication workflow with a single dry-run-default command.

**My role.** Senior Full Stack Engineer and Website Team Lead. Recruited directly by founder Dr Mahsa Mohaghegh (McCauley) — AI/NLP researcher and Head of Computer and Information Sciences at AUT — specifically to deliver the AI and full-stack senior engineering that Webflow couldn't, and that the She Sharp team didn't have in-house.

On the main platform the split was back end and front end: I owned the back end and database, and Lesley Gao owned the front end of the new website, including much of the mentorship dashboard. Mine: product architecture, database schema (39 pgTables, 33 pgEnums, 32 SQL migrations), AI matching pipeline (5-weight rubric + Upstash Redis cache + rule-based fallback + admin human-in-the-loop), Stripe billing with the form→checkout→invitation-code activation flow, Slack ecosystem (read-only event-collector, 3 scheduled Cron digests, interactive event handlers), the `sync-event-from-slack` Claude agent skill with strict Zod validation and dry-run default, admin systems, deployments, observability, and operational support. Beyond the main platform I also built the data-migration crawler that bootstrapped the launch (she-sharp-crawl), the Her Waka teaching site (her-waka) and its complete four-workshop + 12-tutorial curriculum, and the professional SEO audit and recommendations report (serpdata-api-test) on shesharp.org.nz — working across engineering, instructional design, and strategic analysis under one role.
