## Open source

### echook

AI-operated hooks plugin for Claude Code, Cursor IDE, and Codex CLI — install, configure, and use with natural language only; grew from audio notifications into a context-window status line and richer session telemetry

- Repository: https://github.com/ChanMeng666/echook
- Started: November 2025
- Status: active
- Tech stack: Python 3.9+, Claude Code Plugin SDK, Cursor IDE 3.2.16+ third-party hooks, Codex CLI hooks API, hooks.json native matcher routing, NDJSON structured logging (schema audio-hooks.v1), ElevenLabs TTS API, Slack / Discord / Teams / ntfy webhooks, PowerShell MediaPlayer (Windows), afplay (macOS), mpg123 / ffplay / paplay / aplay (Linux auto-detect), GitHub Actions CI (Ubuntu/Windows/macOS × Python 3.9/3.12/3.13)
- GitHub stars: 88 (measured 2026-10-15; renamed from claude-code-audio-hooks)
- Version: v7.1.0, released 2026-10-15, the first release run against the real Codex binary (0.143.0 and 0.162.1); 62 releases (plugin `audio-hooks` on the chanmeng-audio-hooks marketplace)
- Hook events: 39 canonical events (3 on by default), plus 47 matcher variants — separately switchable matchers beneath a canonical event (`session_start_resume`, `stop_failure_rate_limit`), not extra events; mapped per harness: Claude Code 30 of 39 canonical + all 47 variants · Cursor 18 native (8 via auto-bridge) · Codex 11
- Harnesses: 3 (Claude Code · Cursor IDE · Codex CLI) from one canonical source, CI-enforced no-drift
- Runtime: Python 3.9+ standard library only (no third-party runtime deps); distributed via plugin marketplaces + source, not npm
- CLI: 41 JSON-in/JSON-out subcommands; a `manifest` command emits the entire surface (subcommands, hooks, config keys, error codes) as machine-readable JSON so an agent can self-orient
- Status line: 33 configurable segments (context-window color bands, quota bars, model/branch/cost), auto-reflowing to terminal width
- Channels: audio · desktop toast · TTS (speaks the agent's actual final message) · webhook (Slack/Discord/Teams/ntfy, versioned payload)
- Tests / CI: 795 unittest cases (v7.1.0, run 2026-10-15) on a 3-OS × 3-Python matrix (Ubuntu/Windows/macOS × 3.9/3.12/3.13) + build-drift gate

An audio-and-status notification system for Claude Code, Cursor IDE, and Codex CLI. The core idea: you never have to learn the tool. You talk to your AI agent in plain English — "install audio-hooks," "switch to chimes," "snooze for 30 minutes," "send alerts to my Slack" — and the agent runs the commands, reads the results, and reports back. It ships 39 hook events (3 on by default), two audio themes, warnings before you hit your 5-hour and 7-day usage limits, webhooks to Slack/Discord/Teams/ntfy, text-to-speech that reads the agent's actual reply aloud, and a 33-segment status bar that tracks how much of the context window is left. Now on v7.1.0 with 795 automated tests running on Ubuntu, Windows, and macOS across Python 3.9–3.13. Open source under MIT; runs on the Python standard library with no extra dependencies. A sister repo, echook-promo-video, ships an 88-second product film built entirely in code.

**Impact.** A notification system for AI coding assistants — Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex — that you install and set up just by talking to the AI in plain English. It plays sounds, reads the agent's reply aloud, warns you before you hit usage limits, and shows a live status bar.

**Problem.** Developers running long AI coding sessions on Claude Code, Cursor IDE, and Codex CLI have no easy way to *hear* what their agent is doing. They alt-tab to check progress, miss usage-limit warnings, and only notice a stuck session by looking at it. Add-on notification tools exist, but they all share the same flaw: the human sits downstream of the command line. You have to read docs, memorize flags, copy commands, and re-learn the same surface every time it changes. That breaks down the moment a serious user rotates between three editors, each with its own configuration language and its own muscle memory. The real mismatch isn't audio — it's the working contract between humans, AI agents, and developer tooling.

**Audience.** Software engineers operating Claude Code, Cursor IDE, or Codex CLI at the "AI-first" level — people comfortable telling their coding agent to install, theme, snooze, webhook, or reconfigure things in plain English rather than memorizing subcommands. Also: power users debugging long-running workflows where a sound is faster than watching a screen; teams rolling out shared notification defaults across several developers; and researchers who want a working reference implementation of an AI-first plugin contract.

**Product logic.** echook flips the usual relationship: the human is upstream, and the AI agent learns the tool on the human's behalf. One install prompt — *"install the audio-hooks plugin from github.com/ChanMeng666/echook"* — starts the whole flow. The agent runs `claude plugin marketplace add` and `claude plugin install`, the user types `/reload-plugins` exactly once (the only manual step in the tool's entire lifetime, because Claude Code's reload has no command-line equivalent), and from then on every interaction is a sentence. *"Switch to chimes." "Snooze for 8 hours." "Send alerts to my Slack at this webhook and test it." "Turn everything off except stop and permission requests."* The `/audio-hooks` skill reads the intent, runs the right `audio-hooks` command, reads its JSON output, and tells you what happened. You memorize nothing. Cross-editor parity is part of the same contract: every prompt works the same way on Cursor's agent and on Codex CLI, because all three drive the same Python program against the same JSON interface.

**Business logic.** Open source under MIT — no paywall, no premium tier, no telemetry. The value is build-in-public credibility: echook is the demonstration piece for Chan's AI-first product philosophy, and it shows up in Engram-cohort interviews, recruiter conversations, and the README of downstream client projects. A sustained release cadence (now v7.1.0), a three-OS continuous-integration matrix, and a 795-case test suite guarding the cross-editor contract make it visibly production engineering, not a weekend script. The Remotion promo-video sister repo extends the same proof — it shows Chan can ship not only the product but the marketing film for it, end to end and entirely in code, with no video-production tooling.

**Technical approach.** AI-first design at every layer. The `audio-hooks` command-line tool exposes a stable, JSON-only interface with 41 subcommands, no prompts and no spinners, versioned NDJSON event logging (schema `audio-hooks.v1`, 5 MB rotation × 3 files), and a fixed set of error codes (`AUDIO_FILE_MISSING`, `WEBHOOK_TIMEOUT`, `DUAL_INSTALL_DETECTED`, and so on) where each error carries a `suggested_command` field so an agent can recover on its own without scraping text. Hook coverage spans 39 canonical events — session start and end, tool execution, permission requests, file changes, MCP elicitation, and usage-limit warnings (5-hour and 7-day windows with configurable 80%/95% thresholds, each `(window, threshold, resets_at)` firing exactly once via debounce markers), and beneath those events sit 47 matcher variants — a variant is a separately switchable matcher under a canonical event (`session_start_resume`, `stop_failure_rate_limit`), not an event of its own. Two audio themes ship: an ElevenLabs "Jessica" voice or modern UI chimes; rebuilds are declarative via `config/audio_manifest.json` plus the ElevenLabs generator. Webhooks fan out to Slack, Discord, Teams, and ntfy through a fire-and-forget subprocess with a versioned `audio-hooks.webhook.v1` payload, so they never block the hook. The status bar offers 33 configurable segments, including color-coded context-window and usage bars with absolute token counts (e.g. `Context: 83% (166K/200K)`) so users see the "agent dumb zone" before they reach it. The deepest piece is the cross-editor architecture: canonical sources live in `/hooks/`, `/bin/`, `/audio/`, `/cursor-hooks/`, and `/codex-hooks/`, and `build-plugin.sh` syncs them into the Claude Code plugin layout — one source of truth, three editor targets — with continuous integration enforcing no-drift via `build-plugin.sh --check`. Cursor rides its 3.2.16+ auto-bridge so most users get support for free; Cursor-only installs use a native `~/.cursor/hooks.json` registration guarded by a `DUPLICATE_BRIDGE` error that aborts if both paths would run at once. The Codex path handles OpenAI's required `[features]\ncodex_hooks = true` flag by writing a fresh `~/.codex/config.toml` when none exists and emitting machine-readable `next_steps` for the agent to edit an existing one — echook never round-trips a user's TOML, because that would destroy comments and formatting. Canonical events with no Codex equivalent no-op cleanly under the Codex invoker with a debug log line, never blocking the session.

**Outcomes.** The defining release sequence: v5.0 (April 2026) shipped the AI-first redesign — JSON command interface, `/audio-hooks` skill, NDJSON logging, plugin-native install; v5.2.0 (May 2026) added native Codex CLI support with +33 contract tests; v5.2.1 (May 2026) executed the echook rebrand — a "door-only" GitHub rename from `claude-code-audio-hooks` to `echook` (leading with "Claude Code" had become misleading once native Cursor and Codex paths shipped) that preserved every existing install via GitHub's repo redirect and kept the `audio-hooks` command name, the `chanmeng-audio-hooks` marketplace name, and all state directories unchanged. The Engram Architect Cohort Engagement Letter (May 9, 2026) explicitly names *claude-code-audio-hooks* among Chan's preserved IP — formal recognition by a commercial agentic-infrastructure firm that this is portfolio-grade engineering, not a hobby script. The sister repo echook-promo-video then closed the loop on the thesis: an 88-second 1080p product film composed entirely in code (React + Remotion, with Suno-generated background music and ElevenLabs voice and effects — no video-editing suites and no human voice actors), fully reproducible from two commands.

**My role.** Sole author of both repos. On echook proper: designed the AI-first contract (JSON interface + NDJSON log + fixed error codes + `suggested_command` recovery), wrote every hook-event integration, engineered the three-editor synchronization pipeline (canonical sources synced into the plugin layout via `build-plugin.sh`, with CI enforcement), authored the Codex TOML feature-flag bootstrap pattern, and executed the 5.2.1 rebrand without breaking compatibility. On echook-promo-video: designed the nine-section narrative arc, built the reusable visual primitives (TypewriterText, Terminal, SoundWave, GreenGrid, CounterNumber, GlowText), orchestrated the Remotion transitions, wrote the ElevenLabs audio-generation script, and tuned the volume-ducking so the background music dips under voiceover and demo playback. Maintains both repos today.

### AI Programming Education Platform

- URL: https://programming.chanmeng.org/
- Repository: https://github.com/ChanMeng666/ai-programming-teaching-project
- Started: November 2024
- Status: live
- Tech stack: Docusaurus 3.8.1, @docusaurus/faster, React 18, MDX, Cloudflare Workers, Workers AI (Llama 3.1 8B Instruct (fp8)), Cloudflare Vectorize, BGE Base EN v1.5 (768-dim embeddings), Cloudflare KV, Cloudflare Pages, Notion API, Algolia DocSearch (contextual), Typst, Mermaid (dual-view), i18next (EN + 简体中文), Server-Sent Events

Production teaching platform at programming.chanmeng.org where beginners learn to build real software with AI tools, taught across three years of cohorts. Five course versions stay online side by side — from the 2024 class to three separate 2026 tracks (TechNest, Peyvand Academy, Her Waka) — each with video lessons, lab guides, and downloadable Typst-generated PDF notes. A built-in AI tutor (a RAG assistant on Cloudflare Workers AI, Llama 3.1 8B) answers questions from a student's own cohort material, and a Demo Day page publishes the projects students shipped. Bilingual EN + 简体中文. Actively maintained through the 2026 TechNest cohort.

**Impact.** A public website that teaches beginners to build software with AI — three years of cohorts kept side by side (five course versions, three running in 2026), plus an in-site AI tutor that answers from each class's own lessons and a Demo Day page for students' finished projects.

**Problem.** AI-programming cohort programmes typically die between cohorts: the lecture deck is rebuilt from scratch each round, students from the previous cohort lose access to their materials, and the "AI tutor" experience — when it exists at all — is a chatbot tab the student opens separately, with no idea which cohort's curriculum they're studying. Meanwhile the instructor has no way to keep older cohorts permanently retrievable without disturbing the live one. The result: every cohort feels like a one-shot, course content compounds nowhere, and the AI-assisted-development experience is itself unassisted by AI.

**Audience.** Three concentric layers. Active cohort students — the 2026 TechNest AI Track, plus the 2026 Peyvand Academy and academyEX Her Waka programmes — who watch video recordings, follow lab guides, download PDF handouts, and ask the in-site AI tutor version-aware questions. Past cohort alumni (2024 Winter, 2025 Summer) who keep stable URLs to their original materials. Public learners and prospective employers who reach programming.chanmeng.org from the profile and use it as proof of production-grade EdTech built with native AI, not just slides.

**Product logic.** Visitors land on programming.chanmeng.org and the docs default to the 2026 TechNest version (the active cohort), while the version switcher exposes 2026 Her Waka, 2026 Peyvand Academy, 2025 Summer, and 2024 Winter side by side — an alum of any cohort hits a stable permalink. Each version ships its own Video Tutorials section, weekly lab guides as both web docs and downloadable Typst-generated PDFs, and a Mermaid dual-view diagram (the same diagram in two presentations so visual and textual learners both succeed). A floating AI Chat Assistant answers in natural language by retrieving the current cohort's content first (version-aware retrieval), then falling back to other cohorts and the blog.

**Business logic.** Theory of change: one teaching platform that compounds cohort over cohort instead of resetting each round. Once the 2024 Winter materials are versioned in, they stay at the same URL forever; the next cohort's materials sit alongside them without conflict. The AI tutor means a student writing code at midnight gets context-aware help against their own cohort's syllabus, not generic chatbot answers. For Chan personally: the platform is production-grade EdTech engineering (Cloudflare Workers AI + Vectorize + versioned bilingual docs + a PDF pipeline) built while doing actual teaching work — every commit is both a portfolio artefact and student value.

**Technical approach.** Built on Docusaurus 3.8.1 with the experimental @docusaurus/faster build pipeline. Five cohort versions coexist through Docusaurus versioned docs — each version is a self-contained doc tree with its own sidebar, blog feed, and tags. Bilingual i18n is end-to-end: EN primary, 简体中文 secondary, with Algolia DocSearch set to contextual locale + version filtering so a Mandarin-speaking 2026 TechNest student gets 2026 TechNest results in Chinese by default.

RAG AI assistant on Cloudflare Workers AI. A separate Cloudflare Worker (worker/src/index.ts) handles POST /api/chat behind the custom domain programming-api.chanmeng.org:

- the query is embedded with BGE Base EN v1.5 (768-dim) and sent to Cloudflare Vectorize, which returns the top chunks from the indexed corpus (about 1,200 chunks from the English pages of all five cohort versions + the blog, counted by a seeding dry run on 2026-10-15; keyed by stable content-addressed chunk IDs so re-indexing is idempotent)
- retrieval is version-aware: a 2026-technest student gets 2026-technest results by default, with older cohorts available on explicit ask
- the context is passed to Workers AI Llama 3.1 8B Instruct (fp8) which generates the answer, streamed back to the in-site ChatWidget over Server-Sent Events; per-session history persists in Cloudflare KV
- the chat endpoint is rate-limited (per-IP, plus a Cloudflare WAF burst rule) with an explicit CORS allow-list

Typst PDF handout pipeline. A Mermaid dual-view component renders every diagram twice (rendered + source) so visual and textual learners both succeed.

**Outcomes.** Live at programming.chanmeng.org; it was the official platform for the 2026 TechNest AI Track (April–July 2026) and the 2026 academyEX Her Waka programme. Five cohort versions run side by side without interfering. The RAG index covers all five versions + the blog (about 1,200 chunks, measured 2026-10-15), with version-aware retrieval and stable chunk IDs. After Cloudflare deprecated the original chat model, the assistant was restored on 2026-07-10 by swapping to Llama 3.1 8B Instruct (fp8), alongside a move to a custom API domain, per-IP rate limiting, a CORS allow-list, and a WAF rule. DeepWiki provides an external AI doc-Q&A surface at deepwiki.com/ChanMeng666/ai-programming-teaching-project.

**My role.** I migrated production from Vercel to Cloudflare Pages in 2026-02 (the site's URLs moved on 2026-02-09; the docs caught up on 2026-04-29), and in 2026-07 hardened the chat backend (custom domain, rate limiting, CORS allow-list, WAF) and restored it onto Cloudflare's current model after the old one was deprecated. I continue to ship the current cohort's recordings and lab content each week.

### Google News MCP Server

Early-ecosystem MCP server (shipped 5 weeks after Anthropic's Nov 25 2024 MCP launch) — PulseMCP "Top Pick", featured in Skywork AI deep-dive review, distributed across 15+ MCP catalogs

- URL: https://github.com/ChanMeng666/server-google-news
- Started: December 2024
- Status: production
- Tech stack: TypeScript, Node.js, @modelcontextprotocol/sdk, stdio transport, SerpAPI, axios, ES modules, npm (scoped @chanmeng666)
- npm package: @chanmeng666/google-news-server
- Registry listings: 15+ MCP catalogs: 9 directory sites (PulseMCP, Glama, mcp.so, mcpservers.org, MCP Market, Augment Code, Archestra, MCP Server Finder, AgentSeal) and 12 curated lists and registries on GitHub, led by punkpeye/awesome-mcp-servers
- Press: DataCamp, "Top 10 MCP Servers & Clients for AI Workflow Automation in 2026" (no. 10, by Abid Ali Awan, 2025-07-10); PulseMCP Weekly Pulse newsletter; a dedicated Skywork AI article
- npm downloads: 10,354 between 2025-04-13 and 2026-10-13 (the 18 months npm reports)
- PulseMCP badge: Top Pick · 38k estimated visitors · #1,060 global rank
- Glama quality: A (license) · A (quality) · 122 stars by Glama's own count
- Skywork review: One dedicated article, "The AI Engineer's Guide to Real-Time News Integration"
- Stars: 129 GitHub (measured 2026-09-24) · 21 forks · listed on Glama, PulseMCP (Top Pick), Archestra, mcp.so, MCP Market, Augment Code
- Forks: 21
- Early MCP contrib: Issue #76 (Nov 27 2024 — Windows/NVM workaround)

An early Model Context Protocol server — the open standard Anthropic launched in November 2024 to connect AI assistants to outside tools. Its first commit landed 35 days after that launch. It lets assistants like Claude, Cursor, and Cline search live Google News through SerpAPI, automatically sorted into topics (technology, business, science, health) and offered in 10 languages. Published on npm as `@chanmeng666/google-news-server`, it carries a PulseMCP "Top Pick" badge.

**Impact.** Lets AI assistants like Claude search live Google News — sorted into topics, in 10 languages. One of the first tools built for Anthropic's Model Context Protocol: shipped 35 days after the standard launched, and it's now listed across 15+ MCP directories.

**Problem.** Anthropic published the Model Context Protocol in November 2024 — the open standard that lets AI assistants like Claude reach outside their training data to real tools and live sources. In the first weeks after launch the ecosystem had only a handful of reference servers, and none of them let an assistant search current news. That was a concrete gap: people were already asking their AI assistant "what's happening with X today," a question no model can answer from training data alone, and there was no Google News option in the MCP catalog.

A second friction appeared at the same time: Windows users running Node Version Manager couldn't get *any* npm-based MCP server to connect to Claude Desktop, because PATH resolution through NVM's shim layer broke the desktop client's ability to launch the server process. That blocked a large share of early Windows adopters from using MCP at all.

**Audience.** AI assistants and the developers wiring them up. Direct consumers: Claude Desktop, Cursor's agent mode, Cline, Continue, and any MCP-compliant client whose setup includes news search. Downstream: the people asking those assistants about current events — analysts and journalists monitoring coverage, developers building research and content agents. The project is deliberately listed on multiple MCP registries because that is how AI developers actually find servers — they browse catalogs, not GitHub search.

**Product logic.** A user asks their AI assistant something like "what's happening with [topic] in [region] this week." The assistant calls the server's one tool, `google_news_search`, with a query plus optional `gl` (country) and `hl` (language) codes. The server passes the request to SerpAPI's Google News engine, gets structured results back, sorts them into topics (AI & Technology, Business, Science & Research, Healthcare, General) with lightweight pattern matching, and returns clean output with each article's source, date, snippet, and link intact. It also supports search by news topic, publisher, full-story coverage, and section via token parameters. Chinese (`zh`), which SerpAPI's Google News engine rejects as an interface language, is sent as English; other language codes are passed through as given.

The server runs over MCP's stdio channel — the default for desktop AI clients — and runs in one command from npm (`npx -y @chanmeng666/google-news-server`, with `SERP_API_KEY` set). The repo also carries a packaged `.mcpb` bundle, not yet tested as a one-click install in Claude Desktop.

**Business logic.** Open source, MIT licensed, no direct monetization. The intent is ecosystem positioning: be a canonical Google News server during the formative months of the Model Context Protocol, so the project keeps surfacing wherever a developer looks for an MCP tool. Distribution across many registries (mcp.so, Glama, PulseMCP, Awesome MCP Servers, Archestra, and others) is the discovery strategy. The README also carries JSON-LD `SoftwareApplication` metadata and an `llms.txt` guide so that AI agents themselves can read the server's identity, parameters, and use cases without parsing marketing prose — the same discovery-by-machine approach used across the rest of this portfolio.

**Technical approach.** TypeScript on Node.js, built against `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` v1.x, shipped as an ES-module CLI binary (`google-news-server`) declared in `package.json`. Transport is stdio, so the server runs as a subprocess the desktop AI client launches. HTTP calls go through axios; SerpAPI is the underlying data source, called once per tool call (the server itself adds no rate limit, concurrency cap or cache). On top of the raw API the server adds a thin intelligence layer: parameter validation, topic categorization, multi-language formatting, and error handling with clear messages. Releases are tagged on GitHub; 1.0.1 (2026-10-15) is built from the current source and reads the user's own `SERP_API_KEY`.

The repo also ships production packaging — a Dockerfile, a Smithery config, a `manifest.json`, a JSON-LD `structured-data.json`, an `llms.txt`, and a `.mcpb` bundle — plus a full set of community-health docs (CONTRIBUTING, SECURITY, SUPPORT, GOVERNANCE, CHANGELOG, issue/PR templates) added in 2026.

The third contribution is community, not code: **issue #76** in the official `modelcontextprotocol/servers` repo (opened Nov 27 2024, two days after MCP's launch) documented the Windows + NVM PATH failure that stopped Claude Desktop from launching npm-based MCP servers. The fix — point the client config at the absolute path of `node.exe` instead of relying on PATH — is the troubleshooting section of this server's documentation (`docs/overview.md`).

**Outcomes.** The server is published on npm as `@chanmeng666/google-news-server` and listed across multiple MCP discovery surfaces, with third-party recognition:

- DataCamp's "Top 10 MCP Servers & Clients for AI Workflow Automation in 2026" lists it as no. 10
- PulseMCP "Top Pick" badge, and a mention in its Weekly Pulse newsletter the week the server shipped
- Glama A grades for license and quality
- Listings on mcp.so, MCP Market, Augment Code's registry, Archestra and other directories
- Carried in punkpeye/awesome-mcp-servers and eleven other curated lists and registries on GitHub
- A dedicated article by Skywork AI
- Republished on npm by a third party (@iflow-mcp)

Each of these was checked against the page itself on 2026-10-13; the rows are in `meta.x_brand.reach`.

Alongside it, the companion `server-google-jobs` (first commit late December 2024) applies the same pattern to Google Jobs search *(Jobs-repo specifics not verifiable from the News clone — see flags)*. Issue #76 remains visible in the official MCP servers repository as a record of an early ecosystem contribution.

**My role.** I wrote the server and maintain it — the code, the README, the npm publish, the registry submissions and the issue-tracker responses. Outside contributors added the Dockerfile and Smithery config and an end-to-end evaluation, which I reviewed and merged. I also filed the early issue #76 troubleshooting contribution. Together these make the early-MCP-developer story concrete: not a theoretical early adopter, but someone who shipped, distributed, documented, and supported a working MCP server within the protocol's first month.

### a11y-loop

A Claude Code skill plus CLI that makes AI coding agents write accessible UI by default, then proves what it can prove with a real Playwright + axe-core browser audit across the states the agent built — and states plainly what it could not check

- Repository: https://github.com/ChanMeng666/a11y-loop
- Started: July 2026
- Status: active
- Tech stack: Claude Code Skill (Agent Skills open standard), Node.js >= 20, Playwright, axe-core 4.12, WCAG 2.2 AA, JavaScript, GitHub Actions CI
- npm version: v0.2.6 (10 published versions; npm registry, 2026-10-15)
- License: MIT

Accessible interfaces usually fail at the moment the code is written, not at the audit months later. a11y-loop moves the check to that moment: it gives an AI coding agent the rules up front so it writes accessible markup by default, then drives a real browser over what it built — Playwright plus axe-core, across the actual interaction states rather than one static snapshot — and reports what passed. Its distinguishing habit is the honest part: it publishes an explicit list of what it could NOT verify, so a green run never implies full WCAG 2.2 AA coverage it has no standing to claim. Ships as both a Claude Code skill and a standalone CLI (`npx a11y-loop`), with a contrast checker that proposes fixes and a CI mode. MIT.

**Impact.** Makes AI coding agents write accessible UI by default, verifies it in a real browser, and lists what it could not check so a pass never overclaims WCAG 2.2 AA. Built for the accessible-UI challenge set at the Aotearoa AI Hackathon 2026 by the organisation now adopting it.

**Problem.** AI coding agents produce interfaces fast, and they produce inaccessible ones by default: missing focus indicators, unlabelled controls, contrast that fails at a ratio nobody measured. The usual remedy is a late audit against a static page, which misses every state a user actually reaches and reports a pass the tool has no standing to claim.

**Audience.** Developers who build UI by directing coding agents, and the teams who inherit that code — plus anyone who needs a defensible accessibility position rather than a badge.

**Technical approach.** Two halves sharing one rule set. The authoring half is an Agent Skill on the open standard, so Claude Code, Cursor and Copilot pick up the same defaults. The verification half drives Playwright over the built states and runs axe-core 4.12 against WCAG 2.2 AA, then partitions the result into checked, failed, and — the part most tools omit — not checkable by automation.

**Outcomes.** Built 26 Jul – 1 Aug 2026 and published to npm (v0.2.4, 31 Jul) — dates verifiable from the repo's own commit history, and both *before* the **Aotearoa AI Hackathon Festival 2026** (7–8 Aug, AUT City Campus), where **My Life My Voice**, a disability-led NZ organisation, had set *Accessible UI Generation for Developers* as a problem statement arguing that the bottleneck is workflow rather than developer intent. Chan mentored at that festival. All three carried the project's own §3 honesty rules rather than suspending them for outreach: no compliance claim anywhere, coverage cited with its denominator (17 of the 55 WCAG 2.2 A/AA success criteria have any automated rule at all), and an explicit statement that automation does not replace testing with disabled people. The README's most flattering number — the 35 → 1 → 0 benchmark — was deliberately left out of all three, because N=6, single-run and self-audited cannot be caveated properly in an email or a social post; the fully reproducible 163 → 0 demo was used instead. **Validated on 2026-09-04 by the organisation that set the problem.** Chan gave **Timothy Young**, CTO of My Life My Voice, a live screen-share walkthrough that day — pull the public repo, ask the coding agent to install the Agent Skill and the CLI, then invoke it with `/a11y-loop` — run against Chan's own production sites, such as ArchLang's (archlang.uk) and ArchCanvas's (archcanvas.uk). Young wrote that challenge brief, and he had moved from the organisation's Chief Executive role into the CTO seat to lead its Workforce Futures–funded programme putting AI resources into New Zealand's social-sector organisations, which is why an accessibility tool for developers sits inside his remit at all. His verdict is recorded with its hedge intact: it **"won't do the entire job, but it looks like it will be a big help."** The stronger evidence is what he said about the gap itself — that vibe-coding tools can be asked to follow the accessibility guidelines and will do "an okay job", but **"what we really needed was a tool for programmers"**. That is a11y-loop's own thesis, arrived at independently by the author of the problem statement. He judged that applying it "doesn't seem like it would be that hard", is putting it in front of the organisation's own developer to work in, and the two discussed how to promote it so more people use it. The work continues with Chan advising: in the same call she walked him through installing Cursor and standing up a local development environment — GitHub CLI, git, Node.js — from scratch. Three and a half weeks separate the unsolicited handover, made with nothing at stake, from that walkthrough. **Adoption (confirmed by Chan, 2026-09-17).** After the walkthrough Young told Chan that My Life My Voice will adopt a11y-loop and promote it within its development team — the first organisation to take the tool up. What it is **not**: a paid contract, a signed partnership, or yet evidence that the tool is running in production. The §3 honesty rules above bind harder as the tool reaches real teams, not less. **Dogfooded on her own live product (v0.2.5, 2026-09-13).** Running it over archcanvas.uk exposed a blind spot in the tool itself: a correctly trapped portalled dialog (the Base UI mobile menu) was reported as broken, because the keyboard survey only recognised a native `<dialog>` as modal. Measured on that menu and recorded in the public changelog: v0.2.4 reported 2 `keyboard-unreachable` and 1 `focus-order-diverges` row in each of three runs, and 1 `dialog-focus-not-trapped` in two of them; v0.2.5 reported 0 of each in all five runs, while the no-trap fixture still reports all three of its failures.

**My role.** Sole author. Published to npm as `a11y-loop`; the repo is written agent-first, with an AGENTS.md alongside the README so an agent can orient itself without a human intermediary.

### Google Jobs MCP Server

Companion early-MCP Google Jobs server (Dec 31 2024, 36 days post-MCP-launch) — subject of dedicated Skywork AI deep-dive review, 4-language localized, listed across 10+ MCP catalogs

- URL: https://github.com/ChanMeng666/server-google-jobs
- Started: December 2024
- Status: live
- Tech stack: TypeScript, Node.js, @modelcontextprotocol/sdk 1.25.1, stdio transport, SerpAPI, node-fetch, ES modules, npm (scoped @chanmeng666), Dockerfile, .mcpb compiled binary, mcp-evals (v2.0.0 early adoption)
- npm package: @chanmeng666/google-jobs-server
- PulseMCP: 4.6k visitors · registered Jan 1 2025
- Skywork review: "one of the most elegant, production-ready solutions" (Oct 27 2025)
- Glama quality: A (license) · MIT
- Locales: English, Simplified Chinese, Japanese, Korean (24 strings each)
- GitHub stars: 22 stars (measured 2026-09-18) · 10 forks · npm @chanmeng666/google-jobs-server · Glama + serp.ai listings

A Model Context Protocol (MCP) server — the open standard that lets AI assistants call outside tools — that searches Google job listings through SerpAPI and returns results in English, Simplified Chinese, Japanese, or Korean. Built on Dec 31 2024, just 36 days after MCP's public launch, as a companion to the Google News MCP server from the same author. Installs from npm (`npx -y @chanmeng666/google-jobs-server` with `SERP_API_KEY` set), Docker, or a one-file `.mcpb` bundle, and is listed across MCP discovery catalogs including Glama, PulseMCP and mcp.so (catalog ratings and visitor counts are external claims — needs registry check).

**Impact.** The companion to the Google News server: lets AI assistants search Google job listings in English, Chinese, Japanese, and Korean. Built 36 days after MCP's launch — early enough that the founders of two major MCP catalogs contributed code to it.

**Problem.** When it was built at the very end of December 2024, the Model Context Protocol was only weeks old and there was no ready-made way for an AI assistant to look up job listings — least of all in more than one language. A job seeker in Greater China, Japan, or Korea who wanted Claude Desktop to find relevant openings had to translate their own query and hand-assemble search-URL parameters.

**Audience.** Three groups: (a) developers wiring job search into an AI application; (b) multilingual job seekers using Claude Desktop or another MCP-aware assistant; and (c) other early MCP authors looking for a worked example of locale-aware integration with a third-party API. (Skywork AI's write-up describes it as a reference pattern from the early MCP ecosystem — external claim, needs registry check.)

**Product logic.** The server exposes Google Jobs (through SerpAPI) as a single MCP tool, `search_jobs`. A caller passes a `query` plus optional filters — `location`, `radius`, `employment_type`, `salary`, `posted_age`, `sort_by`, and `page` — and picks the output language with `hl` (`en`, `zh-CN`, `ja`, or `ko`). It returns up to 10 results per page, with every label, status message, and suggestion translated into the chosen language (24 translated strings per locale) so the assistant can present results directly without extra formatting.

**Technical approach.** TypeScript on Node.js, built against the official `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` (kept current at 1.25.1). Rather than branch on language throughout the code, the four locales live in one translation table keyed to shared field names, so the same query logic serves every language and only the output strings swap. Distribution is deliberately wide for an early MCP server: npm (`@chanmeng666/google-jobs-server`, run with `npx -y @chanmeng666/google-jobs-server` and `SERP_API_KEY` set), a Dockerfile for containers, and a self-contained `.mcpb` bundle. `package.json` also carries a structured `ai:` block (use cases, capabilities, target audience) so LLM-driven catalogs can index it — the same discovery-oriented authoring pattern across this portfolio's MCP work.

**Outcomes.** Carries security-assessment badges from MseeP.ai and Glama.ai in the README. Listed across MCP discovery catalogs — Glama, PulseMCP, mcp.so and others (the A-rating, PulseMCP visitor count, and the Skywork AI deep-dive review are external claims — need registry/catalog check). Shipped one day after its companion Google News MCP server, making the pair one of the earliest public sets of locale-aware MCP servers.

**My role.** Sole author. I designed the single-table localization approach, wrote every translation, built the multi-channel distribution (npm, Docker, `.mcpb`), and maintain it alongside its Google News MCP counterpart. External contributions have been dependency bumps and catalog-integration commits; the tool design and localization are mine.

### Github README Suno Cards

GitHub Marketplace Action + Vercel-hosted SVG service that turns any Suno creator's catalog into auto-updating animated cards in their GitHub README — three id input formats (UUID / suno.com URL / short code), 36 GitHub Action inputs, 2 layouts x 2 presets x 3 themes (12 base combinations), CJK-safe text via SVG foreignObject + CSS keyframe equalizer.

- URL: https://github-readme-suno-cards.vercel.app
- Repository: https://github.com/ChanMeng666/github-readme-suno-cards
- Started: April 2026
- Status: live
- Live service: https://github-readme-suno-cards.vercel.app (Vercel serverless runtime)
- Action inputs: 36 (handle, manifest_path, song_ids, sort, max, include_tags, exclude_tags, min/max_duration)
- Card combinations: 12 base (2 layouts x 2 presets x 3 themes)
- Customization toggles: 11 element show/hide flags + hex color overrides
- id input formats: 3 (UUID / suno.com URL / suno.com/s/<shortcode>) — parser-normalized
- License: MIT

Show your AI-generated Suno music as animated, always-current cards on your GitHub profile, portfolio, or docs. Paste one line for a single song, or add a scheduled GitHub Action that keeps a whole catalog in sync — new tracks, play counts, and likes update on their own. 12 built-in card styles, correct rendering of Chinese/Japanese/Korean titles, and full English/Chinese/Japanese localization, from an MIT-licensed pnpm monorepo running on Next.js 15.1 and Vercel.

**Impact.** Turns any Suno creator's AI-generated songs into animated cards for their GitHub profile — kept up to date automatically. 12 built-in styles, correct display of Chinese/Japanese/Korean titles, and a one-line setup that syncs a whole catalog.

**Problem.** Suno AI creators have no graceful way to surface their music where developer audiences actually gather: GitHub READMEs, portfolio sites, technical blog footers, project docs. The three workarounds all fail. Linking out to suno.com loses the visual hook and breaks if Suno changes its URL shapes. Screenshotting the player goes stale the moment you publish a new song. Hand-editing Markdown is fine for one song and unmanageable past three. Worse, many Suno creators are bilingual and release tracks with Chinese, Japanese, or Korean titles — and plain SVG `<text>` (the usual way to draw text inside an embeddable image) never inherited HTML's rich text-shaping rules, so those titles render incorrectly. The gap: a service that renders animated, visually rich Suno cards as embeddable images, shapes CJK text correctly, supports both zero-setup single embeds and CI-driven auto-syncing grids, and works both as a browse-and-build website and as a fully programmatic GitHub Action.

**Audience.** Three concentric audiences. (1) Developer-musicians using Suno who want their GitHub profile README, portfolio, or project docs to show a live, auto-updating catalog of their music — including CJK-named tracks. (2) Music creators more broadly who keep a GitHub-shaped public presence (developer-relations folks, indie-game developers, bedroom producers with side projects, researchers releasing music under handles) and want a polished visual surface for their Suno output. (3) Engineers reading the project as a worked example of (a) extracting a clean public repo from a larger internal monorepo, (b) sharing a single validated parser across two independent products, and (c) the SVG-`<foreignObject>`-plus-CSS-keyframes technique for animated, CJK-safe cards that plain SVG can't produce.

**Product logic.** Two complementary paths, plus stats surfaces. **Path 1 — Direct Embed (zero setup).** Paste one Markdown line pointing at the hosted card endpoint: `[![](https://github-readme-suno-cards.vercel.app/api/card?id=YOUR_SONG_ID)](https://suno.com/song/YOUR_SONG_ID)`. The `id` accepts three formats — a raw UUID, a full `suno.com/song/<uuid>` URL, or a `suno.com/s/<shortcode>` short code — which the parser canonicalises to one internal ID. The hosted `/builder` lets you preview the 12 base combinations (2 layouts × 2 presets × 3 themes), flip 11 element toggles, override colors with hex codes, and copy the finished embed URL. **Path 2 — GitHub Action auto-sync.** The Action reads any of its 36 inputs — a Suno handle (auto-discovery of every public song), a YAML manifest of song IDs, or an inline CSV; plus sorting, tag and duration filters, layout/preset/theme/ language, and color overrides — fetches and ranks the matching songs, and surgically replaces only the content between the markers. Beyond single songs, a profile summary card (`/api/profile`) and an auto-discovered card stack (`/api/cards`) render whole-catalog views. All surfaces share one parser and one renderer, so cards look identical whichever path produced them.

**Technical approach.** A pnpm monorepo with three workspaces: `apps/` (the Next.js 15.1 frontend on Vercel), `packages/` (two reusable kernels), and `action/` (the GitHub Marketplace Action). The two packages are the architecturally important part. **`@suno-cards/parser`** is a Valibot-validated (v0.42.1) client for Suno's public oEmbed-style API on `studio-api-prod.suno.com` — anonymous, CORS-enabled, public-by-design endpoints Suno advertises via the W3C oEmbed protocol; no scraping, no auth, no headless browsers. That hierarchy now distinguishes an HTTP `422` malformed-request (`SunoInvalidRequestError`) from a `404` unknown-handle (`SunoHandleNotFoundError`), alongside not-found, private, not-ready, schema, and network error types. A 2026-07 health audit also quarantined `/api/trending` — it turned out to be an abandoned September-2024 snapshot, not a live feed, so `fetchTrending` was removed from the parser's public exports to stop anyone building on stale data. **`@suno-cards/render`** is the pure-function SVG engine — deterministic, cacheable, and callable from both Vercel's serverless runtime and the Action's Node 20 runner. The defining rendering technique: SVG `<foreignObject>` carries inline HTML `<span>`s so CJK text shapes correctly (plain SVG `<text>` can't), with CSS `@keyframes` animating those spans into the equalizer bars — a hybrid plain SVG can't produce cleanly, and one that survives GitHub's Camo image proxy because CSS keyframes pass its SVG sanitization. Text ships localized in English, Chinese, and Japanese. Two-level caching: Vercel's upstream data cache (3600s for single cards) plus downstream `Cache-Control` headers that let Camo manage distribution. The Action is built by an esbuild bundle (`action/build.ts` → committed `action/dist/index.js`, Node 20) so it needs no install step at workflow time. Quality: Biome for lint/format, Vitest suites across parser, render, and action.

**Outcomes.** Live production service at github-readme-suno-cards.vercel.app with `/gallery` and `/builder` routes and three SVG endpoints (`/api/card`, `/api/profile`, `/api/cards`). The current public repository is the clean-extract release — first commit `73f4fa8` "initial commit — github-readme-suno-cards v0.1" on 2026-04-13, immediately followed by `295756e` "clean remaining internal reference" (the post-extraction sanitization sweep) — carried forward to its latest commit `86167f4` on 2026-07-06, which recorded a 2026-07-05 health audit confirming all three render surfaces against live Suno data. That audit produced two durable API decisions: the `/api/trending` fossil was quarantined out of the public parser surface, and HTTP 422 got its own error type. Roadmap: waveform card variant, lyrics-excerpt cards, playlist cards, a JSON API, and PNG export via `@resvg/resvg`.

**My role.** Sole author across both the original internal monorepo and the public v0.1 extraction.

### Aotearoa AI Hackathon 2026

Industry-partnered AI event assistant for the Aotearoa AI Hackathon Festival — relaunched for 2026 (AUT City Campus) as a single-page voice-first agent: an audio-reactive Three.js orb driving a two-way OpenAI Realtime voice conversation (WebRTC + ephemeral keys) plus gpt-4o-mini text chat, over a Neon knowledge base + transcripts with KV rate-limiting, on Vercel. The 2025 edition (AUT × AI Forum NZ × She Sharp) shipped a 3D sprite mascot with 6-tier affection gamification + a Notion-as-database FAQ on Cloudflare Workers; generalized into an open-source MIT template

- URL: https://hackathon.shesharp.org.nz/
- Repository: https://github.com/ChanMeng666/event-qa-ai-template
- Status: live
- For: She Sharp
- Tech stack: Next.js 16.1 (App Router), React 18 + TypeScript 5, Tailwind CSS v3 + Framer Motion v12, Vercel AI SDK v4.3, @ai-sdk/openai (GPT-4o-mini-2024-07-18 streaming), Three.js 0.182 + @react-three/fiber 8.16, Custom Quantum Orb 3D mascot (CSS 3D transforms + Three.js particles), Sprite affection gamification engine (gesture detection, mood weighting, time-of-day bias), Notion REST API (raw fetch, CF Workers compatible — replaced @notionhq/client SDK), shadcn/ui + Radix primitives, @opennextjs/cloudflare adapter, Cloudflare Workers deployment (migrated from Vercel), wrangler v4 CI/CD, localStorage state persistence (50-msg chat history + sprite affection state), 5-min FAQ client cache + optimistic vote/view updates, AI rate limiting + per-session token budgets + prompt guardrails (2026-07 security hardening), OpenAI Realtime API over WebRTC — two-way voice (2026 relaunch), Ephemeral client secrets minted server-side (OPENAI_API_KEY never reaches the browser), Audio-reactive Three.js orb voice UI + live captions (2026), Vercel deployment (2026 edition — she-sharp1/aihackathon-2026)

Real industry-partnered AI event assistant built for the **AI Hackathon Festival 2025** (Auckland, Aug 15–16, 2025), co-organised by **Auckland University of Technology**, **AI Forum New Zealand**, and **She Sharp**, with **UN Sustainable Development Goals** as the innovation brief. The platform serves participants and mentors through three interlocking systems: (1) an **interactive 3D sprite mascot** with a 6-tier "Stranger → Soulmate" affection system, 7-state dynamic mood engine, 17 emotion categories, gesture recognition (circle/pat/swipe), negative-behaviour penalties, streak bonuses, and time-of-day emotion biases — a fully gamified personality layer that responds to how users actually touch the page; (2) a **Notion-as-database community FAQ** with up/downvote ranking, view tracking, 5-minute client cache, and graceful static fallback when Notion is unreachable; (3) an **OpenAI GPT-4o-mini streaming chat** with markdown-rendered responses and one-click FAQ-to-chat hand-off. After the live deployment, the codebase was generalised into a reusable open-source template (`event-qa-ai-template` on GitHub, MIT) so any future hackathon / conference can fork-and-config the same stack. Chan was subsequently recognised among the **14 expert mentors** at the festival. For the **2026 festival** (Aotearoa AI Hackathon Festival 2026, AUT City Campus) the project was **rebuilt from the ground up** as a single-page **voice-first** agent: the whole site is a centered, audio-reactive Three.js orb that starts a **two-way voice conversation over the OpenAI Realtime API via WebRTC** (the client exchanges SDP directly with OpenAI using a short-lived ephemeral secret, so the real API key never reaches the browser), with a text-input fallback answered by gpt-4o-mini via the Vercel AI SDK, live captions, and a collapsible event-info panel. Agent instructions build from a Neon `knowledge` table (graceful fallback to config), transcripts persist best-effort, and Upstash KV rate-limits token minting. Deployed on Vercel (`she-sharp1/aihackathon-2026`, live at aihackathon-2026.vercel.app).

**Impact.** Voice-first AI event agent for the Aotearoa AI Hackathon Festival — relaunched 2026 (AUT) as an audio-reactive orb driving two-way OpenAI Realtime voice + gpt-4o-mini text chat; the 2025 edition served 11 teams / 80+ participants with a gamified 3D sprite mascot + Notion FAQ.

- Tech stack: Claude Code Plugin, Node.js, Playwright, sharp, @resvg/resvg-js, HTML/CSS, SVG

**Impact.** A config-driven Claude Code plugin that renders store-ready promo assets across 17 platform targets and 5 themes from one config — two render engines (HTML/CSS + Playwright raster, native SVG + resvg) with dimension/alpha/size-cap validation and pure-CSS device frames.

### slack-waterline

A Claude Code skill that reads every message in a Slack workspace and proves nothing was missed — thread-aware catch-up, a daily or weekly DM digest, drafted replies, and two audit gates that fail differently. Zero dependencies, many workspaces from one install

- Repository: https://github.com/ChanMeng666/slack-waterline-skill
- Started: September 2026
- Status: active
- Tech stack: Claude Code Skill (Agent Skills open standard), Node.js 18+ (zero dependencies, plain fetch against the Slack Web API), node --test, GitHub Actions

**Impact.** Catches the Slack messages unread-counts cannot see — replies buried in old threads — and refuses to mark anything read until a payload was actually delivered, so a missed message cannot quietly disappear.

### Contributions to other open-source projects

- modelcontextprotocol/servers #75, "Solution for MCP Servers Connection Issues with NVM/NPM (Windows)" (closed, November 2024): Step-by-step Windows + NVM/NPM workaround for the early Claude Desktop MCP connection failure: install MCP server packages globally, locate `node.exe` and global npm root via `where node` and `npm root -g`, then rewrite `claude_desktop_config.json` with absolute paths instead of `npx` commands. Posted as a comment on TristanLib's issue #75 ("How to configure windows filesystem?") two days after MCP's public launch on 2024-11-25. https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/issues/75#issuecomment-2502877979
- wshobson/agents #62, "feat: Add comprehensive security coding expert agents with improved descriptions" (merged, September 2025): Added comprehensive security-focused Claude Code expert agents and refined existing agent descriptions across the canonical community-maintained agents catalogue. 448 lines added across 3 files. https://github.com/wshobson/agents/pull/62
- CopilotKit/CopilotKit #2068, "chore(demos): Add FemTracker Agent + CopilotKit Demo to the demos_2025 folder" (merged, June 2025): Added the 8-agent FemTracker Agent demo (a women's-health AI tracker built on CopilotKit + LangGraph) to CopilotKit's official `demos_2025` folder. 341 lines added. https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit/pull/2068
- CopilotKit/CopilotKit #2529, "docs: add Claude Code setup instructions to MCP server guide" (merged, September 2025): Added Claude Code-specific setup instructions to CopilotKit's official MCP server documentation page so developers using Claude Code (rather than Cursor or Claude Desktop) get a first-class onboarding path. 62 lines added. https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit/pull/2529
- modelcontextprotocol/servers #76, "Connection failures with npm-based MCP servers while uvx-based servers work correctly (Solved, see the comment in this post)" (closed, November 2024): Filed a standalone issue (companion to comment on #75) documenting the Windows + NVM/NPM connection failure and its workaround — chosen as the canonical "Chan-authored" reference issue Anthropic maintainers and the broader community could link to. Self-resolved with the detailed step-by-step solution in the comments. https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/issues/76
- michaellatman/mcp-get #62, "Add Google News MCP Server" (merged, January 2025): Registered Chan's `@chanmeng666/google-news-server` MCP server in the `mcp-get` package registry — one of the early community MCP discovery tools — making it installable via `npx @michaellatman/mcp-get@latest install`. https://github.com/michaellatman/mcp-get/pull/62
- punkpeye/awesome-mcp-servers #163, "Add Google News MCP Server & Add the content in Chinese README and Japanese README that is not synchronized with the English README" (merged, December 2024): Two-in-one PR: (1) registered the Google News MCP Server in the `awesome-mcp-servers` curated list, (2) synchronised the Chinese and Japanese README translations with content that had drifted behind the English source. https://github.com/punkpeye/awesome-mcp-servers/pull/163
- modelcontextprotocol/servers #445, "Add Google News MCP Server in README" (closed, December 2024): Proposed adding server-google-news to the official modelcontextprotocol/servers README community-servers section. https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/pull/445
- kyechan99/capsule-render #71, "Added Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese and Traditional Cantonese README translations" (merged, December 2024): Authored full README translations into Simplified Chinese (zh-Hans), Traditional Chinese (zh-Hant), and Traditional Cantonese (yue-Hant) for `capsule-render` — the popular GitHub profile banner generator used by thousands of profile READMEs. 1,330 lines added across 7 files, merged the same day. https://github.com/kyechan99/capsule-render/pull/71
- Kiran1689/Awesome-Dev-Portfolios #258, "Fix: Add ChanMeng666's Portfolio" (merged, December 2024): Registered chanmeng.dev in the curated Awesome-Dev-Portfolios list, after first opening companion issue #257 to request the addition. https://github.com/Kiran1689/Awesome-Dev-Portfolios/pull/258
- anthropics/claude-code #46524, "[FEATURE] Make every slash command agent-invokable (and their output agent-readable) — /reload-plugins as a concrete AI-first blocker" (closed, April 2026): Filed a feature request arguing that every Claude Code slash command should be invokable from inside an agent loop and its output should be readable back to the agent, using `/reload-plugins` as the concrete blocker. Framed the request inside the broader "AI-first developer tooling" design principle. https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/46524
- CopilotKit/CopilotKit #1957, "🐛 Bug: Custom LLM Service Adapter Integration Fails with "serviceAdapter.process is not a function" Error" (closed, June 2025): Reported a reproducible bug in CopilotKit's Custom LLM Service Adapter integration where `serviceAdapter.process` was undefined at runtime when supplying a user-defined adapter, with a minimal reproduction case. https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit/issues/1957

Deployed on Cloudflare Pages.

**Impact.** Three production systems in one repo: animated portfolio + an IBM watsonx.ai digital twin + an 11-stage autonomous AI newsletter pipeline that ships every Monday 8 AM NZ time fully unattended since April 2026 — Lighthouse 95+ across all metrics.

### GAVIGO Website

- URL: https://gavigo.com/
- Started: December 2025
- Status: live
- For: GAVIGO Inc.
- Tech stack: Next.js, React, TypeScript, Neon Postgres, Drizzle ORM, MDX / Markdown (remark + rehype, gray-matter), React Email + Resend, Motion, Tailwind CSS, Google Cloud Run (europe-west1)
- Live URL: https://gavigo.com (Google Cloud Run, europe-west1)
- Role: the standalone company/investor site, decoupled from the IRE product runtime (ire.gavigo.com) it links to
- Content: Markdown/MDX pipeline (remark + rehype + gray-matter) so non-engineers can edit copy without touching code
- Capture: Resend + React Email lead capture wired to Neon Postgres (Drizzle ORM)
- Company: GAVIGO Inc. (Delaware C-Corp); Chan was Founding Principal Engineer on the flagship IRE platform, Oct 2025 - Oct 2026
- Related projects: GAVIGO IRE

GAVIGO Inc.'s public marketing and investor-readiness website at gavigo.com — the company's standalone brand surface, deliberately decoupled from the IRE product runtime (ire.gavigo.com) so marketing copy and investor messaging can change without redeploying the product.

**Impact.** GAVIGO's company + investor site (gavigo.com) — a standalone brand surface decoupled from the IRE product runtime it links to, with a Markdown content pipeline + Resend capture on Cloud Run.

**Problem.** A startup's product and its story move at different speeds. GAVIGO's IRE platform is a fast-changing, latency-critical runtime; its public company narrative — the pitch to investors, partners, and early users — needs to change even faster, and by people who aren't shipping the product. Running the marketing site inside the product codebase couples the two: a copy tweak risks the runtime, and a non-engineer can't touch either. GAVIGO needed a company surface that is polished, investor-ready, editable without engineering, and completely decoupled from the product it represents.

**Audience.** Primarily investors and strategic partners evaluating GAVIGO during fundraising and business-development conversations — the site is the first credible impression and the bridge to the live IRE demo. Second, prospective early users and press arriving at gavigo.com who need to understand "Skip the Store. Start the Play" and reach the product in one click. Third, GAVIGO's own non-technical team, who edit copy and read captured leads without asking an engineer.

**Product logic.** The site is deliberately a **separate surface from the product**. It presents GAVIGO's positioning and brand, animates key moments with Motion for a premium feel, and routes every call-to-action to the live IRE demo (ire.gavigo.com/mobile) so the story hands off directly to the working product. Content is authored in **Markdown/MDX** through a remark + rehype + gray-matter pipeline, so marketing copy, announcement posts, and page sections are editable as plain files without touching React — the whole point being that the company narrative can move without an engineer in the loop. A **Resend + React Email** capture flow collects interested-party leads into Neon Postgres, turning the site from a brochure into a working top-of-funnel instrument for investor and partner outreach.

**Business logic.** This is founding-team company infrastructure, not a revenue product. Its job is fundraising and credibility: a standalone, polished, fast-to-update investor-readiness surface that GAVIGO (a Delaware C-Corp) can point investors and partners to, that always reflects the current pitch, and that funnels interest straight to the live IRE demo and into a captured lead list. Decoupling it from the product runtime is the strategic choice — the company can iterate its story continuously while the latency-critical IRE platform ships on its own cadence.

**Technical approach.** A Next.js + React + TypeScript site deployed as a container on **Google Cloud Run** (europe-west1) — deliberately separate hosting from the IRE platform. Copy and content run through a **Markdown/MDX pipeline** (remark + rehype + gray-matter) so pages are file-editable; **Motion** drives brand animation; **Tailwind CSS** carries the design system. Lead capture is a **Resend + React Email** flow persisting to **Neon Postgres via Drizzle ORM**. The build is small and focused by design — the engineering value is in a clean, maintainable, non-engineer-editable company surface with a real capture backend, shipped and operated solo.

**Outcomes.** It stands as the company's public front door and the hand-off point into the live IRE product demo, decoupled from and shipping independently of the product runtime.

**My role.** Sole developer and maintainer of the site end-to-end — the Next.js build, the Markdown/MDX content pipeline, the Motion brand animation, the Resend + Neon lead-capture backend, and the Google Cloud Run deployment — as GAVIGO's founding principal engineer (the same role under which I lead the flagship IRE platform).

Named an **Outstanding Mentor** at the **Aotearoa AI Hackathon Festival 2026**, held 7–8 August 2026 at AUT City Campus and hosted by Auckland University of Technology with She Sharp and AI Forum NZ, with Fisher & Paykel Healthcare. The **second year running**: Chan received the same recognition at the 2025 edition of the festival.

### Reproducible Is Not Correct: Reflexive Gates and the Self-Descriptions We Ship to Language Models

- Publisher: Zenodo (preprint)
- Date: 2026-09-25
- URL: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22958002

Sole-authored software-engineering paper (cs.SE; CC BY 4.0). Software now ships descriptions of itself written for language models — schemas, grammars, context files, a server's self-reported identity — and the gate usually guarding them only proves the file regenerates, not that it is true. The paper names the precondition that makes that gate sound, and measures what happens without it: a census of the npm packages behind the Model Context Protocol registry, third-party compiler cases, and a depth study of ArchLang, the floor-plan language Chan built. Preprint published on Zenodo 2026-09-25 (software archive DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22950936); submitted to arXiv the same day, awaiting announcement as of 2026-09-29.

A walkthrough of the 4D framework for working well with AI — Delegation, Description, Discernment, Diligence — with the three modes of human-AI interaction, prompt-engineering technique, and where generative AI currently falls short.

### The Future is Small: Why Small Language Models (SLMs) Are Powering the Next Wave of AI Agents

### Aotearoa AI Hackathon Festival 2026 — MC & Mentor

- Type: hackathon
- Date: 2026-08-07 to 2026-08-08
- Location: AUT City Campus, Auckland, New Zealand
- Organiser: AUT × She Sharp × AI Forum NZ × Fisher & Paykel Healthcare
- URL: https://www.shesharp.org.nz/events/aotearoa-ai-hackathon-festival-2026

**MC'd the opening** of the two-day 2026 festival — welcome and Karakia Tīmatanga from the AUT podium — and returned as a technical mentor, a year after the 2025 edition that produced the first Outstanding Mentor Award. **Received the Outstanding Mentor Award a second consecutive year** for the 2026 festival (`awards[Outstanding Mentor Award (2026)]` — recorded on Chan's own testimony; see the self-attestation note there). She was in the room in **two capacities at once**: on the public mentor roster in her own right, and as part of the **She Sharp team** that ran the venue, working mentor recruitment alongside the organising group in the weeks before. On the public roster she is billed as **Founding Engineer, ArchCanvas**, alongside mentors from AUT, Fisher & Paykel Healthcare, Southern Cross Health Society, Red Hat and Possibl.ai.

**How many mentors — two figures, both real.** The host's public "Meet the Mentors" roster lists **17**; the organisers' own running count reached **28**, which includes volunteers and staff who registered under the mentor code. Neither is wrong; they count different things, and this database records both rather than picking the flattering one.

**Scale and outcome.** 125 registered. **Twelve teams** built against five real-world UN SDG themes; free online pre-event training ran through July, and roughly **a third of participants had never been to a hackathon before**. On the Saturday each team pitched for five minutes to a local judging panel: one team took the venue prize with two runners-up, and the winning pitch went forward to national judging. **Four national finalists** pitch at the Aotearoa AI Summit, 8–9 September 2026 in Wellington. The festival's voice-first event assistant is `ai-hackathon-assistant`, relaunched for 2026.

A second thread outlived the festival. One of the problem statements — **Accessible UI Generation for Developers** — was set by **My Life My Voice**, a disability-led NZ organisation whose *AI For People* programme argues for AI built to work for disabled people rather than the reverse. Its brief names the same bottleneck the `a11y-loop` project attacks: accessibility as a manual, late audit sitting outside the tools developers use, auditing what is already broken instead of preventing it.

**That handover got a live walkthrough on 2026-09-04.** Timothy Young — CTO of My Life My Voice, and the author of that challenge brief — took a screen-share demonstration of `a11y-loop` running against Chan's own production sites, such as ArchLang's (archlang.uk) and ArchCanvas's (archcanvas.uk), and described the gap it was built for in his own terms: vibe-coding tools can be asked to follow the accessibility guidelines and do "an okay job", but "what we really needed was a tool for programmers". His verdict on the tool itself keeps its hedge — it "won't do the entire job, but it looks like it will be a big help." He is putting it in front of the organisation's own developer to work in, and Chan is providing technical guidance. On 2026-09-17 Chan recorded that, after the walkthrough, he told her My Life My Voice will adopt a11y-loop and promote it within its development team: being adopted, by her first-hand account. Not a paid contract, not a formal partnership, not a written endorsement, and not yet a production deployment; the meeting is evidenced by a transcript Chan holds privately and has not published (see the SELF-ATTESTED note above the `a11y-loop` entry). Full record: `projects[a11y-loop].narrative.outcomes` and the `my-life-my-voice` organisation entry.

## Engineering stories

### The threads through my engineering work

#### Who I am as an engineer

I build products in which an AI does part of the work and something deterministic decides whether that work is right: a compiler, a real browser, a checker, a person with an approve button. Across my own products, client platforms and open-source tools the same habits recur: I make the output checkable, I do not trust a green check until I have seen it fail, and I write down what a number does not measure. Many of the people I build for are not engineers (a charity founder, a festival organiser, the commissioner of a research cohort), so a large part of the job is handing the system to them: content they can edit, review screens, runbooks. I am often the only engineer on a project, working from Auckland with AI coding agents, which is why my tools treat agents as first-class callers. When something breaks I trace it to one cause, then change the process (a rule, a test, a checklist) so that the whole class of failure cannot come back. My records say plainly what failed and what I would do differently.

#### The threads

#### Thread 1. Making AI output checkable

The model proposes; something that cannot be talked round decides.

- ArchCanvas S1 ("A floor plan you can check has to be a program"): I stopped asking a model to draw floor plans and gave it a language whose output a compiler can measure, diff and edit.
- ArchLang S2 ("Errors as data: a hand-written parser and fixes a tool can apply"): every error carries a stable code, a byte span and, where provable, a fix an agent can apply without reading prose.
- a11y-loop S1 ("A loop, not a better prompt and not a one-shot linter"): the agent writes, a real browser and axe-core judge, and the loop ends when the checker says so, not the agent.
- She Sharp S2 ("AI mentor matching that never pairs anyone on its own"): the model scores mentor pairs against an explicit rubric, and an admin approves every match.

#### Thread 2. Green is not the same as working

The failures I learn most from are the ones that looked like success.

- ArchLang S3 ("The agent reference was wrong while every check was green"): a drift check stayed green because it certified a generator that restated the grammar by hand.
- ArchCanvas S7 ("A check that can never fail is not a check"): when every layer mocks the database, the one probe that touches it must be allowed to block the release.
- GAVIGO IRE S7 ("Redis had gone, and the health check said healthy"): production ran without Redis while the health endpoint said healthy; I made the client self-heal and the status honest.
- She Sharp S4 ("Incidents that taught me to break my own guards"): a guard is not verified until it has been handed the input it should refuse.

#### Thread 3. Designing for handover from the first week

A system is finished when someone else can run it without asking me.

- She Sharp S6 ("Designing the handover so the answer is a file, not a person"): every recurring obligation got exactly one named owner, and the handover answers "what stops working when I stop answering?".
- Tam-AI-Ti S5 ("Handing production to the client without signing anyone out"): production moved into the client's accounts mid-cohort with no downtime and no one signed out.

#### Thread 4. Building for owners who do not write code

The owner should be able to change the product the day they decide something.

- Eatropolis website S2 ("Letting a non-technical client edit the site: GitHub as the CMS"): the repository became the CMS, with a schema that stops a bad edit before visitors see it.
- FemTech Weekend website S4 ("Letting the founder run selection without an engineer"): the founder approves or rejects summit applicants in batches, and each decision sends its own email.
- Tam-AI-Ti S7 ("Building for a client who directs the product, not the code"): a demo video at every milestone, then teaching videos so the commissioner could read her own data.
- She Sharp S5 ("Writing a charity's recurring work down as 11 agent skills"): a charity's recurring work written down as agent skills a volunteer can run and check.

#### Thread 5. Agents as the user

More and more of my tools are operated by an AI agent on someone's behalf, so I design the interface for that caller.

- echook S1 ("Designing the CLI for an agent, not for a person"): JSON in and out, stable error codes with a suggested recovery command, and a manifest that describes the whole surface.
- echook S8 ("An agent ran `install --help`, and the CLI installed"): after an agent's `--help` triggered an install, help became side-effect-free and unknown input changes nothing.
- ArchLang S7 ("CLI first for agents, MCP only as a doorway"): CLI first because it costs an agent nothing until called; MCP as a separate doorway.
- Google News MCP Server S3 ("Designing a tool whose caller is a language model"): one tool, a validated schema, and two error channels so the model can recover from an upstream failure.

#### Thread 6. Saying what a number does not measure

A figure goes out with its boundary, or it does not go out.

- GAVIGO IRE S1 ("Choosing the checkpoint approach that could be measured on our own cluster"): three controlled, application-level measurements, published with a note that they are not a production SLA.
- GAVIGO IRE S6 ("Renaming a metric instead of overclaiming"): when an ad could satisfy "reached first play", I renamed and redesigned the metric rather than report a flattering number.
- a11y-loop S3 ("Saying what it could not check"): the tool lists what a machine cannot check and is not allowed to call a page "accessible".
- Eatropolis website S6 ("Proving the site would hold up on launch day"): the load test passed, and the report explains why its latency figure is limited by the load generator.

#### Which story for which question

| A technical decision you would defend | ArchCanvas S1 ("A floor plan you can check has to be a program") with ArchLang S1 ("Turning a drawing problem into a language") (a language instead of a better prompt); GAVIGO IRE S1 ("Choosing the checkpoint approach that could be measured on our own cluster") (four checkpoint options, one measurable) |

#### Recruiter version

I am a full-stack engineer in Auckland, New Zealand, who builds AI products and the checks that keep them honest. I founded ArchCanvas, an AI tool that turns a plain-English brief into a dimensioned floor plan, and wrote ArchLang, the open-source language behind it. As founding engineer at GAVIGO, a US startup, I built the platform behind its game feed and moved it to Google Cloud with about 30 minutes of downtime. For She Sharp, a charity for women in tech, I replaced a no-code website with a platform it owns and moved its 1,549-person mailing list with zero failed sends. I built Auckland's Eatropolis festival website, which passed a 1,000-visitor load test without an error, and an AI coach in te reo Māori and English used by a 19-person research cohort. My free tools for AI coding assistants include a Google News server named in DataCamp's Top 10.

#### Engineer version

Most of my work is LLM systems with a deterministic referee. In ArchCanvas (Next.js, Vercel AI SDK, Neon, Drizzle) an orchestrator calls tools, a separate designer model writes ArchLang, and a ship gate compiles, repairs and lints every candidate before anything is saved or charged; the loop is bounded on calls, tokens, wall-clock time and per-call timeout, and a founder-run offline benchmark passed 26 of 26 briefs. ArchLang is a zero-dependency TypeScript compiler: hand-written recursive-descent parser with error recovery, 139 stable diagnostic codes with span-level fixes, count-based resource budgets, and exact arithmetic where a verdict turns on a tie. At GAVIGO I wrote the Go orchestrator (WebSocket hub, scorer, rules engine, warm-pool manager driving the Kubernetes API), moved production from DigitalOcean to GKE, and chose application-level checkpointing over Pod Snapshots, CRIU and DMTCP. Results: 78% Application-Level Reduction, 4.45 s → 1.00 s Controlled Startup Path Comparison, ~140 ms Preserved AI State Restore; controlled application-level measurements, not a production SLA. The failure class I meet most is the check that is green and blind: a drift check certifying a hand-typed grammar, a tool-free benchmark missing an API rejection, a health endpoint reporting healthy without Redis, a non-blocking accessibility job. My fixes are structural: liveness split from readiness, a canary that must reach the real database, guards tested against the input they should refuse. I design CLIs for agents as callers (JSON only, stable error codes, side-effect-free `--help`), and hand systems to non-engineers through schema-validated content in Git, review screens and runbooks.

### a11y-loop — story

Role: Creator and sole developer · Period: 2026-07 – present

#### In one breath

AI coding assistants now write a lot of website code, and by default much of it shuts out people who use a keyboard, a screen reader or high-contrast settings. I built a11y-loop, a free open-source tool that teaches the assistant the accessibility rules before it writes, then checks the result in a real browser, has the assistant fix what failed, and checks again. It also says plainly what a machine cannot check. I built it in a week and published it to npm before the Aotearoa AI Hackathon Festival 2026, where a disability-led New Zealand organisation, My Life My Voice, had set exactly this problem; after a live walkthrough its CTO said they will adopt it and promote it within their development team.

#### The problem

AI coding agents produce interfaces fast, and inaccessible ones by default: missing focus indicators, unlabelled controls, contrast that fails at a ratio nobody measured. The obvious fix, telling the model to "be accessible", does not work: the research the project cites (W4A'25) measured a slightly *higher* violation rate with accessibility-oriented prompts than without.

The usual remedy is a late audit against one static page load. That misses every state a user actually reaches (an open dialog, an expanded menu, a form showing its errors), arrives after nobody wants to touch the UI, and often reports a "pass" the tool has no standing to claim. My Life My Voice's challenge brief at the hackathon named the same bottleneck: accessibility sits outside the tools developers use, as a manual check at the end.

#### What I built

Two halves sharing one rule set, plus an optional third. An Agent Skill on the open Agent Skills standard tells the agent what to decide while planning, what to write by default, how to run the audit loop and how it is allowed to describe the result; the same `SKILL.md` works in Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot and other clients. A Node CLI does the verification: it drives Playwright and Chromium over the built page and its interaction states, runs axe-core against WCAG 2.2 AA plus checks of its own, and partitions the result into failed, needs review, and not checkable by automation. An optional Claude Code plugin enforces the planning step.

- `a11y-loop audit`: five rendering passes per run (default, dark mode, forced colors, reduced motion, a 320 px reflow viewport), plus states the agent scripts with `--interact`. JSON report with the WCAG success criterion and ACT rule per finding, a generated manual-review checklist, SARIF as a secondary format, and exit codes 0/1/2 as a stable contract.
- Own checks axe-core cannot run: tab order, focus visibility, dialog focus trap, Escape and focus return, target size, reduced-motion effectiveness, ambiguous link text, clickable `div`s.
- `a11y-loop diff`: matches findings across two runs by a stable fingerprint and marks each FIXED, NEW or REMAINING; a NEW violation fails the run.
- `a11y-loop contrast --fix`: checks a colour pair and proposes passing colours in OKLCh that keep the hue.
- A `PreToolUse` hook on plan approval that declines, once, a UI plan with no accessibility section.
- Released from GitHub Actions to npm by OIDC trusted publishing with provenance; a promo film made under the same "nothing mocked up" rule.

#### S1. A loop, not a better prompt and not a one-shot linter

- **Kind**: decision
- **Situation**: I wanted coding agents to produce accessible UI. The cheapest option was a paragraph of instructions; the conventional one was a linter or an audit at the end. The published evidence said instructions alone barely move the result, and a single page-load audit misses the states where interfaces actually break.
- **What I did**: I split the job by what each half can be trusted with. The model gets rules up front (the skill), because prevention is cheaper than repair. Judgement of the result goes to a deterministic engine: a real browser, axe-core, and my own checks, across five rendering passes and the states the agent says it built. The skill makes the loop mandatory: audit, fix in the source, re-audit to a new file, diff, and repeat until there are no violations and no NEW findings. Exit codes are the contract, so the agent branches on `0/1/2` rather than parsing prose.
- **Result**: on the seeded demo page the loop takes 163 detectable failures to 0, reproducibly.
