Two days into the build the client widened the requirement: hide the entire site from the public until launch, while their team and the Tātaki Auckland Unlimited reviewers could still see the real production site. A redirect rule has no way to let reviewers through.
- **What I did**: I put the site behind Cloudflare Zero Trust Access: allowlisted reviewers sign in with an email one-time passcode and see production exactly as visitors will, cookies, forms and anti-spam included. Narrow bypass applications, which Access matches before the site-wide one, exposed what had to stay public: the teaser and its newsletter path, the legal pages, the hero video, and the email webhook. The webhook case surfaced when Resend's delivery events started bouncing off the login screen. Testing that path end to end, I found a second bug: the webhook returned success while no rows were saved, because Postgres rejects an `ON CONFLICT` target that matches only a partial unique index. I replaced the partial indexes with plain unique ones in a migration and confirmed a real delivery event landing in the database.
- **Result**: One gate and a handful of path-scoped bypass applications ran the pre-launch window; the newsletter bypass used all five destination slots an Access application allows. Launch on 5 June was a single switch, followed by one announcement email to everyone who had signed up during the teaser phase.
- **Engineer's angle**: Edge-level access control versus application code; why the redirect rule was kept as a disabled draft for a future event; how an upsert that "succeeds" can silently drop data when the conflict target and the index disagree.
- **Plain version**: Until launch day only the client's reviewers could see the site, and opening it to everyone took one click.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *Why not password-protect it in the app?* Reviewers needed to see the same deployment the public would get, and a gate at the edge needs no code change between phases.
  - *How did you catch the database bug?* By following one real email from send to delivery event to database row, instead of trusting the 204 response.

#### S4. An AI event guide that cannot make up the facts

- **Kind**: implementation
- **Situation**: The contract asked for an AI assistant. A festival guide that invents a price or a date does damage, and an open AI endpoint on a public site is an invitation to abuse.
- **What I did**: I built the guide on the Vercel AI SDK behind a one-file provider abstraction, streaming answers from an OpenAI model, with voice in (speech-to-text) and voice out (text-to-speech). Its knowledge is compiled at build time from the site's own content, so it knows every dish, partner and FAQ without a database read. When the ticket structure changed, the guide kept giving the old answer: the visible pages had been updated but the generator never read the tickets file and the system prompt still described the old model. I fixed it, then removed the cause: every atomic event fact now lives in one schema-validated file that feeds the guide's "verified facts", the pages, the structured data and `llms.txt`, and the persona prompt holds no facts at all. In front of the model I added a Turnstile check on the first message, a per-visitor rate limit in Cloudflare KV and a short session cookie, and later a router that answers the most common atomic questions directly from the facts file.
- **Result**: The guide is live on every page with voice enabled, and everything it says traces back to content the client edits. When the client sent a master event knowledge base as the single source of truth, it went into the same facts layer the pages read.
- **Engineer's angle**: Grounding by build-time context instead of retrieval or tool calls, because the corpus is small and fixed; streaming canned answers over the same protocol as model answers; keeping the generated prefix stable for prompt caching.
- **Plain version**: The site has a chat helper that only knows what is on the site, so it cannot tell visitors something wrong.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *Why not RAG?* The whole knowledge base fits in the prompt; retrieval would add a moving part with no accuracy gain at this size.
  - *How do you stop abuse?* An anti-bot check before the first message, then a session cookie, and an hourly per-visitor limit stored at the edge.
  - *Was it worth building?* It was in the contract, and it answers from the same facts as the pages. I would collect traffic data before adding more optimisation (see In hindsight).

#### S5. WCAG 2.2 AA with a brand red that failed contrast

- **Kind**: implementation
- **Situation**: Tātaki Auckland Unlimited reviewed the site against the NZ Government Web Accessibility Standard (WCAG 2.2 AA). The brand's signature red did not reach 4.5:1 on the light backgrounds or on black, and the accessibility job in CI had been allowed to fail without blocking, which hid a wave of regressions when a site-wide banner went in.
- **What I did**: I split the colour into roles: the bright red only for decoration and large display type, a deeper red for all body text, links and buttons, and a lighter variant for red on black. When the client asked for a blue accent, the brand blue measured 4.13:1, so I added a darker blue for text and kept the bright one for non-text roles. I rebuilt the ticket selector from nested interactive `div`s into real radio inputs with labels, completed the standard keyboard pattern for the navigation dropdown, added a target-size check, and made the axe job blocking.
- **Result**: 39/39 axe-core tests passing on every push across Chromium, WebKit and Firefox; Lighthouse accessibility, SEO and best-practices scores at or above 90 on the measured routes; a written conformance statement delivered with the handoff.
- **Engineer's angle**: Design tokens as the enforcement point for contrast; why a non-blocking CI check is worse than none; what axe cannot check (keyboard flow, focus order, screen-reader sense), which I covered by hand.
- **Plain version**: I kept the brand's look but adjusted where each colour is used, so people with low vision can read every line.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *What did automation miss?* Keyboard-only navigation, focus visibility, heading order and screen-reader checks, done manually.
  - *How do you keep it from regressing?* The axe suite gates every push, and the colour rules are written into the project guide.

#### S6. Proving the site would hold up on launch day

- **Kind**: delivery
- **Situation**: The contract required a 1,000-concurrent-visitor load test and a strong mobile Lighthouse score. The Worker's starting plan was too tight: CPU time under load, and bundle size once the database and email code shipped; the client moved the Worker to Cloudflare's Standard plan.
- **What I did**: I ran a k6 profile against production on launch morning: ramp to 1,000 virtual users, hold, ramp down, across the busiest public routes, checking that each response was a real page and not an error page. For mobile performance I found that OpenNext on Workers did not run Next's image optimiser, so phones were downloading full-size photos; I built an offline AVIF/WebP pipeline with a `<picture>` component, trimmed font weights, lazy-mounted the AI widget and deferred the hero video.
- **Result**: 0.00% error rate over 113,320 requests in five minutes. The latency percentile ran above target, and the report explains why: a single home connection was generating all 1,000 users, while the same machine at 100 users stayed well inside the target. On the dishes page, mobile Performance went from 71 to 84. The home page, with a full-screen autoplay video the client chose, stayed below the target after I made the poster image load first; dropping the video on phones was the client's design call, so I documented the option rather than make it alone. In September the client replaced the hero video with a rotating dish-photo slideshow, a change he made himself.
- **Engineer's angle**: Separating server capacity from load-generator limits; the preload scanner ignoring `<video poster>`; why a field measurement (PageSpeed Insights) beats a local Lighthouse run on a congested connection.
- **Plain version**: I simulated a thousand people visiting at once and the site did not drop a single one.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *Did you hit the performance target?* Accessibility, SEO and best practices, yes. Mobile performance improved but the home page did not reach it while it carried the autoplay video; I said so in the report, and the client later replaced the video with a photo slideshow.
  - *How would you get a trustworthy latency number?* A distributed load generator, so the test is not limited by one uplink.

#### S7. After launch: the analytics showed nothing

- **Kind**: incident
- **Situation**: After launch the Google Analytics dashboard stayed empty, and Cloudflare Web Analytics showed zero visits. The client needed numbers to show sponsors.
- **What I did**: First I moved Google Analytics to Consent Mode v2 so measurement would not depend on the cookie banner. The dashboard was still empty, so I checked the output instead of the setup: no page-view request and no analytics cookie on a live visit. The cause was one line. My `gtag` shim pushed an array onto the data layer; gtag.js only treats an `arguments` object as a command, so every consent and config command had been silently ignored. I fixed the shim and confirmed real hits arriving. For Cloudflare's analytics I proved with network probes that its collection host was being blocked on the connections I tested from, not misconfigured, and wrote the rule that its numbers are a floor and never shown alone. During the same review a "near-empty database" turned out to be my local environment pointing at the development database branch; I re-queried production and corrected the record.
- **Result**: Google Analytics became the authoritative source with conversion events for tickets and forms, and the project docs now carry a "verify the output, not the plumbing" checklist.
- **Engineer's angle**: Why `function(){ dataLayer.push(arguments) }` is not equivalent to a rest-parameter array; how to distinguish a code defect from client-side blocking; checking which database a query actually hit.
- **Plain version**: The visitor counter was broken by a one-line mistake; I found it by checking what the page really sent, not what the settings said.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *How long was it broken?* From launch until I caught it within the first week of maintenance.
  - *What would have caught it earlier?* A launch checklist step that looks for a real visit in the analytics real-time view.

#### S8. The ticketing partner changed twice

- **Kind**: requirements
- **Situation**: The contract named "a third-party ticketing partner" without naming one. I built a Ticketmaster integration with tracked outbound links; then the festival chose Universe, Ticketmaster's self-serve platform.
- **What I did**: I replaced the integration with Universe's in-page checkout widget. In production the checkout showed "This content is blocked": the link's `target="_blank"` beat the widget script, the script loaded too late for early clicks, and the page's Permissions-Policy blocked payments inside the iframe. I fixed all three, then found Universe's embed endpoint itself failed for this listing. I switched to Universe's direct-link pattern, so no iframe of theirs could break the site, and kept the button disabled until the on-sale time. On launch day I removed the on-site tickets page: every "Get Tickets" button links straight to Universe with tracking parameters, the old URL redirects, and the ticket link lives in the event-facts file the AI guide reads.
- **Result**: Tickets sold through Universe from the on-sale date with no checkout running on the festival site, and traffic to the checkout measurable through tracked links.
- **Engineer's angle**: Debugging a third-party embed across CSP, Permissions-Policy and script-loading order; choosing the dependency with the smallest failure surface over the nicer UX.
- **Plain version**: When the ticket seller's widget kept failing, I sent buyers straight to the seller's own page so the website could not be the thing that broke.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *Was the first integration wasted?* Partly. I would now wait for the partner decision before building against an API.
  - *Why not keep fixing the embed?* The failing part was on Universe's side; a link out was reliable and kept attribution.

#### In hindsight

- **Preview on the real runtime from day one.** Most early failures were "works in Node, fails on Workers". Running the Workers preview before every push would have caught them before production did.
- **Raise the hero video trade-off before building it.** A full-screen autoplay video and a mobile performance target pull against each other. I measured the conflict after launch; I should have put the choice to the client at design time.
- **Check analytics output at launch.** The `gtag` bug sat unnoticed for days because I verified the setup, not a real hit. A launch checklist now does that.
- **Wait for data before optimising the AI guide.** I built a canned-answer router before there was traffic to show which questions visitors actually ask.
- **Build integrations after the partner is chosen.** The first ticketing integration was replaced within weeks.
- **Give the content editor feedback.** A rejected edit fails the build silently from the editor's point of view; a notice back to the editor would close that loop.
- **Use a distributed load generator.** It would have given a clean latency figure instead of one that needs an explanation.

### echook — story

Role: Creator and maintainer · Period: 2025-11 – present

#### In one breath

echook is a free, open-source add-on for three AI coding assistants (Claude Code, Cursor and OpenAI's Codex). It plays a sound, shows a desktop notification, reads the agent's reply aloud or posts to Slack when the agent finishes or needs permission, so a developer can look away from the screen while it works. It also draws a status bar showing how much of the agent's memory is used. You set it up by asking your AI assistant in plain English. I designed and built it and still maintain it: it supports three editors from one codebase, runs on Windows, macOS and Linux, and has 88 GitHub stars.

#### The problem

AI coding agents work for minutes at a time and then stop, either finished or waiting for a "may I run this command?" answer. The developer either watches the terminal or misses the moment. The editors' own notifications are thin: a bell or a single chime, nothing per event, and nothing that speaks, posts to a phone or warns before a usage limit.

The obvious answer is a one-line shell hook that plays a sound on "stop". That works on one machine and then breaks on the next: Windows plays audio differently from macOS, WSL cannot reach its own files from the Windows media player, and each editor registers hooks in its own format, which changes between releases. And a tool configured through flags and config files asks the developer to learn yet another surface, when the agent they already talk to could do that for them.

#### What I built

A Python program, standard library only, that each editor calls on every lifecycle event with the event's JSON. It decides from the user's preferences whether to play a sound, show a toast, speak or post a webhook, never blocks the agent, and logs each decision as structured JSON lines. Around it, a command-line tool with a JSON-only interface that the user's AI agent drives on their behalf, and a skill that maps a sentence ("snooze for an hour", "send alerts to my Slack") to the right command.

- 39 hook events (3 on by default) plus 47 separately switchable matcher variants, mapped per editor: Claude Code, Cursor and Codex.
- Four output channels: audio (two themes, voice or chimes), desktop notification, speech that reads the agent's actual final message, and webhooks to Slack, Discord, Teams or ntfy.
- Warnings before the 5-hour and 7-day usage limits, each fired exactly once.
- A status line with 33 configurable segments, including context-window and quota bars.
- A CLI with 41 subcommands, stable error codes with a suggested recovery command, and a `manifest` command that describes the whole surface as JSON.
- One canonical source synced into the shipped plugin by a build script, with CI failing on any drift; tests on Ubuntu, Windows and macOS across Python 3.9, 3.12 and 3.13.
- A product film made in code from the product's own interface (echook-promo-studio).

**Who owns it.** I build general-purpose tools like echook in my own time, on my own equipment, alongside full-time work, and I keep the IP. So I ask for a carve-out for that work in employment agreements. When I joined Engram's architect cohort in May 2026, the cohort agreement named claude-code-audio-hooks (echook's earlier name) and the rest of my prior work as my own property (`10-career.yaml` › engram). If an interviewer asks about IP clauses, that is the answer: I read the clause, and I ask for the carve-out up front.

#### S1. Designing the CLI for an agent, not for a person

- **Kind**: decision
- **Situation**: By early 2026 the tool had interactive installers and a configure script with menus. Users increasingly asked their AI agent to install and change it, and the agent stumbled on every prompt, spinner and "edit this file" instruction.
- **What I did**: In v5.0 (April 2026) I redesigned the contract around the agent as the operator. One CLI, `audio-hooks`, takes arguments and returns JSON only: no prompts, no menus. Every error has a fixed code (`AUDIO_FILE_MISSING`, `WEBHOOK_TIMEOUT`, `DUAL_INSTALL_DETECTED`, ...) and a `suggested_command`, so the agent recovers without scraping text. `audio-hooks manifest` emits every subcommand, hook, config key and error code as one JSON document so an agent can orient itself. A skill maps plain-English requests to commands. Anything an agent cannot do is returned as machine-readable `next_steps`. When a user tested v5.0.2 and found that my README claimed the agent could run `/reload-plugins` (it cannot: slash commands are REPL-only), I published v5.0.3 the same day correcting the claim and documenting the honest four-step install. In August I went further and replaced every claim in the README that a single search could refute with claims that can be checked, including an event count with its denominator.
- **Result**: The rule "the CLI is the only interface, JSON in, JSON out, no human-only path" is the first rule in the repo's agent guide and is enforced by tests for read-only commands and error-code coverage. 41 subcommands today.
- **Engineer's angle**: Designing for a non-human caller changes what "usability" means: determinism, stable codes and self-description matter more than friendly text. The `suggested_command` field turns an error into a plan. The cost is that the CLI has to be strict about input, which S8 shows the hard way.
- **Plain version**: I built the tool so that your AI assistant can operate it for you, so you never read the manual.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *Why JSON and not plain text with good messages?* An agent parses JSON reliably; text changes between versions and breaks whatever scrapes it. Error codes stay stable.
  - *What could the agent still not do?* Reload plugins inside Claude Code. That is the one manual step, and the CLI says so in `next_steps` instead of pretending otherwise.
  - *How do you stop the docs overclaiming?* Counts come from `audio-hooks manifest`, not from memory, and claims are worded so they can be checked against the code.

#### S2. Diagnosing silence and clipped sound from a user's report

- **Kind**: difficulty
- **Situation**: Two user reports, two platforms. On macOS 15 a user ([#4](https://github.com/ChanMeng666/echook/issues/4)) got "all is fine" from setup and then no sound at all. On Windows another user ([#14](https://github.com/ChanMeng666/echook/issues/14)) found that the last ~0.4 s of the permission-request sound was always cut off, and offered three possible fixes.
- **What I did**: For macOS I traced it to Sequoia's per-app notification permissions: the sound was being played through `osascript`, which runs via Script Editor, which has no notification permission by default, so the command exited 0 and did nothing. I moved sound to `afplay`, which needs no permission, and kept the popup as best effort. For Windows, the PowerShell player was torn down after a fixed `Start-Sleep -Seconds 3` while the clip was 3.4 s. Of the three options I chose to wait for the real clip length: poll the media player for its duration, sleep that plus 500 ms, with a bounded 10 s fallback. I rejected a bigger constant (it only moves the cliff) and detaching the player (the player lives inside the PowerShell process, so exiting early kills the sound), and wrote the reasoning back in the issue.
- **Result**: Both fixed the same day they were diagnosed (v4.1.0 for macOS, v5.1.2 for Windows); the macOS user confirmed "Now I have the sound." The fix covered all four PowerShell playback sites, including the WSL path, and two other clips that were also being clipped.
- **Engineer's angle**: "Exit 0 with no effect" is the hardest class of bug in a notification tool, because success and failure look identical from the caller. The Windows fix is about where the asynchrony really is: the Python layer was already fire-and-forget; the blocking wait was inside the child process, and that is where the clip length has to be known.
- **Plain version**: Users told me the sound was missing or cut short; I found the exact operating-system cause each time and fixed it the same day.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *Why not just make the sleep 5 seconds?* Any future clip longer than 5 s would break silently again; reading the real duration removes the constant.
  - *How did you test a sound bug?* By the numbers: file size, bitrate and ID3 tag gave the 3.4 s duration, and the fix was checked against the actual clips on Windows 11.
  - *What about the desktop popup on macOS?* It still needs the user to grant permission once; I documented that rather than hide it.

#### S3. A crash on every command, and the CI matrix it produced

- **Kind**: incident
- **Situation**: Days after the v5.0 plugin release, a user reported ([#10](https://github.com/ChanMeng666/echook/issues/10)) that every `audio-hooks` command crashed at import with `NameError: name 'Tuple' is not defined`. A module-level type annotation used `Tuple` without importing it, and Python evaluates those at import time. The release had also been tagged with the code still reporting the previous version.
- **What I did**: I applied the one-line import fix the reporter proposed, and chose it over `from __future__ import annotations` so that no runtime annotation introspection elsewhere would change. Then I added the guard that should have existed: a GitHub Actions workflow that, on every push and pull request, imports the runner (both the source copy and the plugin copy), runs `version`, `status`, `diagnose` and `test all`, and runs the unit suite, on Ubuntu, Windows and macOS with Python 3.9, 3.12 and 3.13. I also aligned every in-tree version string.
- **Result**: Shipped as v5.1.1 the next day. That 3 x 3 matrix is still the project's CI; by v7.1.0 it ran 795 test cases, and it later gained a no-drift check of the plugin copy and Claude Code's own plugin validator.
- **Engineer's angle**: The bug was trivial; the lesson was that nothing had ever imported the shipped file on a clean interpreter. The smoke job tests the artefact users run, not just the functions, and across the OS and Python versions users actually have.
- **Plain version**: One missing line broke the tool for everyone; I fixed it the next day and added automatic checks on three operating systems so that kind of break cannot ship again.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *Why three Python versions?* 3.9 is the oldest commonly installed; 3.12 and 3.13 are what new machines get, and annotation and typing behaviour differs across them.
  - *Why test the plugin copy separately?* Users run the plugin copy, which a build script produces; testing only the source would miss a stale or broken copy.

#### S4. One source, three editors

- **Kind**: decision
- **Situation**: Cursor (from 3.2.16) and Codex CLI added hooks. Each has its own registration format, event names and payloads, and Cursor can also run Claude Code's plugin hooks by itself. Three copies of the logic would drift.
- **What I did**: I kept one canonical source (`hooks/`, `bin/`, `audio/`, `config/`, `cursor-hooks/`, `codex-hooks/`) and a build script that syncs it into the shipped plugin layout, with CI running `build-plugin.sh --check` to fail on any drift. Per editor, only the registration template differs; the runner detects which editor called it from arguments or environment. For Cursor I handled the double-fire risk: a native Cursor install aborts with `DUPLICATE_BRIDGE` when the Claude Code plugin is present, and if forced, the runner suppresses the duplicate at run time. For Codex, hooks needed a feature flag in the user's own TOML config. I chose never to rewrite an existing file, because a round trip would destroy the user's comments and formatting: the installer writes the file only when none exists and otherwise returns `next_steps` telling the agent exactly what to add. Events Codex lacks are clean no-ops.
- **Result**: Native Cursor support shipped in v5.1.6 and Codex in v5.2.0 (May 2026), each with its own bridge-contract tests. Today the manifest maps Claude Code to 30 of the 39 canonical events plus all 47 variants, Cursor to 18 native events, Codex to 11. Codex support was not run against the real Codex binary until v7.1.0 (October 2026). That first live run, `codex exec` on Codex 0.143.0 and 0.162.1, found Codex refusing both of echook's hook files over extra top-level keys, so no Codex user had heard anything. v7.1.0 fixed the files, made `Stop` synchronous so headless runs play it, and was verified against the real binary on both versions and both install routes.
- **Engineer's angle**: The interesting failure mode is silent: a misnamed matcher becomes a permanent no-op, not an error. A contract test pins the chain from registration to handler to sound file in both directions, which is what makes such a break loud.
- **Plain version**: I made one program serve three different AI editors without copying the code three times.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *Why not edit the user's TOML with a parser?* The standard library cannot write TOML and a round trip loses comments; handing the edit to the agent is safer and keeps the tool dependency-free.
  - *How do you know which editor called?* An explicit `--invoker codex` argument for Codex, which sets no identifying variable, and environment variables for Cursor and Claude Code.
  - *What happens when an editor lacks an event?* The runner logs a debug line and exits 0; it never blocks the session.

#### S5. Renaming a project without breaking a single install

- **Kind**: delivery
- **Situation**: The project was called claude-code-audio-hooks. Once native Cursor and Codex support shipped, the name told newcomers it only worked with Claude Code. But the name was also baked into install commands, a plugin marketplace, data directories and users' saved settings.
- **What I did**: In v5.2.1 (May 2026) I did a "door-only" rename to echook: the GitHub repository, display names, docs, logo and status-line brand changed; the CLI command `audio-hooks`, the plugin slug, the `chanmeng-audio-hooks` marketplace name and every data path stayed exactly as they were. I relied on GitHub's permanent redirect for clones, pulls and marketplace fetches, documented the one-line marketplace refresh in case a client did not follow it, and kept old changelog entries verbatim as history.
- **Result**: No data migration, no rewritten config, no reinstall. Existing installs kept updating; stars, forks and issues carried over.
- **Engineer's angle**: Separating the brand (what people see) from the identifiers (what machines key on) made the rename a zero-migration change. The price is a visible inconsistency between the product name and the command name, which I accepted.
- **Plain version**: I renamed the product so the name matched what it does, without making any existing user do anything.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *Why not rename the command too?* It would break every script, alias and saved agent instruction that calls it, for a cosmetic gain.
  - *What if GitHub's redirect is ever broken?* Someone creating a new repository with the old name would break it; the changelog documents the manual marketplace refresh.

#### S6. Following an upstream hook API that keeps moving

- **Kind**: difficulty
- **Situation**: The editors' hook systems change often. In November 2025 Claude Code v2.0.32 began rejecting the settings format my installer wrote; a user reported it with a patch ([#1](https://github.com/ChanMeng666/echook/issues/1), [PR #2](https://github.com/ChanMeng666/echook/pull/2)). In July 2026 a subtler one: I had registered a sound on Claude Code's `WorktreeCreate` event, which turned out to be a *provider* hook. With any command registered on it, Claude Code hands worktree creation to that command and expects a path back; my hook returned none, so every worktree-isolated subagent failed. I found this one in my own use, not from a user report.
- **What I did**: For the format change, I integrated the user's fix the same day with credit and added automatic conversion of old entries. For `WorktreeCreate`, I shipped v6.3.4 removing both worktree registrations and their sounds, since they could never fire safely on any supported editor. Then I changed the process: before trusting an event's name, register a capture shim, provoke it, and record what it does in a measured behaviour log (`docs/EVENT_BEHAVIOR_NOTES.md`). Each upstream sync now reads Claude Code's release changes and binary, records which matcher values exist, and keeps a list of what was looked at and deliberately not registered (blocking or provider hooks among them).
- **Result**: The project is synced against a named Claude Code version (2.1.292 at v6.8.0, the last sync), with a re-sync procedure, and I filed upstream issues where Claude Code itself misbehaved (for example [anthropics/claude-code#90997](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/90997)).
- **Engineer's angle**: An event name describes when it fires, not what the host does with your handler. Some hooks are observational, some gate an action, some provide a result; registering on the wrong kind breaks the host, not your tool. Measuring before registering is the fix.
- **Plain version**: The AI editors keep changing how add-ons plug in; I learned to test each new plug-in point before using it, after one of them broke a feature of the editor.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *How did you find the WorktreeCreate problem?* In my own sessions: the editor's error said the hook "returned no worktree path", which only makes sense for a hook expected to produce output; the documentation confirmed it is a provider hook.
  - *How do you keep up with releases?* A written re-sync procedure against each new version, and a table of upstream issues being watched.

#### S7. "Upgrades killed the hooks": the bug was ours

- **Kind**: incident
- **Situation**: In late summer 2026 desktop notifications and spoken summaries went silent on Windows, and it looked as if recent Claude Code upgrades had broken hooks. I noticed it on my own machine; no user had filed it.
- **What I did**: I checked first whether upstream had changed: I compared the Claude Code binary across versions and found the payloads, event fields and hook discovery had not moved. The real cause was mine. The Windows toast and the speech path escaped text with an escaper written for macOS `osascript` and then placed it in a PowerShell string, where that escaping is wrong; any `"` (routine in a permission request that quotes a git command) made the script unparseable, so nothing appeared. The correct PowerShell escaper already existed in the same file. I verified the fix against PowerShell's own parser (three parse errors before, zero after), replaced the old tray-balloon API with a real Windows toast and an ordered fallback chain cached per OS release, and made the notification and speech functions report their real outcome, because they had returned success the instant a process started.
- **Result**: v6.5.1 (2026-09-01) repaired four failures, three of which had been invisible. Two error codes that had been defined since v5.0 and never emitted (`NOTIFICATION_FAILED`, `TTS_FAILED`) now fire with a reason.
- **Engineer's angle**: The deeper bug was observability: a fire-and-forget launch that reports `True` on spawn makes a dead channel look healthy. The fix was to make failure visible at the default log level, not only the escaping.
- **Plain version**: Notifications had gone silent on Windows; instead of blaming the editor update, I proved it had not changed and found a quoting bug in my own code.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *How did you prove upstream had not changed?* By reading the binary of two Claude Code versions for the event payloads and fields, not the documentation.
  - *Why cache the toast backend?* Probing means launching PowerShell, which is slow; a hook should not pay that on every event. The cache expires weekly and per OS release.

#### S8. An agent ran `install --help`, and the CLI installed

- **Kind**: incident
- **Situation**: On 2026-10-03 an AI agent exploring the CLI ran `audio-hooks install --help` on a machine that already had the plugin. The command ignored the flag, ran the legacy script installer, wrote 20 extra hook registrations into the user's Claude Code settings and reported success. Every event fired twice until the file was restored from the installer's own backup about three minutes later.
- **What I did**: I treated it as a contract failure, not a single bug. Following the thread found more: `upgrade --help` ran a real upgrade, several `set` commands wrote config when probed, `uninstall` did nothing on Windows while reporting success, and the test suite could write to the real data directory. In v6.6.0 `install` requires exactly one mode, `--help` in every spelling is side-effect-free for every subcommand, state-changing commands reject unknown arguments with `INVALID_USAGE` and change nothing, a script install on top of the plugin is refused, and uninstall became native on all three platforms: it backs up first and removes a file only if its content carries echook's marker, so a user's own same-named hook is left alone. In v7.0.0 I removed the script installer entirely, about 2,400 lines of shell and PowerShell with almost no CI coverage that no supported path needed, while keeping uninstall working for machines that still had it.
- **Result**: Tests now pin each rule (help is side-effect-free, install argument safety, read-only reporting commands). At v7.1.0 the suite has 795 tests passing; I also split the 4,972-line CLI and 3,155-line runner into one module per concern and checked the split by replaying 431 invocations against the old code with no difference.
- **Engineer's angle**: A tool built for agents will be probed by agents, and `--help` is the first thing they try. "Help must never have side effects" and "unknown input changes nothing" are the agent-era version of input validation. Deleting the legacy path removed the class of bug rather than patching it.
- **Plain version**: An AI assistant asked my tool for help and it installed itself twice; I made every command safe to explore and deleted the old installer that caused it.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *Why remove the installer instead of fixing it?* It duplicated what the plugin and the native Cursor and Codex installs already did, it was the source of the incident, and it had almost no test coverage.
  - *How do you uninstall safely from a user's settings?* Back up first, decide ownership by file content rather than file name, and report what was kept and why.
  - *How did you verify a big refactor changed nothing?* Ran the same invocations against the code before and after and compared exit codes, output, logs and files written; then planted defects to confirm the tests caught them.

#### In hindsight

- I would have put the import smoke test and the OS matrix in from the first release, not after a user found an import crash (S3).
- I would have measured each hook event's real behaviour before registering a sound on it; the `WorktreeCreate` rollback (S6) came from trusting a name.
- I would have made the CLI strict about arguments from the day I decided agents were its callers (S1). The `--help` incident (S8) was the predictable cost of a CLI that was agent-first in its output but still human-lenient in its input.
- Early releases flipped defaults with no migration and, once, three defaults at once (5.1.4), so users whose settings had been reset suddenly heard about three times more sound. I reverted them and added a committed baseline that fails CI on any flipped default; I should have had that rule earlier.
- Early READMEs overclaimed (a hands-free install, "complete" coverage). Wording claims so they can be checked against the code is a habit I wish I had started with.

### FemTech Weekend website — story

Role: Chief Technology Officer and sole engineer · Period: 2025-05 – present

#### In one breath

FemTech Weekend describes itself as China's first organisation built around women's health technology. I am its CTO, and I built and run its website on my own from Auckland: a bilingual English and Simplified Chinese site with research reports, founder stories and opinion pieces, plus everything its Shanghai Summit 2026 needed online: the event pages, application forms for founders and companies, a newsletter, and an admin page where the founder approves applicants in batches. The summit ran June 22–25, 2026, with 33 speakers headlined by Ida Tin, the Clue co-founder who coined the term "FemTech", and 26 organisers and partners.

#### The problem

FemTech Weekend is a small team led by its founder, Zhu Yihan, connecting women's-health founders, investors and researchers in China with the rest of the world. Its readers sit on both sides of that border, so every page has to exist in two languages and load well in both places. Its value is in what it publishes (market research, founder stories, commentary), not in a brochure.

Then the summit arrived. A four-day event needed speaker and partner pages, an agenda, and a way for founders to apply to pitch and for international companies to apply to the programme, with uploaded decks, confirmation emails and a review process. The founder had to be able to run all of that, and keep the site's content current, without waiting for me: I work remotely, in a different time zone, and there is no other engineer.

Tickets went through an external ticketing platform. What that could not carry was the organisation's own application questions, its bilingual editorial site, and a review flow that sends the founder's own branded decisions.

#### What I built

One Cloudflare Pages project. The site is a static Docusaurus build with three content collections (research, stories, opinions) in English and Simplified Chinese. Every server-side concern is a Cloudflare Pages Function deployed with it, so there is no backend server to run. Summit applications land in Neon Postgres; files go to Cloudinary; every email goes through Resend.

- **Editorial site**: research reports, founder stories and opinion pieces as MDX, bilingual on every page.
- **Shanghai Summit 2026**: the summit page (hero, a 3D globe of 40 countries, partners, speakers, programme, audience, venue, global network, sponsors), programme and pitch pages, and a gated agenda download.
- **Application system**: multi-step forms with draft auto-save, field validation, PDF and headshot uploads, duplicate detection and reference numbers, each writing to its own Postgres table.
- **Founder's admin page**: filter, search, annotate and approve or reject applicants in batches; each decision sends a branded email.
- **Newsletter**: subscription into a Resend audience segment with a branded welcome email.
- **Assistant**: a Gemini-backed chat endpoint for questions about the organisation.

**Two related organisations, two separate sites.** What the two share is practice, not code: server logic as Cloudflare Pages Functions, guides written in the founder's language, and, learned here in S3, a deploy that is only verified by a real request.

#### S1. Picking an editorial engine, bilingual from the first day

- **Kind**: decision
- **Situation**: The organisation already had a first-generation site I had built in Next.js with Notion behind it. The site's real job was publishing (research reports, interviews, commentary), for readers split between English and Chinese.
- **What I did**: The founder valued two things above the rest: how an article reads, and how easily a reader can find one. So I started a second generation on Docusaurus rather than growing the Next.js one. I added the Simplified Chinese locale on the first day, so every page, component string and blog collection was built with two languages from the start rather than translated later. Later I split the content into three blog collections (research, stories, opinions), each with its own layout, and moved all component text onto the translation layer so the two languages carry the same set of keys.
- **Result**: A content site the organisation can grow by adding MDX files, with Chinese and English kept in step. It later carried the summit as well, as React pages inside the same build.
- **Engineer's angle**: Docusaurus is not the usual pick for a brand site. It gives MDX, blog collections, i18n routing, sitemaps and search integration out of the box, and it builds to static files, which suits edge hosting. The cost is that anything app-like (forms, admin) has to live outside its model, which is why the server side became Pages Functions.
- **Plain version**: I chose a publishing tool built for articles in two languages, because publishing is what this organisation does.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *Why not stay on Next.js?* The client cared most about article presentation and search. Docusaurus gave both without building them (MDX layouts, blog collections, DocSearch); the app parts fit beside it as functions.
  - *How do you stop the two languages drifting?* Every string goes through the translation layer, and I ran a pass that removed dead keys and filled the missing ones until both languages had the same keys.

#### S2. Moving the server side to Cloudflare and ending with one copy of it

- **Kind**: decision
- **Situation**: The site first ran on Vercel, with its API as Node handlers using the official SDKs for Notion, Resend and Cloudinary, plus an Express server for local development. In January 2026 I moved hosting to Cloudflare Pages so the static site and its functions would deploy together at the edge. The SDKs failed in the Workers runtime.
- **What I did**: I rewrote each function in the Workers style and replaced every SDK call with plain `fetch` against the service's REST API. Because the move went endpoint by endpoint, for about a month the same behaviour existed in three places: the Vercel forwarders, the Express copy and the Cloudflare functions. In February I deleted the first two, ported the last two endpoints that existed only there, and made local development run `wrangler pages dev` so it uses the same runtime as production.
- **Result**: One implementation of every endpoint, one deploy, and local development that behaves like production. Every function since, including the whole summit system, was written once.
- **Engineer's angle**: The Workers runtime is not Node. SDKs that rely on Node internals break, so REST over `fetch` is the portable choice, at the cost of writing your own request and error handling. The bigger lesson was the three copies: a migration that runs in parallel needs an end date, or fixes land in one copy and not the others.
- **Plain version**: I moved the site to faster hosting, then deleted the old versions of the code so only one remained.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *Why Cloudflare?* The site and its functions deploy as one project at the edge, which suits an audience split between China and the rest of the world, and local development can run the same runtime.
  - *What broke in the move?* The SDKs, and the site's own URLs: the crawler and the canonical domain needed fixing afterwards (S7).
  - *What would you check next time?* Behaviour, not files: that each endpoint does the same thing after the move, not just that it exists.

#### S3. A production form that could not see its database

- **Kind**: incident
- **Situation**: On the day I shipped the rebuilt pitch application, submissions in production failed with a server configuration error. The function said the database connection string was missing, although I had set it as a secret.
- **What I did**: I added a temporary diagnostic to the error response and found the variable existed but was empty. Deleting and re-setting the secret with the CLI, and redeploying, did not fix it. Setting the value through Cloudflare's REST API on the project's production configuration, then redeploying, did. I removed the diagnostic the same day and wrote the episode into the project's developer guide, with the other pitfalls from that week.
- **Result**: Fixed the same day. The guide records that a secret listed as present can still be empty, so a deploy is only verified by a real request.
- **Engineer's angle**: `secret list` proves a key exists, not that it has a value. Diagnostics that reveal configuration belong in a response only for minutes, and should show type and length, never the value.
- **Plain version**: The form could not reach its database because a setting had been saved blank; I found it, fixed it and wrote down how to avoid it.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *How did you find it?* By checking the type and length of the variable at runtime instead of trusting the dashboard.
  - *What else went in the guide?* Saved drafts from an older form shape crashing the new form, a React state update overwriting another, PDF uploads needing Cloudinary's raw endpoint, and scroll position after submit.
  - *Would you do it differently?* A post-deploy smoke test that submits a test application would have caught it at deploy time.

#### S4. Letting the founder run selection without an engineer

- **Kind**: implementation
- **Situation**: Pitch and programme applications were arriving in Postgres. The founder needed to review them, decide, and tell each applicant, and she could not wait for me to run queries in another time zone.
- **What I did**: I built an admin page and three admin endpoints protected by an admin key. The page lists applications with filters, search and inline notes; the founder ticks rows and approves or rejects them in one action. The endpoint fetches the selected rows, keeps only those still "submitted", sends one batch of branded emails (approvals from the team address with a reply-to and the applicant's next steps; rejections from a no-reply address), and only then updates their status.
- **Result**: The team ran summit selection themselves, with every decision reaching the applicant as a branded email.
- **Engineer's angle**: Two safety properties. Filtering to "submitted" makes a repeated click harmless for rows already done. Sending before updating means an email failure leaves every row retryable. The remaining gap is the reverse case (emails sent, update failed), which would need an outbox or a per-row sent flag.
- **Plain version**: I gave the founder a screen where she can accept or turn down applicants in bulk, and the right email goes out automatically.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *How is it protected?* An admin key checked on every request; the static page holds nothing without it.
  - *Why batches?* Applications arrive in waves before deadlines, and one decision often covers many applicants.
  - *What would you add?* Per-user sign-in instead of a shared key, and an audit of who decided what.

#### S5. Handing publishing to a non-technical founder

- **Kind**: collaboration
- **Situation**: Speakers, partners, venue details and stories changed weekly before the summit. If every change went through me, the site would always be a day behind the founder's decisions.
- **What I did**: I kept all speaker, partner and agenda data in one typed data module, so a change is one edit in one place, and a wrong field shows as an error in the editor. I wrote a step-by-step guide in Chinese for adding a story in one or both languages, with templates for the front matter and cover images. Because a push to the main branch is the deploy, the founder can publish herself.
- **Result**: The founder has published stories, an opinion piece, new speakers, venue changes, partner logos and team bios herself, without me.
- **Engineer's angle**: The cheapest CMS for a small team can be the repository plus good structure: typed data, one file per concern, and a guide in the editor's own language.
- **Plain version**: I set the site up so the founder can update it herself, in her own language, the same day she decides something.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *Why not a CMS?* The content is versioned with the code, previews come from the same build, and there is nothing extra to host.
  - *What happens when she makes a mistake?* It shows on the live page within minutes of the push, and the change is one revert away in the history.

#### S6. The form was for the wrong applicant

- **Kind**: requirements
- **Situation**: The first version of the summit's programme application asked about individuals. Working through it with the founder, it became clear the programme was for international companies, investors and ecosystem leaders entering the Chinese market.
- **What I did**: I rebuilt it as a three-step company application (basic information, company snapshot, China objectives and readiness) with a company overview upload, and replaced the table behind it four days after the summit pages launched. The programme and speaker tables I replaced that day already held real applications. The same pattern repeated: a day-by-day timeline implied one ticket covered every day, so I replaced it with a selector showing which package fits the days a visitor picks; the speaker application page came down on 2026-03-30 because the line-up had enough speakers, with no new applications accepted and its table and API kept; the full agenda became a download behind a short form with a separate newsletter opt-in.
- **Result**: Each page asked for what the organisation needed to decide on, in both languages, and each agenda download is recorded as a lead with its own newsletter consent.
- **Engineer's angle**: Rebuilding a table is cheap only before it holds data, and these already held real applications when I dropped and recreated them. That was the mistake in this story: the right move was an additive migration that kept the old rows. After those first days the schema only grew additively. Each form kept the same lifecycle columns (status, timestamps, notes, reference number), so the admin page did not change when the questions did.
- **Plain version**: When we realised the form was asking the wrong people the wrong questions, I rebuilt it for the companies the summit was actually for.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *Did the admin page have to change with the forms?* No. Every form keeps the same lifecycle columns, so the review flow stayed as it was.
  - *What did the agenda gate protect?* Nothing secret; it collects interest and consent. A public agenda does not need signed links.
  - *Did anyone lose an application when you replaced the tables?* The tables held real applications when I replaced them. I would not do it that way again: with rows in a table, the change has to be additive.

#### S7. Making a migrated site findable and light

- **Kind**: implementation
- **Situation**: After the move to Cloudflare the site search crawler failed: the bare domain redirected to `www`, tag pages had doubled paths, and Chinese tags produced encoded URLs that returned 404. Separately, summit content had made the site heavy with large speaker, venue and report images.
- **What I did**: I made `www.femtechweekend.com` the canonical URL across config, sitemap, structured data and emails; fixed the tag permalinks; gave Chinese posts proper slugs. Then, in two passes weeks apart, I cut the image weight: in April 2026 I compressed 14 large images and shrank the social card from 6 MB to 240 KB; in May 2026 I re-encoded the heaviest assets.
- **Result**: The crawler errors these caused were fixed, and the May pass cut the site's image weight by about 67%.
- **Engineer's angle**: Every URL the site emits (canonical, sitemap, JSON-LD, email links) has to agree with the domain that serves it, or crawlers treat the redirect as a different site. Non-ASCII tags need explicit slugs.
- **Plain version**: I fixed the links so search could find the site again, and cut the image weight by about two thirds so it loads faster.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *Why does the social card matter?* It is fetched every time someone shares a link; 6 MB is slow or rejected by some platforms.
  - *How did you choose what to compress?* Largest files first, by measuring what the build shipped.

#### In hindsight

- **No automated tests and no CI.** The build was the only check. A smoke test that submits each form after deploy would have caught S3 before an applicant did, and behaviour tests would have made the S2 consolidation safer.
- **Send, then update, without an outbox.** Fine at this scale; a per-row "email sent" flag would close the remaining gap in S4.
- **Schema changes by hand.** Two early migrations replaced tables outright, in the first days after launch, and those tables already held real applications. Today I would use additive migrations run from the deploy, not from my laptop.
- **Three copies for a month.** I would set an end date for the parallel run before starting a migration.
- **Two homes for form data.** Older ecosystem and report-request forms still write to Notion while summit forms use Postgres; one home would make reporting simpler.
- **Shared admin key.** Good enough for one founder; per-user sign-in would give an audit trail.

### GAVIGO IRE — story

Role: Founding Principal Engineer, Activation, Execution & AI Systems (prev. Core Engineer) · Period: 2025-10 – 2026-10

#### In one breath

GAVIGO is a US startup working on a way past the app-install step: you scroll a phone feed and a game plays right in the scroll, with no app-store install. I was its founding engineer. I built the platform behind that feed: an AI orchestrator that watches what people scroll towards, keeps the next game on standby on a Kubernetes cluster and activates it as the viewer arrives, plus the investor dashboard that shows those decisions live. I took it from prototype to production on DigitalOcean, then moved it to Google Cloud in a cutover of about 30 minutes. In GAVIGO's proof stage the work measured a 78% application-level reduction in startup work: a controlled, application-level measurement, not a production SLA.

#### The problem

Every interactive experience on a phone sits behind the same funnel: discover it, open an app-store page, install, onboard, and only then interact. By the time the user arrives, the moment that made them want it has often passed. GAVIGO's founder, Saba Gecgil, wanted to show that the experience could be prepared before the viewer asked for it, and to show it to investors and partners with evidence, not a mock-up.

The obvious answer, "start a container when the user taps", was not enough for two reasons. A cold container start is slow, and most of that time is infrastructure work (scheduling, container creation, networking, readiness) that application code cannot touch. And a startup selling "activation" cannot claim more than it can measure: every number shown to an investor had to survive a technical reader. So the job was two jobs at once: make activation cheaper, and build the instruments that say honestly how much cheaper and where the limit is.

#### What I built

A single Go service, the orchestrator, sits behind a WebSocket hub. Phones and the dashboard stream scroll and focus events to it; it scores each piece of content on weighted personal, global and trend signals, and a rules engine decides which workload to warm, using the Kubernetes API to scale it towards ready before the tap. Every decision and every phase of an activation is timestamped and broadcast, so the dashboard shows the chain from decision to Kubernetes change to observed result rather than asserting it.

- **Orchestrator** (Go): WebSocket hub, scorer, rules engine with seven named triggers, a warm-pool manager with protected slots, an activation-phase timeline, and a proof layer that classifies each activation by the path it took (cold rebuild, prepared, warm reuse, live session return, checkpoint restore).
- **Clients**: a React + Vite dashboard for investors and operators, and a React Native / Expo app whose web build is the public feed. Audience presets (public, investor, operator) are applied when each WebSocket message goes out, so one catalogue serves three audiences.
- **Workloads**: one always-warm game server holding the whole self-hosted catalogue (23 games across four in-house studios), plus two ML/compute workloads used to prove state preservation, and an AI chat service.
- **State**: Redis for warm-pool state, sessions and measurement history; Supabase for sign-in and social data.
- **Delivery**: GitHub Actions with three required checks, images pinned by digest, production on Google Kubernetes Engine after the move from DigitalOcean.
- **Partner layer**: per-partner telemetry and an operator-gated proof report, an intake checklist for outside games, and a separate, switched-off lane for games hosted by third-party providers, walled off from the proof measurements.

#### S1. Choosing the checkpoint approach that could be measured on our own cluster

- **Kind**: decision
- **Situation**: In April 2026 the next proof question was whether an AI workload's state could survive its container being destroyed, and whether bringing it back was cheaper than starting cold. The cluster was a single small node, and the evidence had to be real within one phase of work.
- **What I did**: I evaluated four approaches and wrote the decision record. GKE Pod Snapshots would preserve full process memory but did not run on our machine type or cluster version and was still in limited preview. CRIU needed privileged containers and kernel features the node image might lack. DMTCP had no validation for an async Python web stack. I chose application-level checkpointing: the workload saves the state that matters in a light format and reloads it without its heaviest imports. I then built a three-tier ladder on a Python inference service (full ML library, then numeric arrays, then plain Python) so each step's saving could be measured separately, and a second test on a language-model workload that saved its conversation cache when the pod died and reloaded it in a fresh process.
- **Result**: The measurements GAVIGO now uses in public: a 78% application-level reduction, a controlled startup path cut from 4.45 s to 1.00 s, and about 140 ms to restore preserved AI state into a fresh process. I wrote down beside them where they stop. These are controlled application-level measurements, not a production SLA or a complete end-to-end activation time: infrastructure work still dominates the full path, and the record says so.
- **Engineer's angle**: The interesting part is the boundary. The ladder measured the application savings inside the container's start window, and the same runs showed that the rest of the end-to-end path is infrastructure work the application cannot remove. That turned "make it faster" into a precise next question for infrastructure-level restore, instead of a vague promise.
- **Plain version**: I picked the approach we could actually prove on the hardware we had, measured it, and wrote down honestly what the numbers did and did not mean.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *Why not CRIU, given published speed-ups?* It needed privileged containers and kernel support we could not guarantee on a managed node; too much infrastructure risk for one phase of work. I recorded it as the next candidate.
  - *What exactly is the 140 ms?* The application-level cost of fetching and loading the preserved state into a new process. Pod scheduling and readiness are outside it. (Controlled application-level measurement, not a production SLA.)
  - *Did the 78% make the product 78% faster?* No, and that is the point of the boundary note: it is application-level work removed, not end-to-end activation time. (Controlled application-level measurement, not a production SLA.)

#### S2. Moving production from DigitalOcean to Google Cloud in one evening

- **Kind**: delivery
- **Situation**: The platform first shipped on DigitalOcean Kubernetes in Singapore. When GAVIGO joined the Google for Startups Cloud Program (programme participation), production needed to move to Google Cloud without losing the live demo the company was showing.
- **What I did**: I rebuilt each layer for GKE: container registry to Artifact Registry; the DigitalOcean load balancer to a GCE Ingress with a global load balancer and Google-managed certificates (ending manual certificate renewal); load-balancer annotations to FrontendConfig and BackendConfig, including a long backend timeout so WebSocket sessions are not cut; services reshaped from one public load balancer each to cluster-internal services behind the Ingress. Deployments used the `Recreate` strategy so a single-node cluster could not deadlock on CPU during a rollout. When the first-choice region ran out of capacity, I created the cluster in another European zone. I kept a rollback plan and archived a full migration record in the repository.
- **Result**: Production moved on 2026-03-11 with about 30 minutes of downtime, mostly DNS propagation and certificate provisioning.
- **Engineer's angle**: The traps were platform-specific: WebSocket timeouts at the load balancer, health checks the Ingress requires, and rolling updates that cannot fit two copies of a pod on one small node.
- **Plain version**: I moved the whole live product to a different cloud provider in one evening, and it was down for about half an hour.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *What took the 30 minutes?* DNS propagation and the managed certificate being issued, not the workloads.
  - *What would you do differently?* Lower the DNS TTL well in advance and provision the certificate before the switch.

#### S3. The nightly benchmark that took every game offline

- **Kind**: incident
- **Situation**: In May 2026 the public feed started serving a fallback page instead of games, minutes after the daily benchmark job finished. All the self-hosted games share one always-warm game-server deployment.
- **What I did**: I traced it to an assumption from an earlier phase: one warm-pool slot per deployment. The benchmark re-acquired slots for every game without protecting them; when the slots expired, each eviction asked Kubernetes to scale "its" deployment to zero, and for the games that deployment was the shared one. Fixing that exposed the same symptom by a second route: the pool's budget was smaller than the number of protected games, so the benchmark itself overflowed it. I fixed all three causes: protected slots in the benchmark path, an eviction callback that never scales a shared deployment down, and a budget that fits the catalogue. Then I wrote the five-step checklist for adding a workload, because each step fails silently when skipped.
- **Result**: A full benchmark run afterwards finished with zero evictions and no scale-to-zero. The checklist sits at the top of the repository's agent instructions.
- **Engineer's angle**: An abstraction that is correct for one-to-one content-to-deployment mapping is wrong for a shared deployment; the fix belongs at the eviction callback, not in more protection flags.
- **Plain version**: A routine test was quietly switching the games off overnight; I found why, fixed it at the root, and wrote down how to avoid it next time.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *Why didn't monitoring catch it?* The fallback page returned a normal response. Later I changed the telemetry so the fallback page no longer counts as a successful load.
  - *Why a checklist and not code?* Some steps are configuration and catalogue data that live outside the code; the checklist names each one.

#### S4. Compression had never worked in production

- **Kind**: difficulty
- **Situation**: In July 2026 a partner studio pushed back on our size limit for outside games. Checking whether their build could fit, I measured what our server actually sent.
- **What I did**: The nginx config had compression switched on, yet production sent everything uncompressed: dashboard, mobile app, games and investor deck. The cause was one default. nginx treats a request as "proxied" if it carries a `Via` header, and by default does not compress those; Google's load balancer adds `Via` to every request. Laptops and docker-compose send no such header, so it worked everywhere except production, and survived the cloud migration and every review. I proved it with the same file and one header toggled, fixed it with one directive, tuned the related settings, and told the founder that a telemetry series would now drop, so that a before/after chart would not be misread.
- **Result**: Every asset on the site now goes out compressed. I also told the founder plainly that the partner had been right to push back on our number.
- **Engineer's angle**: A setting that reads correctly and fails only behind the real load balancer; the only place to see it is the live response headers.
- **Plain version**: The site had been sending files much bigger than needed to every visitor, because of one hidden setting; I found it and fixed it.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *How did you prove the cause, not just the fix?* Same nginx, same file: no `Via` header gave compressed output, adding `Via` gave none.
  - *What else did it affect?* The bytes-per-activation telemetry; I flagged the step change rather than letting it look like a product change.

#### S5. Making production hard to hit by accident

- **Kind**: decision
- **Situation**: In July 2026 a second engineer wanted to test changes against the cloud cluster, and the founder offered to grant whatever access was needed.
- **What I did**: Before saying yes I checked what the orchestrator would do on a laptop. Outside a cluster it fell back to whatever `kubectl` pointed at and defaulted to the production namespace, and a permission refusal was only logged as a warning. A local test pointed at the wrong context could have reached the production namespace. I changed the orchestrator to refuse to start outside a cluster unless a namespace is named, showed how to run the same Kubernetes code against a local `kind` cluster, and asked for the existing CI to become a required check on `main`. I then found the rule was configured but not enforced on our GitHub plan, and that the mobile typecheck job was missing from the required list, and raised both.
- **Result**: The founder upgraded the organisation's GitHub plan; `main` now needs a pull request, an approval and three green checks, with no admin bypass. Local-first testing became the agreed rule.
- **Engineer's angle**: A coordination ritual (taking turns on the cluster) cannot prevent a failure that needs only one person. The safety came from explicit namespace selection and enforced CI, and I checked enforcement through the API rather than trusting the settings page.
- **Plain version**: before granting new access I checked where a local test could reach, made the safe default explicit, and made the safety rules enforced rather than just written down.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *Why not a separate test cluster?* The cluster was one small node; a second one was another environment to run, and a local `kind` cluster covered the code under test.
  - *Why is the mobile typecheck job load-bearing?* The Expo export transpiles without typechecking, so type errors would otherwise reach production.

#### S6. Renaming a metric instead of overclaiming

- **Kind**: requirements
- **Situation**: In August 2026 the founder wanted a public beta with games supplied by a hosted-game provider, gated on whether users reached a first playable moment. The first real run showed a long run of video ads before the first game of a session.
- **What I did**: I asked the founder to request pre-roll off from the provider before the account went live, and explained why: our "reached first play" signal was a short dwell, which an ad satisfies without the user seeing the game. I tried to take a start signal from the provider's player and could not receive it without their cooperation. So I redesigned the gate: count only the second and later games in a session, where no ad plays; require a no-error state, which catches titles that play an ad and then fail; rename it "engaged rate" because we cannot observe play inside someone else's game; and keep the excluded first games as our own read on ad exposure. Later I found the counter could not yet be computed, said so plainly, and recommended waiting for a provider call that could change the definition.
- **Result**: The founder accepted the definition and the rule that its four numbers ship together. The acceptance criteria I wrote for providers (no pre-roll before first play, lifecycle events to the parent page, wrapper telemetry, licence verification) became the company's provider questionnaire. The sweep concluded that free ad-funded inventory with a clean first play was not available to us, and the hosted lane stayed off.
- **Engineer's angle**: Designing a measurement that does not move when an outside setting changes, and versioning the definition instead of silently changing it.
- **Plain version**: When a number would have flattered us, I changed what we measured and what we called it, so the company would decide on real data.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *What did the redesign cost?* Smaller samples: one-game sessions contribute nothing, so the gate carries a minimum sample and always reports it.
  - *Why not suppress the provider's ads?* Using their catalogue without their monetisation was not acceptable; we asked whether it was offered, not whether we could force it.

#### S7. Redis had gone, and the health check said healthy

- **Kind**: incident
- **Situation**: In August 2026 I found production had been running without Redis for days. Nothing was persisted, and `/api/v1/health` reported healthy throughout.
- **What I did**: Root cause: the client pinged once at boot and returned nil on failure with no retry, and with both pods starting together on one node, losing that race was the normal outcome. Every write was then dropped quietly behind nil guards. Two things hid it: Go's typed-nil trap (a nil pointer in a non-nil interface) and a status field that was hardcoded. I rebuilt the client to exist even when unreachable, re-probe in the background and self-heal, and made health report "degraded". I kept HTTP 200 on purpose, because the liveness probe judges on status code alone and a 503 would have turned a degraded dependency into a crash loop. Tests run against a fake Redis server and were mutation-checked in both directions.
- **Result**: Redis reconnects on its own after a boot race or restart, and the health endpoint now tells the truth.
- **Engineer's angle**: The typed-nil interface, the probe-design trade-off, and a race the race detector caught in my own first draft.
- **Plain version**: The database cache had silently stopped working while the system said all was well; I made it recover by itself and made the status honest.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *Why not return 503 when Redis is down?* Both probes use that endpoint; 503 would have the pod killed over and over for a dependency it can work without.
  - *How do you know the tests test the bug?* Putting the old `return nil` back fails three tests, one named after the outage.

#### S8. Reviewing a colleague's measurement code against the real cluster

- **Kind**: collaboration
- **Situation**: In July 2026 the second engineer opened a pull request to measure whether image pre-pulling helped real activations, by watching Kubernetes `Pulled` events. I suspected the watch would replay old events on reconnect but was not sure.
- **What I did**: Rather than ask them to prove my hunch, I tested it myself against our cluster: a watch with no resource version replayed every existing object as "added". On every reconnect, old pulls would be counted again, unevenly, skewing the hit rate while still looking plausible. I proposed the standard List-then-Watch pattern with resume on `410 Gone`, and also pointed out the RBAC permission the watch needed. I set the review order across their two PRs so the smaller, safer one landed first. In the write-up I also described my own two false negatives on the way.
- **Result**: The fix was merged in their PR; the measurement counts each pull once.
- **Engineer's angle**: Kubernetes watch semantics (synthetic ADDED events, resource versions, compaction), and a recurring pattern I named: silent failures that look exactly like a clean negative.
- **Plain version**: I checked a teammate's measurement code against the real system, found it would quietly count things twice, and helped them fix it.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *What were your two false negatives?* One test watched a namespace with no events, so "no replay" was an empty question; the other swallowed a file-not-found in a try/catch and reported "no events".
  - *How did you keep the review constructive?* I said their filter was right for the case they were solving and that this was a second case only visible on reconnect.

#### In hindsight

- I would have built the "does this fail silently?" check into the platform from the start. The benchmark outage, the missing compression, the Redis outage and the replayed watch events all looked like success from the outside. A health signal that says "degraded" and a test for each negative should have come first, not after.
- The single-node cluster shaped too much: rollout strategy, test isolation and benchmark noise all followed from it. I would have argued earlier for a separate small test environment, or written down why we did not need one.
- I documented decisions in the repository as I went, which made the handover straightforward. I would also have recorded chat decisions in the repository from day one: the team chat kept only 90 days, and at least one settled assessment had to be redone because its record was gone.
- I sometimes reported a problem as worse than it was before checking (the metric counter that "could never have run" was a line in a spec, not running code). I now check first, then report.

### Google News MCP Server — story

Role: Creator and maintainer · Period: 2024-12 – present

#### In one breath

AI assistants such as Claude cannot answer "what happened today?" from what they learned in training. I built a small open-source plug-in, a Model Context Protocol server, that lets them search live Google News and get the articles back sorted by topic. Its first commit landed 35 days after Anthropic launched the protocol, it was on npm two days later, and it has since been listed across 15+ MCP directories and named no. 10 in DataCamp's "Top 10 MCP Servers & Clients for AI Workflow Automation in 2026".

#### The problem

Anthropic published the Model Context Protocol (MCP) on 25 November 2024: one standard way for an AI client to call outside tools. In the first weeks the catalogue was a handful of reference servers (filesystem, GitHub, Postgres, search), and none of them answered questions about current events. A model cannot know this morning's news, and asking it to browse a search engine gives it pages of markup to read through.

What was needed was not a scraper but a tool shaped for a model as the caller: a small, typed interface the client can describe to the model, results that arrive already cleaned and grouped, and failures the model can read and act on. It also had to install the way early MCP users installed things, through one line of `claude_desktop_config.json`.

#### What I built

A TypeScript server on the official MCP SDK, run by the AI client as a subprocess over stdio. It exposes one tool, `google_news_search`, forwards the call to SerpAPI's Google News engine, and returns the articles as plain text grouped into five topics, newest first, with source, date, summary and link on each. It is MIT licensed and published on npm as `@chanmeng666/google-news-server`.

- **One tool, seven optional string parameters**: `q`, `gl` (country), `hl` (language), and four tokens (topic, publication, story, section) that let a model drill into a topic, a publisher or the full coverage of one story.
- **Validation before the network**: a TypeScript type guard rejects malformed arguments as a protocol error; upstream failures come back as a readable tool result.
- **Post-processing for the model**: results flattened from SerpAPI's nested shape, grouped (AI & Technology, Business, Science & Research, Healthcare, General) and sorted by date.
- **Ways in**: `npx -y @chanmeng666/google-news-server` from npm with `SERP_API_KEY` set, a Docker image built from the repository's Dockerfile, and a `.mcpb` bundle (not yet tested as a one-click install). Smithery also built it from `smithery.yaml` until the listing was withdrawn (gone by 2026-10-15).
- **Readable by machines**: `llms.txt`, a `manifest.json`, schema.org `structured-data.json`, and since 2026-10 a one-screen README with the full text in `docs/overview.md` for the reader's own coding agent.

#### S1. Shipping into a protocol that was five weeks old

- **Kind**: delivery
- **Situation**: MCP launched on 25 November 2024. Its SDK was at 0.6, the directories that now index thousands of servers did not exist yet, and the official servers repository was where people looked.
- **What I did**: I made the first commit on 30 December 2024 against `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 0.6.1 and published version 1.0.0 to npm on 1 January 2025, after moving the build output from `build/` to `dist/` and making the package installable with `npx`. The same days I opened listing pull requests: to `punkpeye/awesome-mcp-servers` (#163, where I also brought the Chinese and Japanese READMEs back in line with the English one), to the `mcp-get` registry (#62) and to the official `modelcontextprotocol/servers` README (#445). I turned on Renovate on 2 January, which moved the SDK to 0.7 and then 1.x that same day.
- **Result**: The awesome-mcp-servers and mcp-get pull requests were merged on 1 January 2025, the mcp-get one within an hour. PulseMCP featured the server in its Weekly Pulse newsletter as "a newly-released, well-documented approach to pulling news data into MCP clients like Claude". I closed the official-repository pull request myself on 9 January 2025, unmerged.
