- **Engineer's angle**: Building on a 0.x SDK in its first month means the API can move under you. Keeping the surface tiny (one `Server`, two request handlers, stdio) is what let a major SDK bump land as a dependency update rather than a rewrite.
- **Plain version**: I built one of the first news tools for a brand-new AI standard and got it into the places people were looking within days.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *Why stdio and not HTTP?* Desktop clients at the time launched servers as child processes and spoke JSON-RPC over stdin/stdout. That needs no port, no auth and no hosting, which is what a first-week user wants.
  - *Why SerpAPI instead of scraping Google News?* It returns structured JSON for the Google News engine, so the server's work is shaping results for a model, not parsing HTML that changes without notice.
  - *What happened to the official listing?* I closed that pull request unmerged on 9 January 2025; the server reached users through the community directories instead.

#### S2. Unblocking Windows users two days after launch

- **Kind**: difficulty
- **Situation**: On 27 November 2024, two days after MCP launched, npm-based servers would not connect to Claude Desktop on Windows machines that used Node Version Manager, while Python servers launched through `uvx` worked. Mine was one of those machines.
- **What I did**: I opened issue #76 in `modelcontextprotocol/servers` with my environment and configuration, and half an hour later posted a step-by-step workaround: install the servers globally, then point the client's `command` at the absolute path of `node.exe` and the `args` at the installed server's entry file, instead of relying on PATH resolution through NVM's shims.
- **Result**: Several Windows users replied in the thread that the steps fixed their setup. A maintainer closed the issue the same day as a duplicate of an upstream bug the team was already fixing, so my steps were a workaround until that fix shipped. The same section is in the server's own documentation (`docs/overview.md`, "Solution for MCP Servers Connection Issues with NVM/NPM").
- **Engineer's angle**: The failure was in process launch, not in MCP: the desktop client spawned `node`/`npx` without the shell environment NVM relies on. Absolute paths remove the dependency on PATH entirely.
- **Plain version**: When the new standard would not start on many Windows computers, I worked out why and wrote the fix that people used until the official one arrived.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *How did you find the cause?* Python servers through `uvx` connected and every `npx` server failed, which pointed at how Node was being located rather than at any one server.
  - *Was it the right fix?* It was a workaround. The real fix belonged in the client, and the maintainers were already on it.

#### S3. Designing a tool whose caller is a language model

- **Kind**: decision
- **Situation**: The "user" of `google_news_search` is a model reading a JSON Schema and a description, deciding what to send, then reading what comes back. Every parameter it misunderstands and every byte of noise in the result costs the person a worse answer.
- **What I did**: I exposed one tool with seven optional strings rather than a family of tools, because SerpAPI accepts either a query or one of four tokens and the model should only have to choose once. `gl` and `hl` default to `us` and `en`. In `src/types.ts` a type guard checks every field before any network call; a bad call is rejected with the SDK's `InvalidParams` error. An upstream failure is not thrown: it comes back as a normal tool result with `isError: true` and SerpAPI's own message, so the model can see what went wrong. Results are flattened and grouped into five topics before they reach the model, newest first, as plain text with source, date and link on every article. `zh`, which SerpAPI's Google News engine rejected as an interface language, is mapped to `en` before the request.
- **Result**: The tool needs no instructions beyond its schema. Glama grades the server A for licence and A for quality.
- **Engineer's angle**: The two error channels. A protocol error tells the client it called the tool wrongly; an `isError` result is data the model reads and can recover from (retry with other terms, or tell the user the service is down). Mixing them up either hides failures from the model or breaks the client.
- **Plain version**: I designed the tool so an AI can use it correctly on the first try and understand what went wrong when it does not.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *Why plain text and not JSON?* The consumer is a model writing an answer for a person. Grouped, labelled text is what it would have to produce from JSON anyway, and it carries the links through.
  - *Why are all parameters optional?* A query and a story token are alternatives; making `q` required would block the drill-down calls.
  - *How do the tokens get to the model?* SerpAPI returns them in its results (the topic menu links carry a `topic_token`), so a model can follow up on a topic it has just seen.

#### S4. Getting found: lists, directories and the people who run them

- **Kind**: collaboration
- **Situation**: MCP users find servers by browsing catalogues, not by searching GitHub. In 2025 a wave of directories appeared, each wanting metadata, a badge or a deployment config.
- **What I did**: I submitted the server to the curated lists myself and reviewed and merged what the directory teams proposed: Smithery's team contributed a Dockerfile and `smithery.yaml` (PR #13) so Smithery could build and run the server from source with the user's key passed in as configuration; the Glama listing badge (PR #1); PulseMCP's Top Pick badge (PR #16); a security-scan badge (PR #19); Archestra's trust-score badge (PR #27); a hosted-deployment link (PR #34); and an end-to-end test with model-graded evaluations from the author of the `mcp-evals` package (PR #18).
- **Result**: By 2026-10-13 the server was on 10 directory sites and in 12 curated lists and registries on GitHub, led by punkpeye/awesome-mcp-servers. Smithery's listing was withdrawn by 2026-10-15, which leaves 9 directory sites. It carries PulseMCP's Top Pick badge, was named no. 10 in DataCamp's Top 10 (2025-07-10), and has a dedicated Skywork AI article. A third party republished it on npm as `@iflow-mcp/google-news-server`. DataCamp was still the top referrer in the repository's GitHub traffic in the 14 days to 2026-10-13.
- **Engineer's angle**: Each channel builds a different artefact. Docker (and Smithery, while it was listed) builds from the repository, so it tracks `main`; the npm package is the snapshot that was published. Knowing which install path runs which code matters when a user reports a bug.
- **Plain version**: I put the tool where AI developers look for tools, and the people who run those catalogues came to feature it.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *Which channel mattered most?* By the record, DataCamp: it was still the top referrer in the repository's GitHub traffic in October 2026, more than a year after the article.
  - *Did you write the Dockerfile?* No. Smithery's team proposed it with the Smithery config; I reviewed and merged it, and it has been kept current by dependency updates since (now `node:24-alpine`).

#### S5. Supporting users of a free tool

- **Kind**: collaboration
- **Situation**: Once the server was listed, people I had never met started installing it from source and asking for things.
- **What I did**: When a user could not find `dist/index.js` (issue #17), I saw that the Quick Start skipped the build step and rewrote it in order: install, build, point the config at the built file, start. When two users asked for news by category and date range (issue #15), I explained that the server did not expose it, that SerpAPI supports it through its `tbs` parameter, and where in `src/index.ts` the change would go. Renovate keeps the dependencies moving; I review and merge its pull requests.
- **Result**: Issue #17 was closed after the README change. The repository has 129 stars and 21 forks, and npm counts 10,354 downloads between 2025-04-13 and 2026-10-13.
- **Engineer's angle**: For an open-source tool, the README is the interface for humans the way the schema is the interface for models. Issue #17 was a documentation bug, and treating it as one fixed it for everyone after.
- **Plain version**: When people got stuck, I fixed the instructions so the next person would not.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *How do you decide what to add?* The server is in maintenance: it is kept healthy and current, and no features are planned.
  - *How much time does it take?* Little: dependency pull requests, the occasional issue, and directory requests.

#### S6. Writing for the machine reader

- **Kind**: implementation
- **Situation**: By 2025 people also found tools by asking an AI assistant, and MCP clients started to accept packaged bundles. Marketing prose in a README is the hardest thing for either to use.
- **What I did**: In September 2025 I added `llms.txt` (a usage guide written for agents), schema.org `structured-data.json`, a `manifest.json` describing the tool, its parameters and the required `SERP_API_KEY`, and a packaged `google-news-server.mcpb` meant for one-click setup in Claude Desktop. In October 2026 I cut the README to one screen (the card, the film, the one config block, one diagram) and moved the full text to `docs/overview.md`, with a pointer telling the reader to hand that file and `llms.txt` to their own coding agent.
- **Result**: The repository reads in seconds for a person and in full for an agent; the same pattern is now used across the product READMEs in this profile.
- **Engineer's angle**: Separate the audiences rather than compromise: a human needs the shortest path to "it works", an agent needs every parameter and failure mode spelled out, and one document serves both badly.
- **Plain version**: I wrote one short page for people and one complete page for AI assistants.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *Does `llms.txt` do anything?* It is a convention, not a standard: a plain text file an agent can read without parsing a styled page.
  - *Why move text instead of deleting it?* Agents and contributors still need the troubleshooting and parameter detail; it moved to `docs/overview.md`.

#### In hindsight

- **Release from a pipeline, not by hand.** For almost two years the npm package was the 1.0.0 published on 1 January 2025, built from an early commit, while the repository moved on (SDK 1.x, later fixes). Smithery (while listed) and Docker built from `main`, so the install paths ran different code. In October 2026 I cut 1.0.1 from the current source (tagged and released on GitHub, notes in the changelog). A tag-triggered publish workflow would have kept them in step from the start.
- **The topic grouping is cruder than it looks.** It is a keyword regex over title and snippet with no word boundaries, so `ai` also matches inside words such as "said" and "again", and a lot of general news lands in AI & Technology. Word-boundary matching, or letting the model group the results, would have been more honest.
- **Document only what the code does.** The docs and manifest state a rate limit, a concurrency cap and a one-hour cache that the server does not implement; those are not mine to promise. Some error strings are in Chinese, which an English-speaking model or user cannot act on.
- **Test the bundle before offering it.** The `.mcpb` bundle was never installed in a client, so it should not be described as a one-click install until it has been.
- **Tests before badges.** The only automated test came from an outside contributor's evaluation package. A small contract test of the tool schema and the result formatting would have caught the points above.

### She Sharp — story

Role: Senior Full Stack Engineer & Website Team Lead · Period: 2025-07 – 2026-09

#### In one breath

She Sharp is a volunteer-run New Zealand charity for women in technology, with 96+ events since 2014. Its founder, Dr Mahsa Mohaghegh (McCauley), recruited me as the senior engineer the charity did not have. Over 13.3 months I replaced its no-code website with a platform it owns (AI mentor matching, member dashboards, Stripe billing), moved its 1,549-person mailing list off a marketing vendor with 0 failed sends, and wrote its recurring work down as 11 agent skills a non-engineer can run. When I left in September 2026, I handed over to two maintainers with a written runbook, and the platform is still the charity's live site.

#### The problem

In July 2025 the charity ran on rented software: the website inside Webflow, the mailing list and its consent history inside Mailchimp, the artwork in Canva, and eleven years of decisions in Slack. Each tool was a sensible choice for a committee of volunteers. Together they meant that the organisation's own record sat somewhere it could neither read in bulk nor take away. The previous move, from WordPress to Webflow in 2023, had cost the second half of that year re-entering every past event by hand.

The obvious answer was a better site builder. It would not have been enough. The mission needed things no drag-and-drop builder expresses: member roles (mentor, mentee, admin), AI mentor matching, paid membership, consent records the charity controls, and Slack-integrated operations for a team of volunteers. And a second migration had to avoid repeating the first: the data had to come out cleanly.

#### What I built

A Next.js 15 application on Vercel, in a repository the charity holds, backed by a Neon Postgres schema of 39 tables and 33 enums. The public site is prerendered from data files; the same app runs the member dashboards, an admin area, a slide-deck player for events and the charity's email. Around it sit Slack bots, three scheduled jobs and the agent skills that let volunteers run the event and newsletter cycle.

- **Member platform**: sign-up by password or Google/GitHub, one account that can hold several roles at once, and three role-permissioned dashboards.
- **AI mentor matching**: a rule-based pre-filter, then gpt-4o-mini scoring against an explicit five-part rubric, a rule-based fallback, and an admin who approves every match.
- **Membership and donations**: Stripe checkout that issues an invitation code tied to the payment, so email, payment and account stay linked.
- **Email the charity owns**: double opt-in, four sender streams, one call site for the email provider, and the consent record in its own database.
- **Slack**: a `/event` command that turns a plain-English request into a validated pull request, weekly mentorship and funding digests, and a weekday triage reader that never marks anything read.
- **11 agent skills**: event setup, newsletter, posters, decks, promo video, mailing list and contact replies, with an orchestrator that checks an event and names the skill that closes each gap.
- **Five builds around it**: the Her Waka teaching site, the Aotearoa AI Hackathon event assistant, the hackathon's 91-slide event deck, the Makey Makey workshop for teenagers, and the Monthly She# newsletter.

#### S1. Choosing the new stack by how the data comes back out

- **Kind**: decision
- **Situation**: The charity's 2023 move from WordPress to Webflow had no plan for the data, so a volunteer team spent half a year retyping events. Webflow in turn had no bulk media export and kept code export behind a plan the charity had already left.
- **What I did**: I made "how does the data come back out?" the first test for every choice, before features. That ruled out another hosted site builder and led to a Next.js app in the charity's own GitHub organisation with Postgres it can dump. Because Webflow could not export, I wrote a Python crawler that pulled the old site's content into structured JSON (1,748 images, 707 MB, 11 files): events, podcasts, galleries, news and pages from the site, plus event details from the ticketing platform's structured data, with banner images re-requested at 1,600 px instead of the 500 px the pages served, URL de-duplication across scrapers, and a Wayback Machine lookup for images that had already gone dead. I rebuilt the legacy images from the old pages' own markup, and added a CI check that fails if any event page loses an image. In the middleware I kept a rule that 308-redirects Webflow's old pagination URLs to clean ones.
- **Result**: The new site launched without retyping, the old links still resolve, and the platform now does what Webflow could not (memberships, matching, billing, dashboards). Its content lives in files and tables the charity holds.
- **Engineer's angle**: A migration is finished when the old world's links still work, not when the new site goes live. The 308 (not 301) keeps the request method; the image check turns "nothing was lost" into a gate rather than a hope.
- **Plain version**: I picked the tools by asking how easily the charity could leave them, so this move would be the last painful one.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *Why not a better no-code tool?* The requirements (roles, matching, billing, consent records) were beyond what builders express, and the lock-in was the original problem.
  - *What could not be exported?* The images and the historic event register; both were recovered from the published pages while they were still being served.
  - *Isn't Vercel also rented?* Yes, but it hosts code the charity owns; moving it means redeploying a repository, not rebuilding a site.

#### S2. AI mentor matching that never pairs anyone on its own

- **Kind**: implementation
- **Situation**: My mandate included AI mentor-mentee matching. A volunteer programme can afford neither wrong pairings nor a feature that stops when an API is down.
- **What I did**: I built a two-stage pipeline. A cheap rule-based filter scores every pair on basics (skills, industry, meeting format) and only promising pairs reach gpt-4o-mini, which scores them at temperature 0.3 against an explicit rubric: skills 35%, goals 30%, MBTI 15%, industry 10%, logistics 10%. Each answer is schema-validated, cached per pair in Redis and retried with exponential backoff. If the model is unavailable, the same weights are applied by rules and the result is marked low-confidence for manual review. An admin approves every match before anyone is paired. In the schema, a person is one user with one row per role, so someone can mentor and be mentored at once with no special case.
- **Result**: Matches arrive with five sub-scores and a written reason, and an admin makes the call. The queue keeps working when the AI does not.
- **Engineer's angle**: Cost control, explainability and availability come from three separate choices: the pre-filter, the explicit weights, and the fallback using the same formula. Mentor and mentee data is split between the imported form and the profile, and a single resolver walks both; reading one table alone is what once made avatars disappear across many endpoints.
- **Plain version**: The AI suggests mentor pairs and explains why, and a person always makes the final decision.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *Why MBTI?* The application forms ask for it. It carries 15%, against 65% for skills and goals together.
  - *What if OpenAI is down?* Rule-based scoring with the same weights, flagged "manual review".
  - *Why not auto-pair above a threshold?* Mentoring relationships are personal; the cost of a bad automatic pair is borne by a volunteer.

#### S3. Moving 1,549 people off Mailchimp without losing consent

- **Kind**: delivery
- **Situation**: The newsletter list and the record of who had agreed to it lived in Mailchimp. Its dashboard showed one "subscribed" number that hid how each person had got there.
- **What I did**: Before moving anyone, I traced every contact to the act that put them on the list and classified them into five tiers. I reported the unflattering result: 75.4% had arrived by an act that was not a subscription. I built double opt-in where confirming needs a button press, never a link visit, because corporate mail scanners follow every link. I put four sender streams behind a single call site for the email provider, kept the consent record in the charity's own Postgres, deleted the provider's own audience objects so the vendor would not become a second source of truth, and held 2,129 non-consenting contacts as one-way hashes so a later import cannot add them back. I moved the sending domain into an organisation-owned account, matching region and Return-Path so the DNS change came down to one record (29 before, 29 after, one value different).
- **Result**: The first send went out on 2026-08-31 in 16 idempotent batches with 0 failures and a 0.45% bounce rate. 179 past newsletters were recovered and are served from the charity's own site. The founder still approves every broadcast; the skill records the test send, the review round and her approval. The same rule, proven rather than inferred, went into a mailbox audit: I sent one real message to each of the 11 addresses printed on the site and read delivery back. 7 did not exist, including the headline contact address; all were fixed.
- **Engineer's angle**: Each batch carried its own idempotency key and strict validation, so a retry could not double-send and one bad address could not silently drop. The DKIM-only swap was safe because the Return-Path did not move and DMARC was at `p=none`; I wrote that caveat down rather than treat it as a general recipe. A CI gate fails the build if an email address or a ticketing access code reaches a committed file.
- **Plain version**: I moved the charity's mailing list into its own system and, on the way, found out honestly who had actually agreed to receive it.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *Why not just export the CSV and import it?* That carries the five tiers over as one "subscribed" flag, which is the problem.
  - *Is Mailchimp gone?* No. The newsletter left it; event campaigns are still written there, and closing the account is the founder's decision.
  - *Why does confirming need a button?* A GET that confirms will be confirmed by link scanners for people who never agreed.

#### S4. Incidents that taught me to break my own guards

- **Kind**: incident
- **Situation**: Three small failures in a row had the same shape. In March 2026, duplicated URL fallback logic put `localhost:3000` links into a batch of real mentor invitation emails. During the move from my personal Vercel account to the charity's, an environment variable copied with a trailing newline would have broken Stripe webhook verification in live mode; I caught it and wrote a rule. In June that rule itself turned out to write empty values with the newer CLI, caught in the same session by reading the values back. In September, a local test with a production key sent a few confirmation emails with localhost links, through the one send path the earlier guard did not cover.
- **What I did**: I fixed each one, recorded it with its date in the repository's runbooks, and changed how guards are written: a guard is not verified until you hand it the input it should refuse. I added a localhost link guard to the single send function and built its test from the real message, not a paraphrase. Writing that test caught a bug in the guard itself: its first pattern would have refused ordinary hosts such as `localhost.example`.
- **Result**: The site's gates carry self-tests, and the rules sit in the repository beside the incident that produced them. On 2026-08-30 the same method found two other checks that read as correct and gated nothing.
- **Engineer's angle**: Green is the state a broken check and a working check share. A check keyed on an annotation inherits the blind spot of the pass that wrote it. And a prevention rule needs the same verification as the fix: the 2026-06 failure was the 2026-03 rule.
- **Plain version**: I learned to test my safety checks by trying to get past them, because a check that never fails might not be checking anything.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *How did you find the September one?* A person opened their inbox; that is why the test is built from the real message.
  - *What changed in your process?* Every guard gets a refusal test, and every rule gets the dated incident that justifies it.

#### S5. Writing a charity's recurring work down as 11 agent skills

- **Kind**: implementation
- **Situation**: Publishing an event meant someone reading a Slack channel, downloading and renaming posters, headshots and bios, and editing the site by hand. Newsletters, posters, decks and video each lived in a different console or in one person's memory, so the work depended on whoever was free.
- **What I did**: I wrote each loop as an agent skill kept in the repository like code: instructions, scripts and reference rules, changed by pull request and type-checked in CI (which needed a second tsconfig, since the root one skips the skills folder). Skills are dry-run by default. The poster skill generates a textless image and sets every word in code, so a changed speaker title is a one-line fix. The video skill renders one composition into four aspect ratios. `run-event-playbook` builds nothing: it runs 10 checks on an event and names the skill that closes each gap. A Slack `/event` command turns a sentence into a schema-validated draft, shows a diff and opens a pull request on confirm. The agent's own rules are split across nine `CLAUDE.md` files by when a rule must load, not by topic.
- **Result**: 11 skills and a guide for teammates who do not code. Work that needed a vendor console now runs from a command and can be reviewed and re-run. I trained the volunteer team in six sessions, including a two-hour workshop in Auckland where I produced promo videos live. I am honest about adoption: the committee still makes most artwork the old way.
- **Engineer's angle**: An AI-native team is one whose work is written down precisely enough for an agent to execute and a person to audit. The structured output is validated before any git write, the default is dry-run, and a human approves. No timing study was run, so I claim no hours saved.
- **Plain version**: I wrote down how the charity's routine jobs are done, so that an AI assistant can do them and a volunteer can check the result.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *How do you stop the model writing nonsense to the site?* Schema validation, a draft branch, a preview, a human confirm and CI.
  - *Did people use it?* The newsletter and the event deck replaced the old way at least once; posters mostly did not. Shipping a capability and shipping its adoption are two projects.
  - *Why skills, not a SaaS tool?* A procedure in a repository can be reviewed, diffed and tested; one in a console cannot.

#### S6. Designing the handover so the answer is a file, not a person

- **Kind**: delivery
- **Situation**: I had built most of the system, so too much of it lived in my head and, at first, in my own accounts: the repository and deployment began under my personal accounts, and the database and an image store were later found to sit there too.
- **What I did**: In March 2026 I moved the repository, deployment and OAuth apps into the charity's accounts. Before leaving, I copied the production database into the charity's own database account, moved user uploads into a store the charity already pays for, and removed the last dependency on my credentials. In August 2026 I ran a refactoring pass aimed at the next maintainer: the schema split by domain behind one import, one auth wrapper for every protected route, zod validation on request bodies that had none, and large media moved out of the repository (with an offline mirror kept before its history was purged). A snapshot of the repository from April 2026 shows the distance: one agent guidance file, no test files, a deploy workflow but no pull-request gate, no agent skills, and most API routes without request validation. By September there were nine guidance files, 33 test files, five CI jobs on every pull request and 11 skills. I wrote the documentation as the work went: 35,062 lines of Markdown across 105 files, a maintainer handover whose first question is "what stops working, silently, when the person who built this stops answering?", two internal playbooks served as live pages and hash-checked in CI against their source, and 52 recorded decisions, including the ones marked won't-do. I named the decisions that only the founder could take and left them with her.
- **Result**: A volunteer I had mentored made their first independent page update in late August 2026. Two maintainers were named in September 2026 with organisation owner rights, each recurring obligation has one name against it, and the remaining team kept shipping changes after my access was removed. The platform and the agent skills are still in use.
- **Engineer's angle**: Access was shared and obligations were not: every recurring job got exactly one owner, because "the maintainers" owns nothing. The handover writes every count with the command that produced it and the date, because a hand-typed number in prose is a claim nobody re-checks.
- **Plain version**: I made sure the charity could keep running everything after I left, without needing to ask me.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *What did you leave unfinished?* A safeguarding reporting route was proposed and not built; I named it as mine.
  - *Why so much documentation?* The Markdown is the interface. It is what turns a one-person system into one an organisation owns.

#### S7. Launching against the founder's bar, not mine

- **Kind**: requirements
- **Situation**: By March 2026 the platform worked on desktop and real mentors already had accounts on it. The founder tested it on her phone and did not want to launch: the mobile layout broke, fonts and colours did not follow the brand kit, nobody but me had tested it, and I was the only person who could change it. The site was also still running on my personal hosting account, which was not a safe home for an organisation's live service.
- **What I did**: I treated her objections as the launch criteria instead of arguing for the platform. I agreed the mobile fixes with Lesley Gao, who led the front end, and moved the repository, hosting and sign-in apps into the charity's own accounts (2026-03-24). A volunteer tester worked through the site, including the event pages from 2014 to 2022, with the results tracked in a shared results sheet, and I fixed what the pass found. On 2026-06-18, with the old site's renewal due and registrations open for that weekend, the founder asked for the cutover within a day and for mentorship, membership and sign-in to be closed. I moved the domain and closed the application forms, but pushed back on closing sign-in: existing mentors and mentees would have been locked out, and new sign-ups already need an invitation code.
- **Result**: The domain moved to the new platform on 2026-06-19 with existing accounts still working. The application forms were paused by redirect, not deleted, with a written runbook for reopening them.
- **Engineer's angle**: Read the request against its purpose. "Close sign-in" meant "stop strangers joining", which the invitation-code gate already did; closing it would have broken the people already using the platform. A reversible pause (a redirect plus hidden buttons, code intact) is cheaper than a removal and a rebuild.
- **Plain version**: The founder's standard for "ready" included her phone and her brand, so I made those the checklist and launched when they were met.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *Why wasn't it ready in March?* Desktop was. Mobile and brand polish were not, and no one outside the build had tested it. I should have asked for a non-developer's test pass much earlier.
  - *Did you ever disagree with the founder?* Yes, on closing sign-in, and I explained who it would lock out. She agreed and the cutover went ahead.

#### S8. Five builds around the platform

- **Kind**: delivery
- **Situation**: The charity's programmes kept needing small, fast tools that did not belong inside the main platform.
- **What I did**: I built each alone. **Her Waka**: a Mintlify teaching site for a Ministry of Social Development-funded employment programme for women at academyEX Auckland (March to June 2026), with the four workshops I authored and 12 self-paced tutorials. **Aotearoa AI Hackathon event assistant**: in 2025, a chat assistant with a 3D mascot and a community FAQ, later generalised into an open-source template; for 2026, rebuilt as a voice-first agent over the OpenAI Realtime API, where the server mints a short-lived secret so the real key never reaches the browser. Minting is guarded by per-visitor limits over three windows, a much larger per-network ceiling so one address cannot farm tokens by forging visitor ids, and per-visitor and event-wide daily budgets; the agent's instructions load from the database in parallel with those checks. **The hackathon's event deck**: 91 slides rendered in the browser from the event's own data, with timers, team slides and the winners reveal, that ran two days at AUT City Campus. **Makey Makey workshop**: a 20-minute slideshow for 12 to 18 year olds, resting on the fact that the board emulates a keyboard: students vibe-code a banana piano, a Simon Says and a catch-and-dodge game in claude.ai in the browser (nothing to install on locked-down school laptops), then play them with fruit. A bonus Super Mario level, every sprite and sound drawn in code on a canvas, showed what the paid tools can do. **The Monthly She#**: the newsletter rebuilt on the charity's own infrastructure (S3).
- **Result**: Her Waka launched in March 2026 on the site I built. I was named Outstanding Mentor at the hackathon festival in both 2025 and 2026.
- **Engineer's angle**: Each picks the smallest stack that fits: docs-as-site for a teaching hub, a zero-build static deck for a classroom, data-driven slides so a changed time is one edit. The voice agent keeps credentials server-side and rate-limits token minting. On the deck I also replaced a sign-up QR code: it pointed at a form with a file-upload field, which forces a Google sign-in, so people scanning it in a hall got stuck. It now opens a public page on the site, and the feedback form became a native form that writes to the database and posts to a Slack channel.
- **Plain version**: Alongside the main website I built the teaching site, the hackathon assistant and slides, and a kids' workshop the charity's programmes needed.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *What happened to the 2025 assistant?* I generalised it into an open-source template other events can configure, and built the 2026 voice agent from scratch.
  - *How does the deck stay correct?* It reads the same event entry as the web page, and CI checks every registered deck.

#### In hindsight

- **I scheduled the capability and not its adoption.** I shipped skills, announced them and expected use to follow. The better move was to sit with the person who owns each loop for its first real use: one accompanied run is worth more than a guide.
- **A non-developer's acceptance test earlier.** The founder's first phone test found what my desktop testing had not. A volunteer test pass in January would have moved the launch forward.
- **A second maintainer earlier.** For most of the build one person held most of the knowledge. The documentation was written as the work went, but naming a co-maintainer months before I left would have tested it sooner.
- **Accounts from day one.** Starting the repository and deployment under my own accounts made the first months quick and cost a migration later, plus two stores I only found during the handover.
- **The safeguarding route.** A reporting form that writes into the platform's own database was proposed and not built. Every part it needs exists; the work was mine and I did not do it.

### Tam-AI-Ti — story

Role: Sole developer (full-stack, AI, deployment and maintenance) · Period: 2025-10 – 2026-03

#### In one breath

Tam-AI-Ti is a financial-wellbeing coach for Māori adults, in te reo Māori and English, built on the Māori health model Te Whare Tapa Whā so that money is talked about alongside family, spirit, body and mind. Riria (Missy) Te Kanawa commissioned it, and I built the whole thing alone: the app, the AI coach that users can talk to by voice, the database and the hosting. A research cohort of 19 people used it for four months and wrote 181 journal entries in both languages.

#### The problem

Mainstream money apps treat money as numbers: budgets, balances, projections. For many Māori users that framing does not fit, because money is tied to whānau, to spiritual purpose and to health. A generic budgeting tool with Māori words painted on top would test nothing. The commission asked a sharper question: will Māori users engage with an AI coach whose cultural framework is part of how the product works, not decoration on it?

That made three things hard at once. The cultural model had to shape the data, not only the labels. The AI had to be useful without being everywhere, and had to sound like a respectful guide rather than a chatbot. And the person directing the product is an executive, not an engineer, so every decision had to be shown, not explained in jargon.

#### What I built

A Next.js app on Vercel over one Neon Postgres database that also holds the vectors. Users take a 26-question assessment across nine psychological factors, set goals through seven action plans (A to G), check in daily on wellbeing measures grouped by the walls of Te Whare Tapa Whā, write morning and evening journals, and talk to a voice coach. Whānau can be invited to support them, seeing only what the user allows.

- **Culture in the schema.** 48 tables. Each daily check-in measure is a typed column named for its wall (wairua, tinana, hinengaro, whānau) on a bounded scale; each action plan has its own tracking fields; 74 whakataukī across 37+ categories are a searchable library; the maramataka (Māori lunar calendar) has its own tables.
- **Three AI paths, one model each.** CopilotKit tool calls on gpt-4o-mini at temperature 0.3; journal enhancement, translation and insight extraction on gpt-4o; a voice coach on OpenAI's Realtime API.
- **Memory.** Journal entries, goal progress notes, goals and coach messages are embedded (1536 dimensions) when saved, so the coach can find what the user wrote before.
- **Te reo Māori first.** The interface opens in te reo Māori, with an English toggle on every page.
- **Hosting handed over.** Production moved in March 2026 from my accounts to the client's, with no downtime and no one signed out.

#### S1. The culture went into the column names

- **Kind**: decision
- **Situation**: The brief was a tool built on Te Whare Tapa Whā. The easy version keeps a culturally neutral schema (minutes of exercise, minutes of calm) and puts Māori labels on the screen. Then the model is only a skin: the data cannot be analysed by wall, and the AI never sees the framework.
- **What I did**: I made each check-in measure a column that belongs to one wall: sleep, water, food and exercise under tinana; time in karakia or ceremony, connection with people and connection with the environment under wairua; mauri tau (calm, mindfulness) and ako (learning) under hinengaro; check-ins and quality time under whānau. When the first version mixed free numbers and minutes, I restructured it in a migration to consistent integer scales, with the meaning of each step written beside the column. I gave the seven action plans their own typed tracking fields instead of a generic JSON note, and later added period tracking so Budget Review (F) and Accountability Partner (G) recur instead of ending once. I also made te reo Māori the default language of the interface.
- **Result**: 48 tables, 494 columns, 22 schema migrations shipped alongside the feature work. The cohort logged 74 daily check-ins, each one readable wall by wall straight from its columns.
- **Engineer's angle**: The trade-off is schema churn. Bounded integer scales instead of raw minutes lose precision but make the answers comparable across people and quick to give on a phone; the history page needed a scale-to-range mapping so charts still read in real units.
- **Plain version**: I built the Māori health model into how the data is stored, so it is part of the product and not just its look.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *Why not a JSON column for flexibility?* Seven plans with different tracking (a debt payment is not a savings rate) needed validation and queries per type; typed fields gave both.
  - *How did you check the cultural content?* The commissioner directed the framework and its content; I implemented it, kept the terms exact (macrons included) and revised the te reo Māori wording of all 26 assessment questions as the content was refined.
  - *What would you change?* Settle the scales before the first users, not after; one restructure meant migrating live rows.

#### S2. I took the AI off five of the eight pages

- **Kind**: decision
- **Situation**: The assistant first ran on eight routes, with dozens of CopilotKit actions, including the goal wizard and goal detail pages. On the dashboard, replies began to time out: the conversation grew, and every request carried the whole page state and long instructions.
- **What I did**: I made the assistant opt-in per route, with "off" as the default for any route not listed. I kept it where it helps: the dashboard (update today's wellbeing by typing), the journal (fill an entry from what the user says) and journal history (search and analyse). I removed it from goals, the maramataka, resources, sign-in, onboarding, whānau invitations and the manual journal: for focus on goal-setting, speed on the cultural pages, and because sign-in and invitations should not have an agent on them. On the pages that kept it, I shrank what the model receives: one small summary instead of the full dashboard, short tool results, one-line instructions, and no automatic suggestion calls.
- **Result**: CopilotKit went from eight routes to three, and the dashboard's requests became small enough to stop the timeouts.
- **Engineer's angle**: Context is a budget. The failure looked like a network error (aborted streams), but the cause was input size growing with each turn. Removing tool surface also lowers the chance the model picks the wrong tool.
- **Plain version**: I made the AI helper smaller and put it only where it actually helps, and it became faster and more reliable.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *Was removing features hard to justify?* The core goal features stayed; only the AI layer on top went. Goal-setting is a guided form, and a chat beside it competed with it.
  - *How did you find the cause?* By watching the message count and request size climb before each abort, then cutting the readable context first and the instructions second.
  - *Would you do it differently?* Start from one page with the agent and add pages on evidence, instead of starting broad.

#### S3. Retrieval that finds the journal, not the echo

- **Kind**: difficulty
- **Situation**: The first coach answered from fixed content and remembered nothing a user had written. After the proof of concept, in October 2025, the commissioner asked for coaching that learns from each person's reflections and progress, because the research depends on it. I added retrieval over embeddings in Postgres. In testing it often found nothing, or found the wrong thing.
- **What I did**: I traced three causes. A question about the journal as a whole ("show me my recent entries") is about the container, not the content, so it scores low against any entry; I detect those questions and relax the match for them, while specific questions ("times I felt stressed") keep a stricter one. My first threshold was too strict for short entries, so I lowered it. And the user's own earlier question to the coach ("did I mention …?") matched more closely than the journal entry it was about, so I changed the default to search journals and goal notes and to include past conversations only when asked. Words like "today" and "this week" become a date filter. Embeddings are written when an entry is saved; if that call fails the entry still saves and a backfill script fills the vector later.
- **Result**: Four tables carry 1536-dimension embeddings with cosine indexes, and the coach answers "what did I write about …" from the user's own entries.
- **Engineer's angle**: A memory store that contains the conversation about the memory will retrieve itself. Separating source records from chat history, and choosing the threshold by query type, mattered more than the embedding model.
- **Plain version**: I taught the coach to look in the user's diary first and not get distracted by its own earlier chat.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *Why pgvector and not a vector database?* The data was already in Postgres, scoped per user, and small; one database meant one backup and joins with the rows themselves.
  - *How did you tune it?* With test queries in more than one language and the similarity score of each candidate printed, then fixing the patterns that failed.
  - *What is missing?* An automated set of test queries with expected results, so a change to thresholds is measured rather than eyeballed.

#### S4. A voice coach without the server touching audio

- **Kind**: implementation
- **Situation**: The commissioner had asked for a financial coach; voice was not in the brief. In November 2025, reading the cohort's feedback, I saw testers asking to speak rather than type, so I proposed a coach they could talk to and built it. Voice means low latency, and audio is personal; relaying it through the server adds delay and puts the API key at risk if done in the browser.
- **What I did**: The server mints a short-lived key from OpenAI for each session; the browser connects to the Realtime API over WebRTC with that key, so the long-lived key never leaves the server and audio never passes through it. I set server-side voice activity detection with 500 ms of silence to end a turn, so users can interrupt. The coach's instructions carry the cultural framing and its limits: education, not investment, tax or legal advice, and humility about cultural authority. Each session is a database row created by an authenticated server action; transcripts arrive in pieces, so each message is saved once, keyed on its position, role and text, and audio is never stored.
- **Result**: 35 voice coaching sessions in the cohort, with text transcripts kept and no audio stored.
- **Engineer's angle**: Ephemeral keys plus WebRTC is the pattern that keeps latency low and secrets server-side. The hard part was the transcript stream: history updates repeat and grow, so saving naively writes duplicates.
- **Plain version**: People can talk to the coach out loud, and only the words are kept, never the recording.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *Whose idea was voice?* Mine. The brief was a financial coach; the testers' feedback asked for speech input, and I proposed and built it.
  - *Why not store audio?* Text is searchable and far smaller; a voice recording of someone's money worries is more sensitive than it is useful.
  - *How do you stop it giving financial advice?* The instructions forbid specific investment, tax and legal advice and tell it to point to professionals; it is positioned as education.
  - *Why the Agents SDK in the browser?* Its realtime session handles WebRTC, turn detection and history events, which left me only the persistence and the UI.

#### S5. Handing production to the client without signing anyone out

- **Kind**: delivery
- **Situation**: The app ran on my personal Vercel account. The maintenance period in our agreement ended in February 2026, and I asked the commissioner to choose between closing the app down and keeping it running. She chose to keep it. In March 2026 it needed to belong to the client: the repository in their GitHub organisation, hosting on their team, their domain, their email sender, with registered users still signing in.
- **What I did**: I chose a manual move over Vercel's project transfer, because storage, its credentials, the domain, OAuth and email all have to be redone either way. The database stayed where it was and was re-pointed. I kept the session secret identical, so existing sign-ins stayed valid. I recreated blob storage and Redis, copied the avatars with a script that can be re-run safely, added the new callback URLs to Google sign-in, moved the domain (first the apex, then the subdomain the commissioner chose), re-verified the email sender, emailed every registered user the new address, and kept the old address running for a week after the cutover.
- **Result**: A zero-downtime cutover, written up as a 12-step playbook I can reuse for the next client handover.
- **Engineer's angle**: The one variable that decides whether users notice is the session secret; the one step that destroys data is deleting the old project before the blob copy. The playbook orders steps around both.
- **Plain version**: I moved the live app into the client's own accounts without anyone being logged out or losing their photos.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *What went wrong?* No downtime. The avatar copy needed to be made re-runnable during the move, which is why the script overwrites safely.
  - *Why not the platform's transfer feature?* It moves the project but not its storage or their credentials; the hard steps remain.
  - *Who owns it now?* The client: the repository, the hosting and the domain. The handover is complete; since June 2026 I no longer deploy it.

#### S6. In-app browsers broke sign-in and the AI

- **Kind**: incident
- **Situation**: People open links from messaging apps, which load pages in an embedded browser. There, Google refuses sign-in, and the CopilotKit bundle crashed the page because the embedded browser did not support a modern regular-expression feature.
- **What I did**: I added detection for embedded browsers (Messenger, Instagram, WeChat and others). On sign-in, registration and whānau invitation pages the Google button is disabled there and a bilingual message explains how to open the page in the real browser, with a copy-link button. The AI provider checks for embedded browsers and for the regex feature, and does not mount the assistant where it would crash; the error boundary recognises that failure if it slips through.
- **Result**: The rest of the app works inside embedded browsers, and users are told in te reo Māori or English how to continue.
- **Engineer's angle**: Feature-detect, not only user-agent sniff: the regex check catches browsers no list knows about. Disabling one feature is better than a white screen.
- **Plain version**: When people opened the app from a chat link it broke, so I made it explain what to do and keep working.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *How did you find it?* The errors were Google's "disallowed user agent" and an "invalid regular expression" crash, both only in embedded browsers.
  - *Why not polyfill?* The syntax error happens when the bundle is parsed, before any polyfill can run; the fix has to be not loading it.

#### S7. Building for a client who directs the product, not the code

- **Kind**: collaboration
- **Situation**: Riria (Missy) Te Kanawa directed the product: the framework, the features ("include the maramataka", "add a financial coach"), the surveys. She is an executive, not an engineer. Dr Mahsa McCauley, founder of She Sharp, had referred me.
- **What I did**: Before quoting, I turned our first meeting into a requirements checklist of open questions, then a development plan with acceptance criteria for each feature. I sent a feature demo video at every milestone, so she could review progress without a technical background. When the proof of concept was ready at the end of September 2025, she had 13 people test it; I worked through every row of her testing summary and feedback deck, marking each change or the reason it waited, before the cohort started in November. I ran the data analysis on the cohort's use. After launch I made teaching videos and ran a live walk-through of the database so she could use Cursor to read it and do basic analysis herself.
- **Result**: The product was built, deployed and used by a 19-person cohort for four months. After that I handed it over in full, and the client runs it herself.
- **Engineer's angle**: Demo video as the review format: it is asynchronous, shows the real product, and leaves a record of what was agreed.
- **Plain version**: I showed my client each step on video, and later taught her to look at her own data.
- **Follow-ups**:
  - *How did you handle changing requirements?* In migrations: the schema changed with each request and was never rolled back.
  - *What did the client get beyond the app?* A way to read her own data and a written handover playbook.

#### In hindsight

- I would write automated tests from the start. The repository has written testing guides but no test suite; retrieval thresholds and the goal calculations were checked by hand, and several fixes (progress counts, income and debt calculations, time-zone day boundaries) are the kind a test would have caught.
- I would start the AI narrow and grow it on evidence, rather than putting it on eight pages and cutting back to three.
- I would fix the wellbeing scales with the commissioner before the first user, so no live data had to be reshaped.
- I would keep the documentation's figures generated from the code. Some counts in the docs drifted from the tree after the AI cut-back.
